p. 63, n. 6 Ezekiel xviii. 27. A certain old man was asked by a toiler in the ascetic life, Doth God accept the repentance of the sinner? After the old man had taught him by many things he said to him, Tell me, my beloved, wouldst thou cast away thy garment because it was torn? The toiler replied, No, I would sew it up and use it again. The old man said, If thou hast pity upon thy garment which is without feeling, shall not God have compassion upon the work which He hath fashioned? A certain brother asked Father Sisoes, saying, What shall I do, father, for I have fallen? The old man said to him, Rise up again. The brother saith, I did rise up, and again I fell. The old man said to him, Rise up again. The brother said to him, I did rise up again many times, and I fell. The old man said to him, Rise up again. The brother said to him, Until when? The old man said to him, Until thou advancest either to good deeds or to ruin, for in that thing in which a man advanceth he will go on, whether it be to death, or whether it be to life. Abba Poemen said, I prefer the man who hath sinned and done wickedly and become good again to the man who hath never sinned and hath never shown repentance; for the former hath a humble opinion [of himself], but the latter considereth himself to be a righteous man. ܐܫܬܐܠ ܣܒܐ ܡܢ ܦܠܚܐ ܚܕ. ܕܐܢ ܗܘ ܕܡܩܲܒܠ ܐܠܗܐ ܬܝܒܘܬܐ ܕܚܛܝ̈ܐ. ܘܗܘ ܣܒܐ ܡܢ ܒܬܪ ܕܬܠܡܕܗ ܒܡ̈ܠܐ ܣܓܝܐܝܬ ܐܡܪ ܠܘܬܗ. ܐܡܪ ܠܝ ܚܒܝܒܢ. ܐܝܗܘ ܕܬܬܲܠܲܚ ܟܠܕܝܢ ܕܝܠܟ. ܫܕܐ ܐܢܬ ܠܗ ܠܒܪ. ܘܐܡܪ ܠܗ ܠܐ. ܐܠܐ ܚܐܛ ܐܢܐ ܠܗ̇ ܘܗܵܘܝܐ ܠܝ ܠܚܫܚܬܝ. ܘܐܡܪ ܠܗ ܣܒܐ. ܐܢܗܘ ܕܐܢܬ ܥܠ ܡܐܢܐ ܕܝܠܟ ܗ̇ܘ ܕܐܝܬܘܗܝ ܕܠܐ ܪܓܫܬܐ ܚܵܐܣ ܐܢܬ. ܐܠܗܐ ܥܠ ܓܒܝܠܬܗ ܠܐ ܚܵܐܣ ܕܐܝܬܝܗ̇ ܥܒܕܗ܀ ܐܚܐ ܫܐܠ ܠܐܒܐ ܣܘܿܣܐܝܣ ܘܐܡܪ ܠܗ. ܡܢܐ ܐܥܒܕ ܐܒܐ ܕܢܦܠܬ. ܐܡܪ ܠܗ ܣܒܐ. ܩܘܡ. ܐܡܪ ܠܗ ܐܚܐ ܗ̇ܘ. ܩܡܬ ܘܬܘܒ ܢܦܠܹܬ. ܐܡ̇ܪ ܠܗ ܣܒܐ. ܘܬܘܒ ܩܘܡ. ܐܡܪ ܠܗ ܐܚܐ ܗ̇ܘ. ܘܬܘܒ ܩܡ̇ܬ ܙܒܢ̈ܬܐ ܣܓ̈ܝܐܬܐ ܘܢܦܠܹܬ. ܐܡ̇ܪ ܠܗ ܣܒܐ. ܬܘܒ ܩܘܡ. ܐܡ̇ܪ ܠܗ ܐܚܐ ܗ̇ܘ. ܥܕܡܐ ܠܐܡܬܝ. ܐܡ̇ܪ ܠܗ ܣܒܐ. ܥܕܡܐ ܕܬܬܩܕܡ ܐܘ ܒܣܘܥܪ̈ܢܐ ܫܦܝܪ̈ܐ. ܐܘ ܒܡܦܘܠܬܐ. ܒܐܝܕܐ ܓܝܪ ܕܡܬܩܲܕܡ ܒܪܢܫܐ ܒܗ ܐܙܠ. ܐܢ ܠܡܘܬܐ. ܘܐܢ ܠܚܲܝܸ̈ܐ܀ ܐܒܐ ܦܘܡܢ ܐܡ̣ܪ. ܕܨܒܐ ܐܢܐ ܒܓܒܪܐ ܕܚܛܐ ܘܐܪܫܥ ܘܛܒ. ܡܢ ܕܒܓܒܪܐ ܕܠܐ ܚܛܐ ܘܠܐ ܚܘܝ ܬܝܒܘܬܐ. ܗ̇ܘ ܓܝܪ ܐܝܬ ܠܗ ܚܘܫܒܐ ܡܡܲܟܟܐ. ܘܠܗܢܐ ܚܫܝܒܐ ܠܗ ܢܦܫܗ ܒܚܘܫܒ̈ܘܗܝ ܙܕܝܩܐ܀ On the acceptance of Repentance from the Questions in the Paradise of Palladius, Nos. ܬܩܨܒ، ܬܩܦܚ، ܬܩܨܘ.
p. 65, n. 1 ܡܲܓܢܹܛܝܼܣ, i.e. λίθος Μαγνῆτις, ܟܐܦܐ ܕܢܬܦ ܠܦܪܙܠܐ ܠܘܬܗ.
p. 65, n. 2 ܓܢܘܿܣܛܝܼܩܘܿܣ, i.e. γνωστικός.
p. 65, n. 3 ܒܒܘܼܚܪܵܢܗܘܿܢ This word is probably corrupt. Hoffmann suggests ܒܚܘܪܗܘܢ or ܒܚܙܘܢܗܘܢ as the correct reading.
p. 66, n. 1 Read ܡܪܢ.
p. 66, n. 2 Genesis xxvii, xxviii.
p. 66, n. 3 ܡܸܙܕܲܒܢܵܢܘܼܬܵܐ, a rare word of which one example only is given by Payne Smith.
p. 66, n. 4 Genesis xxxvii. 28.
p. 66, n. 5 Exodus ii. 12.
p. 66, n. 6 1 Samuel xix.
p. 66, n. 7 For quotations from this chapter see B.O., iii. i, pp. 255, col. 1, and p. 469, col. 2.
p. 67, n. 1 Read ܘܣܲܒܘܿܟܬ, i.e., سيبخت. The name Se-bôcht means three have saved. See Nöldeke, Geschichte der Perser, p. 396, note 1.
p. 67, n. 2 A district on the western or right bank of the Tigris, adjacent to Gezîret ibn ʿOmar. It is the Bezabde of Ammianus (lib. xx. 7).

p. 67, n. 3 I.e., Ἀραζιανηνή, a town and province of Armenia on the borders of Mesopotamia, north of Ḥiṣn Kêfâ. See Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 174, note 1359. The province extended from Gezîret ibn ʿOmar on the east to Diarbekir on the west. The town is represented by the modern أَرْزَن or Erzerûm.
p. 67, n. 5 ܐܲܕܪܡܲܗ = آذَرْماءْ. The name of a bishopric and a place situated between Nisibis and Môṣul. See Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 203; and Yâḳût, 1. p. 177.

p. 67, n. 6 Dâsen was the mountainous tract of country called by the Arabs Gebel Dâsin, (identified with the Gâra mountains), which rising near Dâʾûdîya in the west extends along to the Upper Zâb and away to the east into Gebel Pîr Ḥasan Beg. Dâsen must have been bounded on the north by ʿAmêdîya and the valley of the Ṣapna, and its most southern district was Batnura, or Bê-tannûrê, which lay along the Bedu rivulet, (a small tributary which flows into the Upper Zâb), about six or seven hours from ʿAmêdîya. See Hoffmann, Auszüge, pp. 202–207, and the authorities quoted by him. For Bê-tannûrê and the Bedu rivulet see Badger, The Nestorians, vol. 1, pp. 210 and 380. For Δασεν of the LXX see Lagarde, Materialien, 1867, ii. 90. The modern diocese of Mâr Aurâham of Gunduk which comprises a number of villages south of the Gâra mountains and those round about Aḳra, represents the diocese of Dâsen and a part of the diocese of Margâ.
p. 67, n. 7 Or ܝܼܫܘܿܥ ܙܟܵܐ.
p. 68, n. 1 Reading, with Hoffmann, ܫܘܢܵܝܵܐ ܘܒܘܼܕܵܪܵܐ.
p. 68, n. 2 Read ܗܘ̤ܵܐ.
p. 68, n. 3 ܣܵܒܵܐ, a title of honour.
p. 68, n. 4 ܚܕܘܿܕ or ܚܲܕܘܿܕ, see text p. 214. 6; 238. 11.
p. 69, n. 1 Read ܘܩܵܘܝܼ.
p. 69, n. 2 I.e., in Bêth ʿÂbhê.
p. 69, n. 3 St. Luke xv. 20.
p. 69, n. 4 St. Luke vii. 48.
p. 69, n. 5 St. Luke xxiii. 42.
p. 69, n. 6 ܘܠܡܲܟܣܐ for ܘܠܡܵܟܣܐ.
p. 70, n. 1 St. Luke xviii. 14.
p. 70, n. 2 Jonah iii. 5–10.
p. 70, n. 3 ܚܵܢܲܬ݀ for ܚܸܢܲܬ.
p. 70, n. 4 The MSS. have ܠܦܘܼܓܢܬܵܗ̇, but Assemânî has (B.O., iii. 1, pp. 90, 470) ܦܽܘܓܺܝܬܴܐ Phugitha, and says that it is locus apud Izlense coenobium.
p. 70, n. 5 ܬܹܐܘܿܪܝܼܵܐ ܗ̄. ܗܲܘܢܢܝܬܐ ܘܪܥܝܢܐ ܝܕܥܬܐ ܕܟܝܢܐ ܘܕܠܐ ܒܟܝܢܐ Orient. 2441, fol. 384, col. 2.
p. 71, n. 1 2 Samuel xii.
p. 71, n. 2 Jonah i. 2.
p. 71, n. 3 Read ܕܒܲܒܢܲܝ̈.
p. 71, n. 4 Judges xxi. 13.
p. 72, n. 1 This chapter is quoted in B.O., iii. i, p. 459, col. 1 f.
p. 72, n. 2 See B.O., iii. i, p. 186. His history of Jacob of Bêth ʿÂbhê is praised by Thomas of Margâ. See chap. 24.

p. 72, n. 3 The Monastery of Bar Ṭûrâ must have been near Bêth ʿÂbhê. Both these monasteries were freed from the jurisdiction of the bishop by Îshôʿ-yahbh of Gĕdhâlâ. See Mai, Script. Vet. Nova Coll., t. x, p. 296.

p. 72, n. 4 Ḥĕnân-Îshôʿ I., called the Elder or the Lame, was appointed Catholicus A.D. 686, and practically ruled the Nestorian Church until 701; he was buried in the convent of Jonah near Môṣul See B.O., ii, p. 42; Bar-Hebraeus, Chron. Eccles., ii, col. 135; Baethgen, Fragmente, pp. 32, 117; and Wright, Syr. Lit., p. 843.
p. 73, n. 1 Read ܝܘܼܒܵܠܵܐ.
p. 73, n. 2 ܬܲܫ̈ܥܝܵܬܵܐ ܪܗܸܛܪ̈ܝܵܬܵܐ.
p. 73, n. 3 Read ܒܲܣܩܝܼܠܘܼܬ.
p. 73, n. 4 The greater part of this chapter is quoted in B.O., iii. i, p. 106, col. 1 f.
p. 73, n. 5 Mâr-yahbh was a contemporary of Jacob of Bêth ʿÂbhê, and besides the history of Jacob, to which Thomas refers in this chapter, wrote an Epistle. See B.O., iii. i, pp. 186, 187.

p. 74, n. 1 Aphnî-Mârân, افنيماران the monk, was a disciple of Kâm-Îshôʿ, the fourth Abbot of Bêth ʿÂbhê. He flourished about A.D. 630 while Îshôʿ-yahbh of Gĕdhâlâ was Patriarch. According to ʿAbhd-Îshôʿ he wrote a commentary on the Epistle which Mâr-yahbh composed ܡܪܝܗܒ ܐܝܬ ܠܗ ܐܓܪܬܐ ܘܠܐܦܢܝܡܪܢ ܦܘܫܩܗ̇. See B.O., ii, p. 422, col.; iii. i, p. 187.
p. 76, n. 1 Read ܚܵܐܲܪ.
p. 76, n. 2 I.e., the woman and her daughter referred to in the preceding chapter.
p. 76, n. 3 Here the text is probably corrupt. Hoffmann suggests that we should read ܒܩܲܬܪܵܐ on a rock.
p. 76, n. 4 Compare Guidi, Un nuovo testo Siriaco, p. 17, at the foot.
p. 76, n. 5 Read ܒܟܠܹܗ.
p. 77, n. 1 Lit. Of his coming.
p. 77, n. 2 Read ܕܡܕܲܒܲܪ.
p. 77, n. 3 Read ܘܐܸܬܦܪܸܫ ܕܕܠܐ.
p. 77, n. 4 Literally But how, we give to silence.
p. 77, n. 5 After ܕܐܝܟܢ ܕܝܢ Hoffmann would add two points:
p. 78, n. 1 I.e., Bar-Ḥadh-bhĕ-shabbâ who lived in Mount Shaʿrân جبل شعران, and whom Sabhr-Îshôʿ nominated as his successor. See B.O., iii. i, p. 450, col. 2, at the foot, and p. 470, col. 1.
p. 79, n. 1 Genesis xlvi. 29.
p. 79, n. 2 St. Matthew xi. 29.
p. 79, n. 3 This chapter is quoted by Assemânî, B.O., iii. i, pp. 458, 471.
p. 79, n. 4 I.e., to Margâ.
p. 79, n. 5 ܟܸܣܪܘܼ or ܟܘܼܣܪܘܿ, Pers. خُسْرَوْ, Arab. كِسْرَي Χοσρόης.
p. 79, n. 6 Khusrau II. Parwêz reigned from the summer of A.D. 590 to February 25, (29) 628. See Nöldeke, Geschichte der Perser, table facing p. 434; Guidi, Un nuovo testo Siriaco, p. 24, l. 10.
p. 79, n. 7 Pers. هورمزد, Chald. הורמיז. Hôrmîzd IV reigned from February 579–590. See Nöldeke, op. cit., p. 434; Guidi, Un nuovo testo Siriaco, p. 7, l. 5.
p. 79, n. 8 I.e., about A.D. 595.

p. 79, n. 9 I.e., Îshôʿ-yahbh, the son of Basṭôhmagh, of Kuphlânâ in Adiabene. He was one of those who accompanied Îshôʿ-yahbh of Gedhâlâ on his embassy to Heraclius. On the death of Mâr-emmêh 644–647, he was elected Catholicus, and sat until 657–658. See B.O., iii. i, pp. 114, 115, 472; Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 226; Wright, Syr. Lit., p. 842.

p. 80, n. 1 Though famous among the Nestorians for having built a magnificent temple at Bêth ʿÂbhê, he is equally famous among the Jacobites for having by bribery and other means prevented their building a church at Môṣul. ܗܢܐ ܕܠܩܒ ܠܐܘܪ̈ܬܕܟܣܘ. ܕܨܒܝܢ ܗܘܘ ܠܡܒܢܐ ܥܕܬܐ ܒܡܘܨܠ. ܘܚܣܪ ܡܠܘܐܐ ܣܓܝܐܐ ܒܫ̈ܘܚܕܐ ܕܩܪܒ ܠܕܝܢ̈ܐ ܘܒܛܠܗ ܠܒܢܝܢܐ. See Bar-Hebraeus, Chron. Eccles., ii, col. 127, and B.O., iii. i, p. 144 ff.
p. 80, n. 2 See p. 38, and Thomas of Margâ, Bk. 1, chap. 28, Bk 2, chap. 6.
p. 80, n. 3 A monk of Mount Îzlâ, and the founder of Bêth Rabban. See B.O., iii. i, pp. 255, 471, 472.
p. 80, n. 4 Bar-ʿIdtâ probably refers to the Church of Mâr Sergius. The ܕܝܪܐ ܕܫܝܪܝܢ is mentioned in Guidi, Nuovo testo, p. 16, l. 2.

p. 80, n. 5 Shîrîn, a native of Ḥûzistân, was of Greek parentage and was a Christian. See B.O., iii. i, p. 109, but especially Nöldeke, Geschichte der Perser, p. 283, note 2; p. 287, note 2; and p. 357, note 4. In Guidi, Un nuovo testo Siriaco, p. 10, Khusrau's two Christian wives ܬܪ̈ܬܝܢ ܢܫܘ̈ܗܝ ܟܪܣܛܝ̈ܢܝܬܐ are distinctly mentioned; the one ܫܝܪܝܢ is called ܐܪܡܝܬܐ, and ܡܪܝܡ the other ܪܗܘܡܝܬܐ. Her favourite physician was Gabriel of Sinjâr who let blood from her arm, and who became as a son to her (Guidi, op. cit., p. 14). Bar-Hebraeus states in his Chronicle of Dynasties (Bruns ed. p. 97, ll. 10, 11; Bedjan ed. p. 92, ll. 23, 24) that Khusrau built three great temples to the Mother of God, the Apostles, and Mâr Sergius the Martyr, and that the Patriarch of Antioch consecrated them, ܘܒܢܐ ܟܣܪܘ ܬܠܬܐ ܗܝ̈ܟܠܐ ܪ̈ܘܪܒܐ ܠܝܠܕܬ ܐܠܗܐ ܘܠܫܠܝܚ̈ܐ ܘܠܡܪܝ ܣܪܓܝܣ ܣܗܕܐ܆ ܘܩܕܫ ܐܢܘܢ ܦܛܪܝܪܟܐ ܕܐܢܛܝܟ., and he adds that Christianity was spread abroad in all Persia ܘܐܬܦܬܝܬ ܟܪܣܛܝܢܘܬܐ ܒܟܠܗ̇ ܦܪܣ; but that he was a heathen at heart is evident from his unseemly conduct in the Church at Dârâ. See Theophylactus 5, caps. 13, 14; Evagrius vi. 21. (For an account of Sergius, who is said to have suffered persecution in the reign of Maximian, see Tillemont, Mémoires, tom. v. pp. 73,282, and Butler, Lives of the Saints, October 7.) Khusrau ascribed the pregnancy of his best-loved wife Shîrîn to the power of Saint Sergius, but his professions of Christianity appear rather to have been due to the influence of the woman whose wit and beauty and gift of singing are famous in the romances of the East, than to conviction.

p. 81, n. 1 The Βολογεσίφορα of Stephanus Byzantinus, i.e., the town called by the Syrians and Arabs ܚܲܠܲܚ, حْلْوَان, Ḥalaḥ, Ḥulwân, which was situated beyond the Tigris in Adiabene. It was of some importance, and was one of the towns which had the privilege of electing the patriarch. See Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 67, note 592, and p. 120; Nöldeke, Geschichte der Perser, p. 134, note 3.
p. 81, n. 2 ܐܘܿܪܗܵܝ, اَلرُّها, now called Urfah. For the history of Edessa during the VIIth century see Duval, Histoire d'Édesse, p. 222 ff.

p. 81, n. 3 For the account of Shamṭâ's position under Khusrau and Shêrowai, see Nöldeke, Geschichte der Perser, p. 383, note 3, and for the narrative of his murder of Khusrau, see Thomas of Margâ, Bk. i, chap. 33; and the authorities quoted by Nöldeke, op. cit., p. 382, note 1.

p. 81, n. 4 See Assemânî, B.O., iii. 1, p. 392. Yazdîn, or Yezdîn the tax-gatherer, was a prominent member of a powerful and wealthy Christian family in the neighbourhood of Dastagerd, and as far back as the end of the fifth century, a Nestorian Synod was held in his ancestor's house at Karkhâ dhĕ Bêth Slôkh (Kerkuk). See Nöldeke, op. cit., p. 383, note 3; Bar-Hebraeus, Chron. Eccles., ii, col. 71. Now at that time there was well known in the gate of the king Yazdîn of Karkhâ dhĕ Bêth Garmai, and he was an advocate for the Church like Constantine and Theodosius; and he built churches and monasteries everywhere… And he was beloved by Khusrau even as was Joseph in the sight of Pharaoh, and it is said that on the morning of each day he used to send one thousand ܐܣܬܪ̈ܝܢ to the King. Yazdîn also sent money to rebuild the churches at Jerusalem. See Guidi, Un nuovo testo Siriaco, pp. 17, 22.
p. 82, n. 1 For the manner in which he acquired books at the capture of Dârâ see B.O., iii. 1, p. 451, col. 1, at the top, وكان احذ من دارا كتبًا كثيرة, etc.
p. 82, n. 2 This name means the man with a large family. Hoffmann, Auszüge, note 1800.
p. 82, n. 3 I.e., Îshôʿ-yahbh III. of Kuphlânâ in Adiabene.
p. 82, n. 4 Lines 14–21, p. 47, and ll. 1–3, p. 48 are quoted in B.O., iii. 1, p. 462, col. 2.
p. 82, n. 5 See supra, p. 45, note 3.

p. 82, n. 6 I.e., which he has considered foreign to the purpose of his work and has therefore omitted. We might read ܘܲܝܒܲܪ ܐܢܘܢ ܒܟܝܬܐ and he has passed over them as foreign. See Payne Smith, Thesaurus, coll. 577,2783, and Nöldeke in Z.D.M.G. xxv, p. 672. Hoffmann thinks that perhaps ܥܒܪ ܒܪܝܬܐ in Philoxenus = Gr. παρῆλθη τὴν ἔξω.
p. 83, n. 1 ܓܵܘܵܐ = the assembly or community of the monks.
p. 83, n. 2 Gabriel, surnamed the Dancer, was born at Nisibis. He was ordained by Ṣĕlîbhâ-zĕkhâ at Kerkuk about A.D. 720. See Thomas of Margâ Bk. 2, chap. 33 and B.O., iii. 1, pp. 460–462.
p. 83, n. 3 Read ܒܬܫܥܝܬܐ.
p. 83, n. 4 Read ܒܪܹܫܵܐ. Compare chap. 18, p. 41 (text).
p. 83, n. 5 Read ܫܵܒܩ ܐܢܐ.
p. 84, n. 1 ܚܕܲܝܲܒ or ܚܕܲܝܵܒ, Adiabene. The Syrians generally considered this district to include all the land between the Upper and the Lower Zâb. See Hoffmann, Auszüge, note 1911.

p. 84, n. 2 Bêth Zîwâ lay on the left bank of the Upper or Great Zâb, and as Basṭôhmagh used to cross the river by the King's Bridge to visit Rabban Jacob, Bêth ʿÂbhê must have been situated on the right bank, and at no great distance from the river.
p. 84, n. 3 Read ܥܵܒܲܪ ܗ̄ܘܵܐܒܓܹܫܪܵܐ.

p. 85, n. 1 Syr. ܒܵܣܵܡܵܝܵܐ rendered aromatarius by Assemânî (B.O., iii. 1, p. 472) and Payne Smith (Thes., col. 550). We should probably point ܒܸܣܵܡܵܝܵܐ and translate, the man from Tell-Besme (See Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 115). Tell-Besmê تل بسمة, the ܬܠ ܒܫܡܝ of the Chronicle of Dionysius (B.O., 1, p. 273), was situated to the west of Mârdîn, near Deyrik, and the ancient ruins of this place are indicated on J. G. Taylor's map in Journal Geogr. Soc. London, vol. 38, 1868, p. 355.
p. 85, n. 2 Read, with C, ܒܡܦܩ ܒܪܘܚܝ.
p. 85, n. 3 See supra, p. 19.
p. 85, n. 4 Add some word like ܐܲܟܬܸܒܢܲܢ after ܥܘܗܕܢܗܘܢ.
p. 86, n. 1 We might perhaps read ܢܲܝܬܐ ܥܘܗܕܢܗܘܢ omitting ܡܢ ܕ.
p. 86, n. 2 Read ܐܦ ܕܠܐܚܪ̈ܢܐ or ܐܦ ܠܐܚܪ̈ܢܐ.
p. 86, n. 3 Read ܘܒܕܓܘܢ. This and the seven following clauses are quoted in B.O., iii. 1, p. 441, col. 1.

p. 86, n. 4 Sabhr-Îshôʿ was a native of Pêrôzâbhâd ܦܝܪܘܙܐܒܕ in Bêth Garmai; he became Bishop of Lâshôm, and afterwards patriarch in 596. He died in the year 604 at Nisibis. See B.O., ii, p. 415; iii. 1, pp. 441–449; Bar-Hebraeus, Chron. Eccles., ii, 107; Baethgen, Fragmente, pp. 36, 119; Wright, Syr. Lit., p. 838; Guidi, Un nuovo testo Siriaco, pp. 10, 15.
p. 86, n. 5 Read ܪܹܫܵܐ.
p. 86, n. 6 A.D. 604. He was buried in the monastery which he built at جذان. B.O., ii, p. 415, col. 2.

p. 86, n. 7 I.e., ܕܵܪܵܐ or ܕܵܐܪܵܐ, Arab. دَارَا, Δάρας between the borders (ܒܹܝܬ ܬܚܘܿܡܹ̈ܐ), or Dârâ of the marches, is situated about eight hours' ride to the S. E. of Mârdîn. It was built on the eastern frontier of the Roman empire towards Assyria with the view of checking the invasions of the Persians. For an account of its fortifications see Procopius, Bello Persico, ii. 13. Dara continued more than sixty years to fulfil the wishes of its founders, and to provoke the jealousy of the Persians, who incessantly complained, that this impregnable fortress had been constructed in manifest violation of the treaty of peace between the two empires. Gibbon, Decline, chap. 40. Concerning the first fortification of Dârâ by the Greeks see Wright, Joshua the Stylite, p. 70. Ibn Baṭûṭah describes it as very old, white in appearance, with a lofty fortress which is now ruined (ed. Defrémery et Sanguinetti, ii, p. 142). The ruins have been well described by Sachau in his Reise in Mesopotamien, pp. 394, 395.

p. 87, n. 1 Bar-Hebraeus states that Dârâ was captured by Khusrau A. Gr. 915 = A.D. 604, after a siege of nine months, and that Sabhr-Îshôʿ, who was with him, died there during the siege Chron. Eccles., ii. 107. According to Guidi (Nuovo testo Siriaco, p. 14, l. 18) Khusrau captured Dârâ in the fourteenth year of his reign.

p. 87, n. 2 ܡܵܚܘܿܙܹ̈ܐ = المداين the double city, i.e., Seleucia and Ctesiphon which were situated on both banks of the Tigris about twenty miles below Bagdad. Seleucia was on the right, and Ctesiphon on the left bank of the river. Within the last six years the building on one side of the famous Arch of Khusrau has fallen, and the destruction of the whole ruin may be expected to follow in a short time, for the fine large bricks are carried away continually in boat loads to build new houses and walls.

p. 88, n. 1 Bar-Hebraeus (Chron. Eccles., ii 107) describes him as a native of Kashkar, and a doctor in the Church of Seleucia. He was an avaricious man, and his disciples bore a bad name for which he was much reproached, not only by his own people but by the Persian nobles. He died four years after he was ordained Catholicus, and was buried in Seleucia. The Persians then subjected his disciples to torture until they revealed the hiding-place of all the money which their master had collected. Gregory is No. 28 in the list of the Eastern Catholics given by Solomon of Baṣra in the Book of the Bee, (ed. Budge, p. 117). Gregory of Seleucia was appointed by the influence of Shîrîn and her physician Gabriel of Sinjâr; compare ܗܝܕܝܢ ܐܬܬܣܝܡ ܩܬܘܠܝܩܐ ܓܪܓܘܪ ܦܪܬܝܐ ܒܡܥܒܕܢܘܬܗ̇ ܕܫܝܪܝܢ ܕܐܝܬܘܗܝ ܗܘܐ ܒܪ ܐܬܪܗ̇ ܟܕ ܛܒ ܒܢ̈ܝ ܥܕܬܐ ܟܠܗܘܢ ܥܡ ܡܠܟܐ. ܠܓܪܝܓܘܪ ܟܫܟܪܝܐ ܕܐܬܛܪܕ ܡܢ ܢܨܝܒܝܢ ܒܥܝܢ ܗܘܘ. ܘܕܒܪ ܒܪܫܢܘܬܗ ܕܘܒܪ̈ܐ ܕܠܐ ܫܦܝܪ̈ܝܢ܀ Guidi, Nuovo testo, p. 15.
p. 88, n. 2 Note 6 refers to ܐܘ ܡܫܠܡ ܚܝ̈ܘܗܝ (p. 50, l. 13) and not to ܘܨܪܘܗܝ.
p. 88, n. 3 Perhaps alluded to in Guidi, Nuovo testo, p. 11.
p. 89, n. 1 This chapter is quoted in B.O., iii. 1, pp. 90,91.
p. 89, n. 2 Gregory died in the nineteenth year of the reign of Khusrau = A.D. 608–609.

p. 89, n. 3 About this time the famous physician Gabriel of Sinjâr flourished. As he was a Jacobite and had great influence with Khusrau, and was a bitter foe (ܣܐܢܐ ܥܫܝܢܐ) of the Nestorians, it is probable that the king's unreasoning oath was due, in a great measure, to this man's power over him. It is certain that for eighteen years the Nestorians had no patriarch. See Bar-Hebraeus, Chron. Eccles., ii. 109 and note 1. The whole question of the appointment of Gregory of Kashkar as Catholicus being a concession to Shîrîn the Queen and Gabriel of Sinjâr is fully discussed by Hoffmann, Auszüge, pp. 118–121.
p. 90, n. 1 This chapter is quoted in B.O., iii. 1, p. 91, col. 1f.
p. 90, n. 2 I.e., Bâbhai of Bêth ʿAinâthâ in Bêth Zabhdai, to be distinguished from Bâbhai bar-Nĕsîbhnâyê. See supra, p. 46, note 4.

p. 90, n. 3 The duty which Mâr Bâbhai undertook was the inspectorship of monasteries. It will be remembered that about the middle of the sixth century Ḥannânâ of Adiabene, the successor of Joseph Ḥûzâyâ in the school of Nisibis, had attacked the doctrines of Theodore of Mopsuestia, and had declared his intention of following the views of Chrysostom. As he was a teacher of importance and had a following of eight hundred pupils, the Nestorian Church ran a great risk of an internal schism. The views which he brought forward were condemned at a synod held under Îshôʿ-yahbh of Arzôn, (581–595), and at another presided over by his successor Sabhr-Ishôʿ (596–604). Joseph of Ḥazzâ or Arbêl adopted the opinions of Ḥannânâ, and his example was quietly followed by a large number of monks and others, and after the death of Gregory of Kashkar the Metropolitans of Nisibis, Adiabene, and Kerkûk persuaded Mâr Bâbhai that it was his bounden duty to visit all the Nestorian convents, and to expel all such as inclined to, or professed, the views of Ḥannânâ and Joseph of Ḥazzâ, together with any of the Mĕṣallĕyânê or praying monks who might be found therein. Mâr Bâbhai was qualified for his task in every way, and the manner in which he carried it out is warmly praised by Thomas of Margâ who, no doubt, expressed the general opinion of the Nestorian Church at this period on this subject. See Hoffmann, Auszüge, pp. 116–121; Wright, Syr. Lit., p. 842, col. 1 and the authorities quoted by him.
p. 90, n. 4 See Guidi, Nuovo testo, p. 17, l. 18.

p. 91, n. 1 See B.O., ii, p. 416, col. 1. For the letter which Îshôʿ-yahbh III. wrote to him see B.O., iii. 1, p. 141, col. 2, p. 142, col. 1 (Nos. 41 and 46). According to ʿAbhd-Îshôʿ he wrote [re-key the Syriac line from p. 91 n. 1] an exposition on Faith and the Mysteries (Sacraments), the cause of the Nativity and Epiphany, and a commentary on Saint Paul. See B.O., iii. 1, p. 215. He was a member of the Mission to Heraclius. See Thomas of Margâ Bk. ii, chap. 4.
p. 91, n. 2 For the letters of Îshôʿ-yahbh III. to Gabriel see B.O., iii. 1, pp. 114, 141, 142.

p. 91, n. 3 The ܡܨܲܠ̈ܝܵܢܹܐ, called by the Greeks εὐχόμενοι or εὐχῖται, Euchites, i.e., those who pray, were a sect of heretics who sprang up in Mesopotamia in the third quarter of the fourth century and spread themselves over Syria and other places; their doctrines were current as late as the twelfth century. They believed that each man received from his ancestors at birth a demon which always led him on to evil. Baptism, they thought, was able to lop off the external branches of sin, but it could never eradicate the demon from the soul in which it was the cause of sin. Prayer was the only means by which the demon could be exorcised, and to do this effectually a man must pray without ceasing, for in that alone could perfection be found. Of them Epiphanius (Haer. 80) says toti in orationes intenti cetera negligebant, et, abjectis propter falsam Evangelii interpretationem, bonis fortunae, otiosi errabant per vicos ac plateas, viris promiscue cum mulieribus dormientibus. They refused to work, and wandered from city to city begging their daily bread; their profession and occupation in life was prayer. Bar-Hebraeus (Chron. Eccles., i. 573) calls them ܡܨܠܝܢ̈ܐ ܛܘܐ̈ܐ. See B.O., i, p. 128, col. 2, (where they are mentioned by Ephraem Syrus together with a number of other heretical sects); Assemânî, Dissertatio de Syris Nestorianis (B.O., iii. 2, p. CLXXIIff.; iii. 1, p. 101, col. 2, at the top); and Cotelerius, Eccles. Graec. Monumenta, t. 1, p. 302ff. A good account of the Mĕṣallĕyânê is given by Tillemont, Mémoires Ecclésiastiques, t. viii, pp. 222–226; and see especially Guidi, Ostsyrische Bischöfe, in Z. D. M. G., Bd. xliii, p. 391.
p. 92, n. 1 Read ܢܸܣܥܘܿܪ.
p. 92, n. 2 Read ܢܣܘܼܓ.
p. 93, n. 1 The first 12 lines of the text of this chapter are quoted in B.O., iii. 1, p. 91, col. 1.
p. 93, n. 2 Read ܡܠܦܢܐ ܗ̄ܘܐ.
p. 93, n. 3 For the list of them by ʿAbhd-Îshôʿ see B.O., iii. 1. 94.
p. 94, n. 1 ܡܲܠܟܝܼܙܕܸܩܹ̈ܢܵܝܹܐ for ܡܲܠܟܝܼܙܕܸܩܹܝܵܢܹܐ; see B.O., i. 386, l. 20.

p. 94, n. 2 The Melchisedekians were a sect founded by one Theodotus an usurer who lived about A.D. 174. They first believed that Christ was a mighty, divine power, μεγάλην τινα καὶ θείαν δύναμιν, and later this power was identified with the Holy Ghost. To these views they added the opinion that Melchisedek had neither father nor mother, and that his beginning and end were incomprehensible (See Theodoret, Haer. fab. ii. 6; and Epiphanius Haer. lv.). St. Jerome proved that Melchisedek was a man, and the governor of a district in Palestine (Tillemont, Mémoires, iii. p. 32). In the Book of the Bee (ed. Budge p. 35) it is said that Melchisedek was the son of Mâlâḥ (in Bezold, Schatzhöhle, p. 36 Mâlâkh) the grandson of Shem the son of Noah, and that his mother's name was Yôzâdâḳ. On a marginal note of the MS of the Book of the Bee which I called A (fol 39a) the name of Melchisedek's father is given as Harḳlêîm, and that of his mother Shêlâthêîl, ܗܪܩܠܐܝܡ، ܫܠܐܬܝܠ. The passages from the lexx. quoted by Payne Smith (Thes. col. 2146) add that he sprang from foreign peoples, and on this account [the name of] his parents were not written in the [Book of] Generations, according to the words of Paul (Hebrews vii. 3). And the names of his parents were made known by revelation to the old man in the desert of Scete who, in his simplicity, meditated upon these things, by the counsel of Theophilus, Archbishop of Alexandria. For the account of the solitary who was brought by Cyril to Alexandria to consult God concerning Melchisedek's origin, see Cotelerius, Eccles. Graec. Mon., tom. i, pp. 423,424; and Tillemont, Mémoires, iii. p. 32.
p. 95, n. 1 Better ܐܝܬ ܗܘܐ ܡܠܦܢ̈ܐ.
p. 95, n. 2 He became Bishop of Alexandria A.D. 385. See Sozomen, Hist. Eccles., vii. 14; Socrates, Hist. Eccles., v. 12.
p. 95, n. 3 The remainder of this chapter is quoted in B.O., iii. 1, p. 218, col. 1.

p. 95, n. 4 I.e., هاغلة, see Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 238, note 1897. Hêglâ Omêd is a Persian name compounded of Hêglâ, and Omêd = امّيد hope. Compare אומית על יזרתי Hoffnung auf Gott in Horn and Steindorff, Sassanidische Siegelsteine, (in Mittheilungen aus den Orientalischen Sammlungen, Berlin, 1891.) p. 28, at the top.
p. 95, n. 5 Read ܠܐܚ̈ܐ, or ܘܠܐܚ̈ܐ.

p. 95, n. 6 Ḥĕnân-Îshôʿ I. surnamed the Lame ܚܓܝܼܪܐ was ordained A.D. 685, and having sat for fourteen years died in the Monastery of Jonah at Nineveh A.D. 699. For a list of his works see B.O., iii. 1, p. 154, and for an account of his dispute with John, Metropolitan of Nisibis, surnamed the Leper, see B.O., ii, pp. 421–424.
p. 96, n. 1 Read, with Vat., ܘܗܘ ܡܢ ܐܝܟ ܝܕܥ ܐܝܟ.

p. 96, n. 2 George, the son of fishermen came from the village of Neshra ܢܫܪܐ in Adiabene, and was Abbot of Bêth ʿÂbhê about A.D. 590. He was buried in the martyrium of this convent with Nathaniel, Ṣĕlîbhâ, and Gabriel surnamed Ṣephrônâ; see Thomas of Margâ, Bk. ii, chap. 20. His life was written by David the Bishop at the request of a Persian nobleman in the Book of the Little Paradise; see Thomas of Margâ, Bk. ii, chap. 24. According to ʿAbhd-Îshôʿ he wrote the Book of Obedience, ܟܬܒܐ ܕܡܫܬܡܥܢܘܬܐ; B.O., iii. 1, p. 217.
p. 96, n. 3 He wrote a commentary on the Psalms of David, and treatises against the followers of Severus of Antioch, the Manicheans and other heretics. See B.O., iii. 1, p. 224.
p. 96, n. 4 According to Thomas of Margâ, Bk. ii, chap. 20, he became Abbot of Bêth ʿÂbhê.
p. 96, n. 5 I.e., Little Sparrow. ܨܦܪܘܿܢܵܐ is explained in Or. 2441 fol. 319b. col. 1 by ܓܢܣܐ ܕܦܪܚܬܐ ܕܩܥܝܐ ܩܕܡ ܡܛܪܐ A kind of bird which sings before rain.
p. 97, n. 1 The first sixteen lines of this chapter are quoted in B.O., iii. 1, p. 473.
p. 97, n. 2 Read ܐܸܨܛܒܝܼ.
p. 98, n. 1 Read ܥܵܠܡܵܝܹ̈ܐ.
p. 99, n. 1 In the text p. 56, note 2, read St. Matthew ix. 6.
p. 100, n. 1 Literally, one who maketh to inherit.
p. 100, n. 2 Read ܚܲܟܝܼܡܵܐ.
p. 100, n. 3 Proverbs xx. 7.
p. 100, n. 4 Proverbs xxi. 15.
p. 100, n. 5 Proverbs xxiii. 24.
p. 101, n. 1 Reading with A, ܘܣܓܸܕܘ.
p. 101, n. 2 Assemânî has (B.O., iii. i, p. 203, cols. 1 and 2) ܐܬܬܠܡܲܕܘ.
p. 101, n. 3 This chapter is quoted in B.O., iii. 1, pp. 203, and 474.

p. 101, n. 5 The text of this letter, edited from two modern copies of Îshôʿ-yahbh's Letters which I had made at Al-Ḳôsh, is given at the end of this chapter. In it Îshôʿ-yahbh gently chides the monks of Bêth ʿÂbhê because they had not consulted him in the matter of the election of a successor to Mâr Jacob, and he advises them to appoint Abbâ John whom Mâr Jacob had nominated as his successor before he died. Îshôʿ-yahbh recommends the monks to appoint Abbâ John on account of his having been a monk for seventy years.
p. 102, n. 1 Assemânî has ܕܥܠܘܗܝ.
p. 102, n. 2 For the list of his works see chap. xxxiv (infra, pp. 110–112).
p. 102, n. 3 His first funeral oration was written upon Mâr Jacob of Bêth ʿÂbhê.
p. 102, n. 4 Dâḳôḳ = Tâʿûḳ. See supra p. 44, note 1. See also Mai, Script. Vet. Nova Coll., t. x, p. 296.
p. 102, n. 5 See Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 274; B.O., iii. 1, pp. 203, 204 and note 1.
p. 102, n. 6 Assemânî writes ܟܽܘܕܳܐܗܳܘܳܝ and ܟܽܘܕܳܐܗܘܺܝ (B.O., iii. 1, pp. 151, 203). ܟܘܼܕܐ = Pers. خُدَا god.
p. 102, n. 7 ܒܹܝܬ ܚܵܠܹ̈ܐ, Arab. باحَالَا (B.O., iii. 1, p. 155, col. 2, l. 9) = دير الطين (B.O., iii. 1, p. 205, col. 2, note 2). This monastery was situated in al-Ḥadîtha near Môṣul.
p. 103, n. 1 Abbâ John wrote a history of Khodhâhwai. See B.O., iii. 1, p. 204.
p. 103, n. 2 I.e., the monks of Rabban Ezekiel.
p. 103, n. 3 A village in the diocese of Margâ. See B.O., iii. 1, pp. 204, 492.

p. 103, n. 4 Mâr Abraham sat from A.D. 837–850. He was originally a monk in Bêth ʿÂbhê, and afterwards became Abbot of that monastery; he next became Bishop of Ḥadîtha, and was finally elected Patriarch. See B.O., iii. 1, p. 508, note 1.

p. 104, n. 1 He wrote certain chapters on heads of knowledge, institutions for beginners, a short Chronicle, a history of Mâr Khodhâhwai, a discourse upon him, and some hymns. ܣܡ ܪ̈ܝܫܐ ܕܩܪܝܢ ܕܝܕܥܬܐ. ܘܐܝܬ ܠܗ ܛܘܟܣ ܫܪ̈ܘܝܐ܆ ܘܟܪܘܢܝܩܘܢ ܒܟܪ̈ܝܬܐ. ܘܬܫܥܝܬܐ ܕܡܪܝ ܟܘܕܐܗܘܝ܆ ܥܡ ܡܐܡܪܗ ܬܘܒ ܘܡܕܪ̈ܫܐ. See B.O., iii. 1, pp. 203–205; and Wright, Syr. Lit., 843.
p. 104, n. 2 Read ܡܪܝ ܚܙܩܝܐܝܠ
p. 107, n. 1 This chapter is quoted in B.O., iii. 1, p. 227.
p. 107, n. 2 Near the Upper or Great Zâb in Adiabene.
p. 107, n. 3 According to ʿAbhd-Îshôʿ he wrote a book of various questions, ܐܒܪܗܡ ܐܝܬ ܠܗ ܟܬܒܐ ܕܫ̈ܘܐܠܐ ܡܦܲܬܟ̈ܐ.; B.O., iii. 1, p. 227.

p. 107, n. 4 The text of this passage is corrupt, and it is perhaps better to follow the reading of the Vatican MS. Hoffmann offers as an alternative ܠܒܢ̈ܝ ܚܕ ܐܒܐ ܘܚܕܐ ܐܡܐ܆ ܐܝܟܢ܆ ܕܐܝܟ ܒܒܢ̈ܝܗ̇ ܕܛܘܒܢܝܬܐ ܫܡܘܢܝ ܢܬܢܲܗܪܘܼܢ܆ ܢܫܲܒܚ. See 2 Maccabees vii. 1; and Wright, Catalogue Syr. MSS., pp. 185, col. 2.
p. 107, n. 5 All the MSS. have ܡܸܪܕܲܐ, but read ܡܲܪܕܹܐ.
p. 108, n. 1 Read ܛܘܼܒܵܢܵܐ.
p. 108, n. 2 I.e., the general work in the monastery which every novice was bound to take part in for a certain time.
p. 108, n. 3 Read ܠܲܚܝܵܪܬܵܐ.
p. 108, n. 4 This mountain must have been situated near Ḥadhattâ below the Upper Zâb in Adiabene.
p. 108, n. 5 A disciple of Ḳâm-Îshôʿ who flourished about the year 630. For his works see B.O., iii. 1, p. 187.

p. 108, n. 6 Sabhr-Îshôʿ Rôsṭâm was a native of the village of Ḥĕrêm in Adiabene, and entered the great convent on Mount Îzlâ under the Abbot Narsai, the successor of Bâbhai. In addition to the lives of Joseph and Abraham he wrote those of Abbâ Abraham of Bêth ʿÂbhê, Abbâ Ḳâm-Îshôʿ of Bêth ʿÂbhê, Abraham of Nethpar, and some others. See Wright, Syr. Lit., p. 843; B.O., iii. 1, p. 455.
p. 109, n. 1 This chapter is quoted in B.O., iii. 1, pp. 440, 472. Sergius flourished at the beginning of the seventh century.
p. 109, n. 2 A place situated in the diocese of Margâ. See B.O., iii. 1, pp. 178, 440; Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 97.
p. 109, n. 3 ܓܲܪܡܩܵܝܵܐ, جر مقانى, a man of ܒܝܬ ܓܪ̈ܡܝ.
p. 109, n. 4 It was situated on the Lower Zâb.
p. 109, n. 6 Seleucia and Ctesiphon.
p. 109, n. 7 Read ܘܫܲܢܝ ܡ̇ܢ ܟܕ.
p. 109, n. 8 A mountainous district in Bêth Zabhdai.
p. 110, n. 1 Read ܘܒܥܕܬܐ ?
p. 110, n. 2 This chapter is quoted in B.O., iii. 1, p. 453, col. 2.

p. 110, n. 3 Sâhdônâ, i.e., the little martyr, was ordained Bishop of Mâḥôzê dhĕ Arîwân in Bêth Garmai by Îshôʿ-yahbh of Gĕdhâlâ. He was one of the members of the Mission sent to Heraclius A.D. 628, and on his way back became a convert to Jacobite views, a fact which caused great scandal in the Nestorian Church. The text of the letters which Îshôʿ-yahbh wrote concerning this matter are given at the end of Bk. ii, chap. 6, in which Thomas of Margâ relates the story. See B.O., iii. 1, pp. 81, 107, 115, 142, 453, 457, 462; Wright, Syr. Lit., p. 842.
p. 111, n. 1 Halmôn, or Halamûn, (the Halamoon of Badger, Nestorians, vol. 1, p. 394) was situated in the north of Bêth Nûhâdhrâ, or Bêth Nûhâdhrê, on the left bank of the Upper Ḥâbûr.

p. 111, n. 2 ܒܹܝܬ ܢܘܼܗܵܕܪܵܐ, باهذرا، بانهذرا، بانهدرا، بانهودرا The Region of Nohodarê was a district or Nestorian Church province, the southerly limit of which was Awânâ near Bâlâdh on the Tigris opposite Eski-Môṣul; the boundary on the north-west was the Monastery of Rabban Aphnî-Mâran dhĕ Khurkmâ, or Dêr az-Zaʿfarân, not far from al-Gezîra by Gebel Gûdî; and the most northerly point was Halmôn. See Hoffmann, Auszüge, pp. 208–216, and the authorities quoted by him.
p. 112, n. 1 The greater part of this chapter is quoted in B.O., iii, 1, p. 91, coll. 1. 2.

p. 112, n. 2 This statement of Thomas of Margâ is supported by historical evidence. In the eighteenth year of his reign Khusrau liess die Einkünfte aus den Steuern seiner Länder sowie allen sonstigen Einnahmequellen zählen, und da berichtete man ihm, dass seine Einkünfte aus der Grundsteuer und den andern Quellen sich in diesem Jahr in gemünztem Gelde auf 420 Millionen Mithqâl an Gewicht beliefen, was, 10 Dirham auf 7 Mithqâl gerechnet, 600 Millionen Dirham macht (about 294,000,000 marks or 360,000,000 francs). All this money was brought into the treasury at Ctesiphon, where there were already stored up 48,000,000 Mithqâl of money coined by Pêrôz, son of Yazdegerd, and by Kawâdh, son of Pêrôz. Dazu kam noch eine Menge von Juwelen, Kleidern, u.s.w., deren Betrag nur Gott zählen kann. Nöldeke, Geschichte der Perser, pp. 353 ff.

p. 113, n. 1 Yazdîn was the director of the land-tax of the whole kingdom and had amassed an enormous fortune, which the king confiscated. See Nöldeke, Geschichte der Perser, p. 583, note 1; Hoffmann, Auszüge, pp. 115–121; Wright, Syr. Lit., p. 837.
p. 113, n. 2 Shamṭâ here appears as the leader of the rebellion. See Nöldeke, op. cit., p. 354, note 4; Guidi, Nuovo testo, p. 23.
p. 113, n. 3 I.e., Ctesiphon and Seleucia.

p. 113, n. 4 The number of Khusrau's sons is given as seventeen by Ṭabarî. When the nobles heard that Khusrau had given orders to slay all the prisoners in the gaols, certain of them came to ʿAḳr Bâbil (which Nöldeke identifies with al-Ḳaṣr, where Khusrau's sons were being educated, a body of soldiers being stationed near to prevent their leaving the place), and taking Shêrôë they brought him by night to Beh-Ardashîr where he was proclaimed King of Kings. Nöldeke, op. cit., pp. 357 & 382.

p. 114, n. 1 Khusrau had intended that Merdânshâh, the son of Shîrîn should succeed him. See Theophanes, Chronographia, ed. Niebuhr vol. 1, pp. 499–501. Merdânshâh was slain with the other sons of Khusrau.

p. 114, n. 2 Chosrau verachtete die Menschen und schätzte gering, was kein verständiger und umsichtiger König geringschätzt. Sein frevler Muth und seine Rücksichtslosigkeit gegen Gott ging so weit, dass er dem Befehlshaber der inneren Leibwache Namens Zâdhân-Ferruch gebot, alle Gefangene in seinen Kerkern umzubringen; ihre Zahl belief sich auf 36,000 Mann. Nöldeke, op. cit., p. 356. The first act of Shêrôë when brought to Beh-Ardashîr was to release all these prisoners, who at once joined with the nobles in proclaiming him king.
p. 114, n. 3 Read ܘܡܛܠ.
p. 114, n. 4 Read ܘܓܲܓܪܵܢܘܼܬܹܗ. ܓܲܓܪܢܘܼܬܵܐ is a rare word.
p. 114, n. 5 According to Ṭabarî Khusrau had determined to slay all the troops which had fled from before the victorious arms of Heraclius. Nöldeke, op. cit., p. 356.
p. 114, n. 6 Read ܥܠ.

p. 114, n. 7 According to Ṭabarî Khusrau fled to one of his gardens called Bâgh-i-Hinduwân whither he was pursued and captured; he was afterwards cast into prison, where seventeen or eighteen of his sons were slain before his face, and where he died or was murdered. According to Guidi, (Nuovo testo, p. 24) ܬܒܥܘ ܫܡܛܐ ܘܢܝܗܘܪܡܝܙܕ ܡܢ ܫܝܪܘܝ ܡܠܟܐ ܒܪ ܟܘܣܪܘ ܕܢܩܛܠܘܢܝܗܝ ܠܟܘܣܪܘ. ܘܟܕ ܐܦܣ ܠܗܘܢ ܥܠܘ ܥܠܘܗܝ ܐܝܟܐ ܕܚܒܝܫ ܗܘܐ. ܘܐܪܝܡ ܫܡܛܐ ܣܝܦܐ ܕܢܡܚܝܘܗܝ ܘܒܟܐ ܟܘܣܪܘ ܠܩܘܒܠܗ ܘܐܡܪ ܠܗ. ܡܢܐ ܚܛܝܬ ܠܟ ܕܬܩܛܠܢܝ. ܘܠܐ ܡܚܝܗܝ ܫܡܛܐ. ܘܡܚܝܗܝ ܢܝܗܘܪܡܝܙܕ ܒܢܪܓܐ ܥܠ ܟܬܦܗ. ܘܬܢܐ ܥܠ ܐܚܪܬܐ. ܘܐܪܩܕ ܥܠܘܗ. ܫܝܪܘܝ ܒܪܗ. ܘܩܒܪܘܗܝ ܒܩܒܪܐ ܕܡܠܟ̈ܐ. For the history of the overthrow of this king see Nöldeke, op. cit., p. 357, note 4, p. 383, note 3; Gibbon, Decline and Fall, chap. 46; Chron. Paschal, tom. 1, p. 728, ed. Dindorf; Theophanes, Chronographia, p. 501; and Eutychius, Annales, ii, p. 251 ff.

p. 115, n. 1 Shamṭâ suffered imprisonment and the loss of his right hand by the order of Shêrôë, and he was shortly after crucified before the door of the Church of Bêth Narḳôs. See Guidi, Nuovo testo, pp. 24, 25.
p. 115, n. 2 Shêrôë's reign lasted eight months.
p. 115, n. 3 I.e., Gudâl, الجُدال, near Môṣul.

p. 115, n. 4 Bêth ʿArbhâyê is described by Bar-Sarôshwai as the district which extends from Bâlâdh, opposite Eski-Môṣul on the Tigris to Nisibis. In a passage quoted by Wright (Catalogue Syr. MSS., p. 1136, col. 2) it is said that marauding bands of the Persians were perpetually coming over their borders and capturing cities from Ras-ʿAin to Nisibis, and from the countries of Maiperḳâṭ and Arzan to the Mountains of Ḳardô; they captured also Ṭûr ʿAbdîn which is in these countries. To prevent these raids two fortresses were built; one on the borders of Bêth ʿArbhâyê, by the mountains, and the other on the Tigris. ܒܝܬ ܥܪ̈ܒܝܐ probably = Βεαρβαες of Theophylact, and بَعَرْبايا of Yâḳût, which is described as being near Môṣul. See also the passages quoted by Hoffmann, Auszüge, note 170, p. 23; and B.O., iii. 2, p. 507.
p. 115, n. 5 See Guidi, Nuovo testo, p. 24, l. 17.
p. 117, n. 1 Genesis iii. 3.
p. 117, n. 2 ܡܫܵܘܫܛܘܼܬܵܐ, from √ܝܫܛ, a rare word.
p. 117, n. 3 Exodus xx.
p. 117, n. 4 ܟܬܵܒܵܐܝܼܬ, literally by writing. There seems to be no example of this word in Payne Smith's Thesaurus.
p. 118, n. 1 ܬܵܘܣ̈ܝܼܦܹܐ, a rare word.
p. 118, n. 2 Read ܒܲܝܬܝܲܬ ܠܲܬܡܝܼܗܵܐ.
p. 118, n. 4 Read ܩܵܡܝܼܫܘܿܥ.
p. 119, n. 1 Read ܘܒܬܪܗ ܗܢܐ.
p. 119, n. 3 Read ܒܹܝܬ ܓܪ̈ܡܝ?
p. 119, n. 4 See Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 277.
p. 119, n. 5 Ḥarbath Gelâl or Gellâl, خَرْبة جَلِيل was probably situated on the Lower Zâb. See Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 261; B.O., iii. ii, p. 756.
p. 119, n. 6 I.e., Îshôʿ-yahbh III. of Adiabene.
p. 120, n. 1 ܡܲܠܦܵܢܵܐܝܼܬ. For ܢܸܪ̈ܕܲܐ read ܢܸܪܕܹܐ.

p. 120, n. 2 Rabban Îshôʿ-yahbh, the founder of the Monastery which bore this name at Môṣul, flourished about A.D. 570, while Ezekiel was Patriarch of the Nestorians. He was surnamed ܒܪ ܩܘܣܝܢ, or ܒܪ ܩܘܣܪܐ = بر قوسرا. For a list of his writings see B.O., iii. 1, pp. 230, 231.
p. 121, n. 1 See supra, p. 72, note 4.
p. 121, n. 2 This chapter is quoted in B.O., iii. i, p. 187, coll. 1, 2.

p. 121, n. 3 He flourished about A.D. 660 under George the Patriarch, and is said to have been the founder of the Dêr al-Zaʿfarân near Môṣul. See B.O., ii, p. 422; iii. i, p. 187. He is one of the monks mentioned by name in the letter which Îshôʿ-yahbh sent to Bêth ʿÂbhê concerning the election of a head. See p. 104, l. 11.
p. 122, n. 1 I.e., Kerkûk, ܟܪܟܘܟ, كركوك. See Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 267.
p. 122, n. 2 St. John vii. 38.
p. 122, n. 3 Exodus xiii. 21.
p. 122, n. 4 ܘܒܫܡܐ ܕܡܨܠܝܵܢܘܼܬܵܐ literally, and in the name of Meṣallianism. For the doctrines of the ܡܨܠܝܢ̈ܐ see supra, p. 91, note 3.
p. 122, n. 5 The monks who treated Aphnî Mâran in this manner wished to indicate that he was an ass, and was only fit to be buried like an ass.

p. 123, n. 1 The Monastery of Rabban Aphnî-Mâran marked the limit on the north-west of the church province of Bêth Nûhâdhrâ (see supra, p. 111, note 2). It is placed by Yâḳût not far from al-Gezîra by or upon Gebel Gûdî. According to Ibn al-Athîr Dêr al-Zaʿfarân or Ḳalʿat al-Zaʿfarân stood upon a high mountain near فرشابور, or Pêrôzshâbhôr, which lay on the banks of the Tigris. See Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 213. Sachau mentions (Reise in Syrien und Mesopotamien, p. 376) Ḳalʿat Zaʿfarân, eine Ruine, 2 1/2 Stunden entfernt, auf dem Westufer des Tigris auf einem Hügel gelegen.
p. 123, n. 2 This chapter is quoted in B.O., iii. i, pp. 105, col. 2, and 475, col. 2.

p. 123, n. 3 Literally the country of the Romans; but Constantinople was nova Roma, Ῥώμη νέα, and hence the Syrians and Arabs use the word ܪ̈ܗܘܡܝܐ and اَلرُّوم, ar-Rûm, to designate the Byzantine Greeks. Wright, Chronicle of Joshua the Stylite, p. 1.

p. 123, n. 4 I.e., Îshôʿ-yahbh II. He sat from A.D. 628–644, and was Bishop of Bâlâdh at the time of his elevation to the patriarchate. See B.O., ii, pp. 416–418; iii. i, pp. 105, 475; Bar-Hebraeus, Chron. Eccles., ii. 113, note 1; and Baethgen, Fragmente, pp. 13, 19, 108, 111. Îshôʿ-yahbh II died A. Gr. 955 = A.D. 643 and was buried at Kerkûk; see Bar-Hebraeus, Chron. Eccles., II 127, note 3; and Wright, Syr. Lit., p. 842. The principal writings of Îshôʿ-yahbh were a commentary on the Psalms, and sundry epistles, histories, and homilies. According to Guidi, (Nuovo testo, p. 24) he was a married man.

p. 124, n. 1 He was educated in the schools of Nisibis, and became Bishop of Môṣul, and afterwards Metropolitan of Arbêl and Môṣul. He sat as Catholicus from A.D. 647–658. The chief events in his life are recorded by Thomas of Margâ in the following chapters.
p. 124, n. 2 All the MSS. here read ܟܘܼܦܠܵܝܵܐ, which is certainly a mistake for ܟܘܼܦܠܵܢܵܐ. See Syriac text p. 78, l. 5.

p. 124, n. 3 Read ܡܵܚܘܿܙܹ̈ܐ ܕܐܲܪܝܼܘܵܢ. See B.O., iii. i, pp. 116, 475; iii. ii, pp. 723, 761; Bar-Hebraeus, Chron. Eccles., 18, note 1; Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 52, note 443, p. 277, note 2180. This town was probably situated on the Lesser Zâb.
p. 124, n. 4 See Guidi, Nuovo testo, p. 24.
p. 124, n. 5 ܥܲܪܒܵܝܵܐ, or ܥܲܪܵܒܵܝܵܐ, عربيّ, a man from the people who dwelt in ܒܝܬ ܥܪ̈ܒܝܐ, اهل باعربايا, i. e., the district between Eski Môṣul on the Tigris and Nisibis.
p. 125, n. 1 ܕܠܝܚܘܬ ܫܝܢܐ, literally, the troubling of peace.

p. 125, n. 2 The Persian Mission of peace was despatched by Bôrân, daughter of Khusrau Parwêz, although overtures of peace had been made to Heraclius by Shêrôë. Bôrân reigned only one year and four months, but during this short period she endeavoured to do away with some of the ill effects of the recent wars. Wie man erzählt, sprach sie am Tage ihrer Thronbesteigung: frommer Handlungsweise will ich mich befleissen und Gerechtigkeit anbefehlen. …… Sie behandelte ihre Unterthanen gut, verbreitete Gerechtigkeit über sie, liess Münzen prägen und steinerne und hölzerne Brücken ausbessern. Die Steuerrückstände erliess sie den Leuten und schrieb an sie insgemein offne Briefe, worin sie ihnen darlegte, wie sie ihnen wohlthun wolle, und die verstorbenen Glieder der Dynastie schilderte…… Sie gab dem römischen Kaiser durch Vermittlung des Catholicus Îshôʿ-yahbh das hölzerne Kreuz zurück. Nöldeke, Geschichte der Perser, pp. 390–392. ܘܐܡܠܟܘ ܥܠܝܗܘܢ ܦܪ̈ܣܝܐ ܠܒܪܘܐܢ ܝܬܬܗ ܕܫܝܪܘܝ. ܗܕܐ ܕܝܢ ܟܕ ܐܡܠܟܬ݀܆ ܒܚܟܡܬܐ ܫܕܪܬ݀ ܠܘܬ ܗܪܩܠܝܐ܆ ܠܡܪܝ ܝܫܘܥܝܗܒ ܩܬܘܠܝܩܐ܆ ܐܝܟ ܕܢܥܒܕ ܠܗ̇ ܥܡܗ ܫܠܡܐ. ܟܕ ܐܬܠܘܝ ܠܗ ܩܘܪܝܩܘܣ ܕܢܨܝܒܝܢ. ܘܓܒܪܝܠ ܕܟܪܟܐ ܕܒܝܬ ܓܪ̈ܡܝ. ܘܡܪܘܬܐ ܕܓܘܣܛܪܐ. ܘܣܓܝ ܚܕܝܐܝܬ ܐܬܩܒܠܘ ܡܢ ܡܠܟܐ ܗܪܩܠܐ ܘܥܒܕ ܠܘܬܗܘܢ ܟܠ ܕܨܒܘ. ܒܪܘܐܢ ܐܢܬܬ ܫܝܪܘܝ ܕܐܡܠܟܬ݀ ܥܠ ܦܪ̈ܣܚܐ܆ ܠܚܪܬܐ ܒܡܘܬܐ ܕܚܢܘܩܝܐ ܡܝܬܬ݀܀ Guidi, Nuovo testo, p. 26. Îshôʿ-yahbh met Heraclius at Aleppo, but he can hardly have given back to him the Holy Cross, which the Persians had carried off when they conquered Jerusalem A.D. 614 (Gibbon, Decline and Fall, chap. xlvi), for that had been restored by Ardashîr III in 628–629, and the festival to celebrate its restoration took place at Jerusalem in 629. (One writer says that ܦܪܐܗܢ, the general of Ardashîr, sent the Cross back to Heraclius; see Guidi, Nuovo testo, p. 25.) See the discussion on this point in Nöldeke, op. cit., p. 392, note 1. In the account of this mission given by Bar-Hebraeus (Chron. Eccles., ii. 113) Îshôʿ-yahbh is said to have given the Greeks to understand that his religion was the same as theirs, ܘܟܕ ܐܫܬܐܠ ܡܛܠ ܬܘܕܝܬܐ ܚܲܘܝ ܕܐܝܟ ܝܘܢ̈ܝܐ ܡܘܕܐ. Îshôʿ-yahbh was far-sighted enough to make an alliance with Muḥammad the Prophet (or, as Wright thought, with Abû Bakr) through the intervention of a Christian governor at Najrân called Sayyed, and Îshôʿ, the Bishop of the believers at that place. Certain of the conditions of the agreement, which was ratified by ʿOmar ibn al-Khaṭṭâb, are given by Bar-Hebraeus Chron. Eccles., ii, col. 117; see also B.O., ii, p. 418; iii. i, p. 108, col. 1. Îshôʿ-yahbh stipulated that the Christians should be protected from the attacks of their foes; that the Arabs should not compel them to go out to war with them; that they should not compel them to change their manners and laws; that they should help them to repair their old churches; that the tax on the poor should not exceed four zûzê, and that the tax on merchants and the wealthy should be ten zûzê per man; that a Christian woman in Arab service should neither be compelled to give up her faith, nor to neglect fasting and prayer; etc.

p. 126, n. 1 See supra, Bk. i, chap. 27, p. 91. For the letters of Îshôʿ-yahbh to this bishop, see B.O., iii. i, p. 141, col. 2, p. 142, col. 1. After his death his cell was spoiled by orders of the governor of Nisibis; see Guidi, Nuovo testo, p. 26, at the foot.
p. 126, n. 2 See B.O., iii. i, p. 116.
p. 126, n. 3 See B.O., iii. i, pp. 141, 142; where letters from Îshôʿ-yahbh to this bishop concerning the people of Tagrîth (Tekrît) are described.
p. 127, n. 1 This chapter is quoted in B.O., iii. i, p. 106, col. 2.
p. 127, n. 2 St. Matthew died and was buried in Antioch. See Acta Sanctorum, xlviii, Sept. 21; Lipsius, Apostelgeschichte, vol. 2, p. 127; Budge, Book of the Bee, p. 106.
p. 128, n. 1 B.O. has ܕܬܬܝܬܐ.
p. 128, n. 2 Literally, While he, Mâr Îshôʿ-yahbh worked like a man (ܐ̄ܢܵܫܵܐܝܼܬ), Christ would protect and defend him like a God (ܐܲܠܵܗܵܐܝܼܬ).
p. 128, n. 3 Read ܐܸܣܬܲܥܪܲܬ.
p. 128, n. 4 This chapter is quoted in B.O., iii. i, p. 107, coll. 1, 2.

p. 128, n. 5 The modern Ḳalʿat el-Meḍîḳ on the Orontes. Apamea lies on the western edge of the plain which extends from the southern slope of the el-Bâra mountains, and the mountains near Ḳalʿat Sêdjar and Ḥâmâ. See Sachau, Reise in Mesopotamien, p. 71 f. Dr. Strassmaier has noted a passage on British Museum tablet SP. 1. 176, in which it is said that the city of A-pa-am-a is situated upon the river Ṣi-il-ḫu.
p. 129, n. 1 Not necessarily Jacobites.
p. 129, n. 2 Literally, confession.
p. 129, n. 3 Read ܕܟܘܿܪܐ.
p. 129, n. 4 Strike out the point after ܘܬܚܘ̈ܝܬܗܘܢ.
p. 129, n. 5 Read ܡܠܵܛܵܐ = μελέτη.
p. 129, n. 6 Read ܦܩܲܕ.
p. 130, n. 1 Read ܚܒܪ̈ܘܗܝ.
p. 130, n. 2 Read ܣܝܡ̈ܐ ܕܡܢܲܟܪܵ̈ܝܲܝ.

p. 130, n. 3 Among the letters of Mâr Îshôʿ-yahbh are five which relate to Sâhdônâ and to his conversion to the views held by the Jacobites, and they form Nos 6, 7, 28, 29 and 30 of those which were written while he was Metropolitan of Ḥazzâ (Arbêl) near Môṣul. Portions of them have been published by Assemânî, B.O., iii. i, pp. 116, 118 and 119, but as the defection of Sâhdônâ caused such a disturbance in the Nestorian Church, and was held to be of a very serious character by Mâr Îshôʿ-yahbh himself, and as the letters are of such importance for the right understanding of certain parts of the history of Thomas of Margâ, it has been thought proper to give the full texts of these at the end of this chapter. They are edited from two copies which I caused to be made from an old MS. at Môṣul while on a mission to Mesopotamia for the Trustees of the British Museum. They afford an interesting insight into the history of Sâhdônâ, and into the character of Îshôʿ-yahbh, and give an idea of the internal troubles which beset the Nestorian Church at that period.
p. 131, n. 1 This chapter is quoted in B.O., iii. i, p. 124, col. 1.
p. 131, n. 2 See Bk. ii. chaps. xii–xv.
p. 131, n. 3 I.e., the diocese of Môṣul. See Payne Smith, Thes., col. 421. For monasteries situated in this district see Hoffmann, Auszüge, pp. 175–179.
p. 131, n. 4 Read ܘܐܬܩܲܕܫ.
p. 147, n. 1 This chapter is quoted in B.O., iii. 1, p. 124, col. 2.
p. 148, n. 1 Read ܕܲܬܥܵܫܵܐ.
p. 148, n. 2 Read ܡܲܝܬܹܐ.

p. 148, n. 3 Neque enim, aiebant, est hoc Monachorum opus, ut in cellis nostris sedentes, audiamus cantiones, et sonos, et tripudia puerorum, et nocturnos vigilantium adolescentium ludos. B.O., iii. 1, p. 126, col. 1.
p. 148, n. 4 ܫܲܗܪܵܐ ……Presbyter…… qui nocturno praesertim officio decantando praeest. See B.O., iii. 2, p. 820 ff.

p. 149, n. 1 ut alter alterum doceremus, aut alium quempiam literis imbueremus; multoque minus, ut Scholares iterum evaderemus. B.O., iii. 1, p. 126, col. 1. ܩܝܵܡܘܼܬܐ i.e., ܩܝܵܡܘܼܬ ܩܠܐ = choral singing.
p. 149, n. 2 Read ܐܢܗܘ ܕ.
p. 149, n. 3 Hoffmann would read ܒܟܠܗ̇, in which case we must translate thy power is in the whole land of Persia.
p. 150, n. 1 Hoffmann would read ܘܕܒܗܕܪܐ ܕܪܘܼܚܝ And in that by the ornament of my spirit I have power over all monasteries and convents, etc.
p. 150, n. 2 This chapter is quoted in B.O., iii. 1, p. 125, col. 1.

p. 150, n. 3 Ḥerpâ is mentioned together with Bêth Bôzî, Bîrtâ, Ḥleptâ, Haṭrâ, Bâshôsh, Rêshʿên in Bk. IV, chap. 21, as being situated in the province of Saphsâphâ, which according to Hoffmann, (Auszüge, p. 223), embraced the region extending from the southern slopes of the Ḥair mountains on the north and east of the plain of Naukur along the Gômel river, and thence along the Upper Ḥâzir river by Shermen and Shôsh to ʿAḳrâ.

p. 150, n. 4 A name compounded of Pers. barz high, and Sûrên the name of a noble Persian family. For examples of distinguished men who bore the name Sûrên, Σουρήνας, Σουρήνης, and a discussion upon it see Nöldeke, Geschichte der Perser, p. 438, note 4. Bĕrâz Sûrîn is mentioned by name in the letter which Îshôʿ-yahbh wrote to Ḳâm-Îshôʿ and the other monks of Bêth ʿÂbhê concerning the election of an abbot. See supra p. 104 and B.O., iii. 1, p. 141, col. 1. The famous convent of Bêth ʿÂbhê lay to the south of Ḥerpâ. See the following chapter (p. 152, l. 19), and Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 226.
p. 151, n. 1 Hoffmann would read, but doubtfully, ܡܛܝܒܘܬ ܨܒܝܢܗ.
p. 152, n. 1 Read ܗܸܘ.
p. 152, n. 2 Read ܟܝܘܠܦܢܐ.

p. 152, n. 3 ܐܲܫܝܼܡܘܿܢܵܝܵܐ. In Payne Smith, Thes. col. 406, ܐܫܝܡܘܢ is explained by ܕܘܟܬܐ ܕܠܐ ܡܝ̈ܐ a place without water, and in Duval's Bar Bahlûl, (Paris 1888, pt. 1, col. 307) it is said to be the name of a place اسم موضع. ܐܲܫܝܼܡܘܿܢ = probably יְשִׁמֹת, or יְשִׁימוֹן.
p. 152, n. 4 The remaining part of this chapter is quoted in B.O., iii. 1, p. 125, col. 2.

p. 153, n. 1 Soon after the expulsion of Sâhdônâ from the Nestorian Church, and the quarrel with the monks of Bêth ʿÂbhê, Îshôʿ-yahbh found himself involved in a serious dispute with Simon the Metropolitan of Rew-Ardashîr (See Nöldeke, Geschichte der Perser, p. 19) in Persia and of the Ḳaṭrâyê, who refused obedience to him as his diocesan, and who held views which were not pleasing to him. Our knowledge of the reasons of the dispute is limited, and can only be obtained from a series of seven letters which Mâr Îshôʿ-yahbh wrote to Simon and the Bishops of Persia, and to the monks and Church of Ḳaṭar, a district on the Persian Gulf near Baḥrên. In them he argues the disputed points with considerable skill, and more than once refers to his own work Huppâkh Ḥushshâbhê ܗܘܼܦܵܟ ܚܘܼܣܵܒܹ̈ܐ (in Arabic عكس الارا B.O., iii. 1, p. 137), or Refutation of (Heretical) Opinions, and they, like the letters which he wrote concerning Sâhdônâ, are excellent examples of his epistolary compositions. The full text of these letters is given at the end of this chapter; and for a complete list of his letters see B.O., iii. 1, pp. 140–143. In addition to these works he wrote Exhortations for beginners [in the ascetic life], thought by Assemânî to have been composed while he was a monk at Bêth ʿÂbhê, and he arranged Ḥudhrâ, or service-book for the Sundays of the whole year, and drew up the offices of baptism, absolution, and consecration. See B.O., iii. 1, pp. 139-141; Wright, Syriac Literature, p. 843; and Badger, The Nestorians, vol. ii, pp. 22-23.
p. 174, n. 1 Parts of this chapter are quoted in B.O., iii. 1, pp. 139, 144.
p. 174, n. 2 Properly ʿĂnâ-n[î]-Îshôʿ. See Hoffmann, Opuscula Nestoriana, p. iv.
p. 174, n. 3 See infra, p. 189 f.

p. 174, n. 4 ʿĂnân-Îshôʿ and his brother Îshôʿ-yahbh were fellow-students at Nisibis with Îshôʿ-yahbh III., and afterwards entered the great convent on Mount Izlâ; they flourished about the year 645. See Wright, Syr. Lit., p. 843; B.O., iii. 1, p. 144, col. 1.
p. 174, n. 5 He afterwards became Bishop of Ḳârdâlîâbhadh. (See p. 177).
p. 175, n. 1 See supra, p. 39, note 3.
p. 175, n. 2 See supra, p. 129.
p. 175, n. 3 Read ܩܕܝܫܘܬܗ.
p. 175, n. 4 I.e., Mount Îzlâ.

p. 175, n. 5 See chap. 18. Narsai succeeded Bâbhai as head of the Monastery of Îzlâ after A.D. 628. See B.O., iii. 1, p. 455, col. 2. He is probably the Narsai to whom Îshôʿ-yahbh wrote Letters Nos. 29 and 50.

p. 176, n. 1 Thomas is no doubt quoting from a letter which he had at hand, but of which no copy seems to have come down to us. No. 16 of the letters written by Mâr Îshôʿ-yahbh while he was Bishop of Môṣul is addressed to the monks of the Monastery of Mount Îzlâ, and refers to the expulsion of some of the brethren. He says that he has twice written to them, and that inasmuch as he has received no answer he is afraid that what he has heard by rumour of the quarrel which had broken out among them, but which he never expected could be true, has really happened. He describes the quarrel as the work of the devil in the form of a man, and in a long exhortation advises them to remember their past glorious state, and to endeavour to bring it back again. Finally he says, Go forth after your brethren, and gather them together, and if it be necessary for you to endure suffering, shrink not from it until ye have made them dwellers together with you, and loving associates. ܘܦܘܿܩܘ ܒܬܪ ܐܚ̈ܝܟܘܢ ܘܟܲܢܫܘ ܐܢܘܢ. ܘܐܢ ܐܠܨܐ ܠܡܚܫ ܚܠܦܝܗܘܢ ܠܐ ܬܬܟܠܘܢ. ܥܕܡܐ ܕܬܥܒܕܘܢ ܐܢܘܢ ܠܟܘܢ ܒܢ̈ܝ ܡܥܡܪܐ ܘܫܘ̈ܬܦܐ ܕܚܘܒܐ (fol 17a.). It is probable that ʿĂnân-Îshôʿ and his brother left the Monastery of Îzlâ on account of the disturbance referred to in the above letter.

p. 176, n. 2 The chief town of Adiabene, situated about 70 miles east of Môṣul. Of Arbêl, Arbîl, or Irbil, إِرْبل (Yâḳût, t. 1, p. 186 ff.) Bar-Bahlûl says ܐܲܪܒܸܝܠ ܡܢ ܚܕܝܒ ܐܘ̇ ܐܝܟ ܚܕܝܒ قرية ببلاد حزّة تُنسن اليها مطرنة الموصل ܚܕܬܐ ܘܐܬܘܪ ܘܡܘܨܠ܀ . Duval, Syr. Lex., col. 280. The site is a very old one, and is mentioned in the cuneiform inscriptions. See Schrader, Keilinschriften und das Alte Testament, p. 441.

p. 177, n. 1 The librum horarum Canonicarum of Assemânî, B.O., iii. 1, p. 145, col. 1. For the regulations made by Îshôʿ-yahbh for times of prayer, etc., see B.O., iii. 1, pp. 139, 305, and especially p. 526.
p. 177, n. 2 Compare p. 88, line 3 (text) where Thomas says I am consumed with love for him, i.e., ʿĂnân-Îshôʿ. Strike out note 2.
p. 177, n. 3 In note 3 read ܐܝܬ ܠܗ. Assemânî has ܕܥܠܘܗܝ (B.O., iii, p. 139, col. 2).
p. 177, n. 4 ܩܝܵܡܘܼܬ ܩܵܠܵܐ.

p. 177, n. 5 Ḳârdâlîâbhâdh, كاردارى آباذ is the old name of Shennâ dhĕ Bêth Râmmân, or Sinn Bârimma, سنُّ بارَّما which was situated at a distance of ten farsaḥ from Tekrît, تكريت, on the east bank of the Tigris, below the spot where the Lower Zâb flows into the Tigris. See Hoffmann, Auszüge, pp. 189, 253. وبارمَّا ايضا قوية فى دجلة الموصل واليها نسب السُّن فيقال سِنُّ بَارِمَّا Yâḳût, t. 1, p. 464, ll. 20–22. According to B.M. Rich 7203, fol. 161 b, col. 1, and B. M. Orient. 2441, fol. 346 b, col. 2, ܩܲܪܕܝܠܒܵܐ also = مدينة السن. Hoffmann suggests that Ḳârdâlîâbhâdh = Ḳârdîn-âbâd (cf. Rûbîl for Reuben), i.e., Ḳârdîn's colony. Cf. Yazdîn-âbâd (text, p. 234. 19, 386. 16).
p. 178, n. 1 Read ܕܡܕܡ.
p. 178, n. 2 Read ܡܸܢܵܗ̇.
p. 178, n. 3 Read ܕܐ ܓܪܬܐ.

p. 178, n. 4 Compare the entry in ʿAbhd-Îshôʿ's Catalogue (B.O., iii. 1, p. 144) ܥܢܢܝܫܘܥ ܣܡ ܫܘܚܠܦܐ ܘܦܘܪܫܐ ܕܩܪܝܬܐ. Assemânî refers to an Exposition of obscure passages from the Book of Paradise, in which unfortunately the name of the author is not given, but says an hujus Ananjesu sint, non ausim definire (B.O., iii. 1, p. 146, col. 2, at the foot). The famous Book of Paradise redacted by ʿĂnân-Îshôʿ is described by Thomas in chapter 15 of this book; see p. 189 f. His work entitled Liber Canonorum de Aequilitteris, i.e., on the different pronunciation and signification of words that are spelt with the same letters, has been published, with the additions of Honain ibn-Isḥâḳ of al-Ḥîrah, (died in 873) and another compiler, by Hoffmann, Opuscula Nestoriana, pp. 2–49.
p. 178, n. 5 In this work he followed in the footsteps of Joseph Hûzâyâ, and anticipated Jacob of Edessa and the monks of Ḳarḳaph˘thâ. Wright, Syr. Lit., p. 843, col. 1.
p. 179, n. 1 We must read here ܕܟܬܒ̈ܐ ܕܐܒܗ̈ܬܐ ܒܦܘܪܫ ܚܫܚ̈ܬܐ ܕܐܝܬ ܒܒܝܬ ܐܪܟ̈ܐ. See Hoffmann, Opuscula Nestoriana, p. V.
p. 179, n. 2 Read ܡܢ ܚܝ̈ܐ ܕܙܒܢܐ.
p. 179, n. 3 Strike out ܡ̣ܢ after ܡܪܝ.
p. 179, n. 4 This chapter is quoted in B.O., iii. 1, p. 149 f.

p. 179, n. 5 George, the disciple of Îshôʿ-yahbh, was first Bishop of Môṣul, then Metropolitan of Adiabene, and finally Patriarch of the Nestorians; he succeeded his friend Îshôʿ-yahbh A.D. 661 and sat until 680. He wrote ܬܫܒܚ̈ܬܐ ܘܥܘܢ̈ܝܬܐ ܘܟܥ̈ܘܙܘܬܐ ܘܒܥܘ̈ܬܐ ܘܡܐܡܪ̈ܐ ܩܠܝܠ ܘܩܢܘ̈ܢܐ. See B.O., iii. 1, pp. 153, 708.
p. 179, n. 6 ܟܲܦܪܵܐ = كفرى, a place on the naphtha mountains between Tûz Ḥurmatli and the Diyâla river. See Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 277.

p. 179, n. 7 ܪܘܼܣܬܵܩܵܐ, a tract of land, Pers. رُسْتَاق, plur. رَسَاتِيقُ, Arab. رُزْدَاق, plur. رُزْدَاقَات, or رَزَادِيق. This word is compared with the Pehlevi רוסטאק by J. Müller; see Lagarde, Gesammelte Abhandlungen, 1866, p. 81.
p. 179, n. 8 Read ܕܒܐܬܪܐ.
p. 180, n. 1 See Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 227 and note 675 (p. 74). Tellâ dhĕ Zâllê and Bêth Ḥabbâ must have been situated very near Bêth ʿÂbhê.

p. 180, n. 2 Nectarius, the senator, a native of Tarsus, was made Bishop of Constantinople by Theodosius; he died about A.D. 397. Thomas of Margâ probably means either Basil the Great or Gregory Nazianzen. Socrates says (Hist. Eccles., iv. 23) that Evagrius was ordained at Constantinople by Gregory Nazianzen, and Sozomen relates (Hist. Eccles., vi. 30) that when Gregory occupied the see of Constantinople, he made Evagrius his archdeacon. See also B.O., iii. 1, pp. 45, 151.
p. 181, n. 1 Evagrius of Pontus born about A.D. 345, died 399.
p. 181, n. 2 I.e., Ḥazzâ or Irbîl, Arbela.
p. 181, n. 3 He claims that in the East (i.e., Persia) more than twenty bishops and two Metropolitans had been ordained by the Church of God; see supra, p. 172, l. 21.
p. 181, n. 4 In his first letter to the monks of Ḳaṭar Îshôʿ-yahbh praises the virtues of this George. See p. 168, l. 28.

p. 181, n. 5 ܦܪܵܬ ܕܡܲܝܫܵܢ, فرات ميسان, i.e., the Euphrates of Maishân, a town on the Shatt al-ʿArab opposite to the modern town of al-Baṣra, البصرة, and including Moḥammera. Baṣra is about 65 miles above the mouth of the Shatt al-ʿArab, and 40 miles below the junction of the Tigris and Euphrates (Shatt al-ʿArab). Moḥammera is ten miles from Baṣra. Maishân was the name given to the district which extended from Ctesiphon and Seleucia to the Persian Gulf.
p. 181, n. 6 See B.O., iii. 1, p. 152, col. 1.

p. 182, n. 1 All the MSS have ܓܝܼܘܪܓܝܼܣ ܐܚܪ̈ܢܐ, but ܐܚܪ̈ܢܐ must be corrupt. We might read ܐܚܪܵ̈ܝܹܐ (compare ܐܚܪܢܐ for ܐܚܪܝܐ in Hist. of Alexander, ed. Budge, p. 1, l. 10) and translate these last [two] Georges, or ܚܐܒ̈ܐ ܦܪ̈ܣܝܐ, Persian noblemen, or ܒܢ̈ܝ ܚܐܪ̈ܐ ܦܪ̈ܣܝܐ or sons of Persian noblemen.

p. 182, n. 2 ܫܘܼܦܲܪ̈ܕܝܼܩܹܐ flatterers, deceivers. In B.M. Orient. 2441, fol. 370b, col. 1, and Rich 7203, fol. 179b, col. 2, we have ܫܘܼܦܲܪܕܝܼܩܐ ܒܨ مراي مملّق خداعين ܘܐܝܟ ܒܪ ܣܪܘ ܡܪ̈ܡܝܢܐ ܐܘ ܫܦܘܪ̈ܬܢܐ المتحسّنين الخداعين الملقين܀ ܫܘܵܦܲܕܝܼܩܘܼܬܐ التملّق ممخرق܀ ܫܘܼܦܲܪܕܝܼܩܵܢܘܼܬܵܐ ܐܝܟ ܒܪ ܣܪܘ المراياه التحسّن المحاباه الممخرق܀.
p. 182, n. 3 Assemânî seductus à quibusdam adulatoribus aientibus. (B.O., iii. 1, p. 152, col. 1.)
p. 183, n. 1 I.e., Ctesiphon and Seleucia. See B.O., 1, pp. 354, 356; and Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 352, note 1997. On p. 84, l. 1 (text), ܡܚܘܙ̈ܐ takes the place of ܡܕܝܢ̈ܬܐ.
p. 183, n. 2 This chapter is quoted in B.O., iii. 1, p. 150, col. 1 ff.
p. 183, n. 3 Read ܬܪܥܝܬܗ.
p. 184, n. 1 St. Matthew xx. 26, 27.
p. 184, n. 2 The Holy Communion.
p. 185, n. 1 Ctesiphon and Seleucia.
p. 185, n. 2 We should perhaps add the word ܕܝܵܬܹܩܹ̈ܐ here. See p. 82. l. 13.
p. 185, n. 3 Genesis xlvi. 29.
p. 185, n. 4 I.e., Nisibis.
p. 186, n. 1 Numbers xvi. 1–35. George means Nay, we think rather that when thou didst find that we were humble thou didst wish etc.
p. 186, n. 2 Strike out ܟܕ.
p. 186, n. 3 Read ܘܐܠܗܐ.

p. 186, n. 4 See also chaps. 16 and 29. Mâr Athḳen was originally a monk at Mount Îzlâ, but he ended his days in the Monastery of Mâr Aphnî-Mâran. Besides the Ecclesiastical Histories here mentioned he wrote a Disputation [addressed to] a wise brother, several letters, a Treatise on the monastic life, etc. See B.O., iii. 1, p. 217.
p. 186, n. 5 Parts of this chapter are quoted in B.O., iii. 1, pp. 145, 150.
p. 187, n. 1 St. John xvi. 33.
p. 187, n. 2 St. John xv. 20.
p. 187, n. 3 See supra, p. 181.

p. 187, n. 4 ABC have ܥܵܩܘܿܠܹܐ, and Vat. has ܩܵܩܘ̈ܠܹܐ, which Assemânî (B.O., iii, 1, p. 150, col. 2) transcribes ܥܴܩܽܘ̈ܠܷܐ. Hoffmann would read ܥܵܩܘܿܠܵܐ. The town ܥܩܘܠܐ, العاقول, is ܟܽܘܦܷܗ, الكُوفَةُ, al-Kûfâ, a city about thirty five miles south of Babylon, ten east of Meshed ʿAlî, and twenty-four from the Euphrates. See Yâḳût iii, pp. 322–326.
p. 188, n. 1 See supra, p. 102, note 7.
p. 188, n. 2 The inhabitants of Ḳaṭar قَطَر on the east coast of Arabia, along the Persian Gulf, opposite Baḥrên. See Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 114 f. We should probably read ܒܹܝܬ ܩܲܛܪ̈ܵܝܹܐ.
p. 188, n. 3 See the letters of Mâr Îshôʿ-yahbh on pp. 154–174.

p. 188, n. 4 Read ܕܪܝܘ ܐܪܕܫܝܪ Rêw-Ardashîr, or Rêv-Ardeshêr, later Rêshahr. This town was situated on the river Tâb, on the frontier between Pêrsistân, and Khûzistân, and is to be distinguished from Rîshahr, near Abûshehr (Bushire) on the Persian Gulf. The residence of the Archbishop of Persia was at Rew-Ardashîr. See Nöldeke, Geschichte der Perser, p. 19, note 4.
p. 188, n. 5 A place on the chief island of Baḥrên in the Persian Gulf. It is the دَارَيْن of Yâḳût, ii, p. 537. See also Nöldeke, Geschichte der Perser, p. 57, note 2.
p. 189, n. 2 This chapter is quoted in B.O., iii. 1, p. 145.
p. 189, n. 3 See Wright, Syr. Lit., p. 843, note 19.
p. 189, n. 4 Read ܒܲܕܒܲܪ ܙܲܒܢܵܐ.
p. 189, n. 5 Literally sons of oil. Assemânî has ܟܘܼܗܵܢܵܐ (col. 2, l. 37).
p. 189, n. 6 I.e., the service book for the whole year.
p. 189, n. 7 This refers to the words, And he entreated the wise and holy father, etc.

p. 190, n. 1 Reading, with Hoffmann, ܘܚܡܫܬܥܣܪ ܒܐܪ̈ܒܥܝܢ i.e., 15×40. Assemânî has Divisit autem universum opus in sexcenta et quindecim capitula, quatuordecim canonibus et distinctionibus comprehensa. (B.O., iii. 1, p. 146, col. 2).
p. 190, n. 2 Read ܡܫܲܐܠ asking.
p. 190, n. 3 Read with Vat. ܕܢܣܝܡ.
p. 190, n. 4 ܡܵܠܲܓܡܵܐ = μάλαγμα.

p. 190, n. 5 The book contained then six hundred chapters on specific points, divided into fifteen books of forty sections each, four hundred and thirty chapters on general matters, and a large number of chapters on miscellaneous subjects.
p. 190, n. 6 Born at Antioch, A.D. 347, died 407.

p. 191, n. 1 This Discourse or Encomium is extant in Syriac in Brit. Mus. MS. Add. 17,174 (Wright, Catalogue, p. 1075, col. 2). The title reads ܩܘܠܣܐ ܕܕܝܪ̈ܝܐ ܕܡܨܪ̈ܝܢ ܡܢ ܡܐܡܪܐ ܕܬܡܢܝܐ ܕܦܘܫܩܐ ܕܡܬܝ ܐܘܢܓܠܝܣܛܐ. ܕܥܒܝܕ ܠܡܪܝ ܝܘܐܢܝܣ ܐܦܝܣܩܘܦܐ ܕܩܘܣܛܢܛܝܢܘܦܘܠܝܣ.

p. 191, n. 2 Abraham is always called ܢܸܬܦܪܵܝܵܐ, or ܢܲܬܦܪܵܝܵܐ by the Nestorians (see B.O., iii. 1, p. 191, note 1), and ܢܷܦܬܱܪܴܝܳܐ by the Monophysites (see B.O., 1, p. 463, note 1; Wright, Catalogue, p. 774, col. 1). The Nestorians derive the word from the district called ܢܸܦܲܪ, نِفّر, in the province of Kashkâr (ܢܬܦܪܝܐ ܟܘܢܝܐ ܕܡܢ ܢܸܦܪ ܐܝܟ ܕܡܫܠܡܝܢ, Payne Smith, Thes., col. 2430), but Hoffmann is inclined to refer it to Νέφθαρ, 2 Maccabees i. 36, where there was a place of sacred fire, although he thinks it quite possible that Niffer was really the birthplace of Abraham, and that he may have identified his town with Nephthar, through a mystic fancy. According to ʿAbhd-Îshôʿ he wrote various compositions, and a work on the monastic life. See B.O., iii. 1, p. 191, and 1, pp. 463, 464; Wright, Catalogue Syr. MSS., p. 1075b.

p. 191, n. 3 Palladius the great friend of Chrysostom was born about A.D. 367. He embraced the ascetic life about 387, was made Bishop of Hellenopolis after 391, and took refuge in Rome from the persecution in 405. He visited several places in Palestine, and travelled in Egypt from Alexandria to Aswân in search of material for his history of the Egyptian ascetics, and was the friend of a large number of the most famous of them. The Paradise or Lausiac History of Palladius is thought to have been composed between the years 414 and 420. See Tillemont, Mémoires, viii, pp. 272, 359; Cotelerius, Monumenta, iii, 563; Assemânî, B.O., iii. 1, p. 49, note 1.

p. 191, n. 4 He died A.D. 420. According to the Catalogue of ʿAbhd-Îshôʿ (B.O., iii. 1, p. 49) Palladius and Jerome ܐܟܬܒܘ ܟܬܒܐ ܕܦܪܕܝܣܐ ܘܡܡܠܠܐ ܕܣܒ̈ܐ ܥܡ ܡܠ̈ܟܐ ܕܒܬܠܬ ܦܢܩ̈ܝܬܐ ܚܪܝܙܝܢ. See B.O., 1, pp. 568, 608.

p. 192, n. 1 The Paradise of Palladius contained the lives of the western ascetics, and the Paradise of Joseph Ḥûzâyâ contained the lives of the eastern ascetics (B.O., iii. 1, p. 102, col. 2); both are to be distinguished from the Paradise of Eden by ʿAbhd-Îshôʿ, Metropolitan of Nisibis, (B.O., iii. 1, p. 325), and the Little Paradise by David, Bishop of Kartaw. See infra Bk. II. chap. 24. For the account of the Syriac version of the Paradise of Palladius and Saint Jerome, and the Questions of Abraham of Nephthar, which is believed to be the redaction made by ʿĂnân-Îshôʿ see pp. 192–206. A portion of this same version appears to be preserved in Brit. Mus. Add. 17,263 (Wright, Catalogue, p. 1079, No. DCCCCXXXI); but Add. 17,264 (Wright, Catalogue, p. 1078, No. DCCCCXXX) is probably the work of Gabriel of Ḳaṭar. See Wright, Syr. Lit., p. 843, note 19.
p. 207, n. 1 This chapter is quoted in B.O., iii. 1, p. 151, coll. 1. 2.

p. 207, n. 2 The text here appears to be corrupt, but I give what I believe Thomas meant to say. Hoffmann would emend the first four lines of the chapter thus: ܐܲܝܟ ܡܵܐ ܕܝܸܠܦܹܬ ܡ̣ܢ ܬܫ̈ܥ̱ܝܵܬܵܐ ܥܹܕܬܵܢܵܝ̈ܬܵܐ ܟܠܗܹܝܢ ܕܗܵܪܟܵܐ ܟܬܝܼ̈ܒܵܢ܆ ܡܸܢܗܹܝܢ ܡ̇ܢ ܡ̣ܢ ܟܬܵܒܹ̈ܐ܆ ܡܸܢܗܹܝܢ ܕܝܢ ܡ̣ܢ ܝܘܼܒܵܠ ܡܸܠܬܵܐ ܘܬܘܼܢܵܝܵܐ ܐܸܫܟܚܹܬ ܕܝܢ ܐܵܦ ܒܐܸܩܠܹܣܵܣ̈ܛܝܼܩܹܐ ܕܲܡܝܲܬܪܐ ܡܵܪܝ ܐܲܬܩܸܢ ܕܲܟܬܝܼܒ ܒܵܗ̇ ܥܠܵܘܗܝ ܥܲܠ ܡܵܪܝ ܓܝܼܘܵܪܓܝܼܣ ܩܵܬܘܿܠܝܼܩܵܐ. Assemânî reads Sicut didici ex Ecclesiasticis historiis circa ea omnia, quae hic scribuntur, et alia quidem ex codicibus, alia vero ex traditione, et historia Ecclesiastica excellentis Mar Atken, hoc praeterea in historia de eodem Mar Georgis Catholico scriptum reperio. (B.O., iii. 1, p. 153.)

p. 207, n. 3 Mâr Athḳên is in error here. George succeeded Îshôʿ-yahbh A.D. 661 and sat till 680, but Ḥasan ibn-ʿAli began to reign A.H. 40 and died A.H. 49, when he was succeeded by his younger brother Ḥusên حُسَين, who died A.H. 61, or about twenty-one years after Ḥasan began to reign. See Wright, Syr. Lit., p. 843; Assemânî, B.O., iii. 1, p. 153, col. 2; Annales quos scripsit Aṭ-Ṭabarî, ed. de Goeje, ser. II, t. 1, pp. 1, 366; Ibn-el-Athiri, Chronicon, ed. Tornberg, t. iii. (A. H. 60–95), Leyden, 1876, p. 383 ff.
p. 208, n. 1 Hoffmann would strike out ܕܥܣܪܝܢ ܘܬܪ̈ܬܝܢ.
p. 208, n. 2 A town, the ruins of which lie a little to the south-east of the modern town of Meshed ʿAlî. See Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 97.

p. 208, n. 3 Mâr Abhâ was originally a Magian. He was baptized at Ḥêrthâ and he studied at Nisibis and Edessa. He was elected Patriarch A.D. 536, and shortly after began to teach at Seleucia. Owing to a dispute with Khusrau I. Anôshârwân (531–579) he was banished to Âdhôrbâigân, but he returned to Seleucia where he was thrown into prison by the king, and died A.D. 552. His body was carried to Ḥêrthâ and buried, and the Nestorians style him Mâr Abhâ the Martyr. For a list of his works see B.O., iii. 1, pp. 75–81. See also Bar-Hebraeus, Chron. Eccles., ii. 89–95 and Wright, Syr. Lit., p. 836, col. 2.

p. 208, n. 4 In pentasyllabic tripartite metre. The extract ends abruptly. Hoffmann emends thus:— ܐܝܬܝܐ ܕܡܢ ܥܠܡ | ܗ̇ܘ ܕܡܬܘܡܐܝܬ | ܐܵܦ ܛܵܒܐ ܐܝܬܘܗܝ | ܐܵܦ ܡܢ ܛܵܒܘܬܗ | ܠܐ ܡܬܘܿܡ ܡܫܬܲܚܠܦ | ܘܲܐܝܟܢ ܫܘܚ̈ܠܵܦܹܐ. Assemânî, considering ܘܐܝܟܢ ܫܘܚ̈ܠܦܐ to be no part of the metrical composition, translates, Quot in ea suavium Cantuum mutationes cernere est, et quot pulcherrimo ordine succedentes sibi strophas et modos!

p. 220, n. 3 Arab. ديلم, a region to the south-west of the Caspian Sea, having Adhôrbâîgân on the west, Ḳazwîn on the south, and Ṭabaristân on the east. With Dêlûm, Gîlân (older form Gêlân) is often mentioned. Dêlûm represents the steep mountainous tract of country, covered with woods and abounding with streams of water, which is opposite Ṭabaristân, while Gîlân جيلان or كيلان is the flat, fertile plains at the foot of the mountains. قال ابن حوقل وبلاد الديلم سهل وجبل فلسهل يسمّى الجيل والسهل هو ساحل على بحر الخزر تحت جبال الديلم See Géographie d'Aboulféda, ed. De Slane, p. 426. The half-savage inhabitants of Dêlûm served as mercenaries in the armies of the Sassanide kings, and some of them were, as we learn from the following extract from Yâḳût (ii, p. 711), settled near Shahruzûr. دَيلَمِسْتَان قرية قرب شهرزور بينهما ىسعة فراسَغ كان الديلم فى ايام الاكاسرة اذا خرجوا للغارة عسكروا بها وخلّفوا سَوَادَهم اَدَيْها وانتشروا فى الارض غايبين فاذا فرغوا من غاراتهم عادوا اليها ورجلوا الى مُسْتَقَرّهم For the chief towns of Dêlûm see De Slane, op. cit., p. 428 f.; for references to the people of Dêlûm as mercenaries see Nöldeke, Geschichte der Perser, p. 479, note 1; and compare Hoffmann, Auszüge, note 1640; and B.O., iii. ii, p. DCCXL f.

He wrote the Solution of the Ḳurʾân, ܫܪܝܐ ܕܩܘܪܐܢ, a Disputation against heretics, and other excellent works, among which was, probably, the History of John of Dêlûm. See B.O., iii. 1, p. 212.

It may have been the Bar-ʿIdtâ who lived in the time of Îshôʿ-yahbh of Arzon (580–595), and who was the contemporary of Jacob the founder of the Monastery of Bêth ʿAbhê; he is often quoted by Thomas of Margâ. See supra, p. 38, note 2. The day of his commemoration was the same as that of Jacob of Bêth ʿAbhê. See Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 181. Cf. also بخازِرَ إِلَى جَنْبِ قَرْيَة يقَال لها باربيثا [بارْعيتَا] بينها وبين مدينة المَوْصِل خمسة فر اسغ Ṭabarî ii, p. 707.

Yâḳût ii. p. 349, l. 18 فدًى لبنى بن شيبان ناقتى. See also Brit. Mus. MS. 23,355, fol. 241 a (Kitâb al-Ansâb, by al-Samʿânî).
p. 231, n. 4 Read ܕܙܲܪ̈ܥܵܬܹܗ.

p. 232, n. 3 The Syriac word ܡܘܿܝܠܵܐ = موْئل or مَوْأَلَة refuge, place of safety. See Kâmûs, Bûlâḳ edition, A.H. 1303, vol. 4, p. 62. It = ܒܝܬ ܨܘܒܐ, or ܒܝܬ ܓܘܣܐ, cf. Neo-Syriac ܡܘܼܠܵܐ barn, granary, Payne Smith, Thes., col. 2036. In Ibn Haukal we have بَيْتُ مُواءَلَةٍ, (which Hoffmann corrects into بَيْت مُوأَلَةٍ) and concerning which De Goeje says proprie domus refugii adhibetur sensu domus spectabilis, but Dozy asks ne serait-ce pas plutôt maison fortifée? See Supplément aux Dictionnaires Arabes, t. 11, p. 777, col. 1; De Goeje, Bibliotheca Geographicorum Arabicorum, Pars secunda, Viae et Regna Descriptio Ditionis Moslemicae Auctore Abùl-Kâsim ibn Haukal, p. 81, line 8, and pars 4, p. 372. For ܒܹܝܬ ܡܘܼ̈ܝܵܠܹܐ Mill-house, see Thomas of Margâ (text) p. 238, l. 11.
p. 232, n. 4 Read ܕܡܲܠܟܐ.
p. 232, n. 5 Read either ܝܵܬܒܹܝܢ, or ܝܲܬܝܼܒܹܝܢ.

p. 232, n. 6 I know of no other word by which to render ܡܘܿܝܠܵܐ, which meant a place where cattle, horses, asses, camels, etc., could be placed in safety for the night, or in time of war (compare the Border peel-towers). Ayâs's building was no doubt a private khân, the like of which exist in great numbers in the east at the present day. They are built in the form of a quadrangle, and have usually one large, strong door which is strengthened with heavy bars of wood, and fastened by massive bolts. On each side of the doorway are rooms for the accommodation of travellers, and along each of the walls are several stalls or chambers, usually open in the front, where the beasts are fed and sheltered. In the centre of the courtyard the camels are unloaded and their burdens piled up for the night. Such khâns usually have a supply of water either in a well in the courtyard, or close at hand outside. They are more expensive to stay at than the large public khâns, many of which have been built for the poor by rich men, and endowed with funds to pay for keeping them clean.
p. 233, n. 1 I.e., the monastery of Rabban bar-ʿIdtâ.
p. 233, n. 2 Acts xii. 1.

p. 233, n. 4 See supra, p. 61, note 4.

p. 233, n. 5 Âwânâ, which marked the limit of the church province of Bêth Nuhâdhrâ, lay on the east bank of the Tigris, a little above Môṣul, and nearly opposite to Eski-Môṣul. According to Yâḳût the Monastery of Abbâ Yâwseph lay on the caravan road near the Tigris about one farsaḥ from Bâlâdh. See the maps in Černik, Technische Studien-Expedition durch die Gebiete des Euphrat und Tigris, (in Ergänzungsheft No. 45 zu Petermann's Geographischen Mittheilungen, Gotha, 1876); and Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 212.

p. 236, n. 2 Bêth Bĕghâsh, Bêth Bâghêsh, or Bêth Bâghâsh, the بابغيش or باعاش of the Arabs, was a district which lay on the Upper Zâb between Adhôrbâîgân and Ardabîl [read Dabîl] along which the Great Zâb flows. In the eighth century of our era the seat of the Bishop of Bĕghâsh was in the Church of Bai [see infra chap. xxxix (text p. 125, l. 3)], probably Ḳalʿa-i-Bai, the residence of Melik Beg, one of the first Kurdish princes of the Sambo dynasty, who with the help of the Syrian Christians in the fortress of Dîz obtained the rule over the Ḥakkârî region. See Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 227. The name Bêth Bĕghâsh is preserved in Basch Ḳalʿe; see Hoffmann in Feige, Die Geschichte des Mâr ʿAbhd-Îshôʿ, Kiel, 1890, p. 10, no. 10, (text p. 26, l. 14, translation p. 25, at the foot). Cf. بابغيش ناحية بين اذربيجان واردبيل يمرُّ بها الزابُ الأَعلَى Yaḳût, vol. 1, p. 446.
p. 237, n. 1 See supra, p. 228.
p. 238, n. 1 ܦܪ̈ܲܩܛܹܐ = φράκτης. See Du Cange, Glossarium, col. 1702.
p. 238, n. 2 The last two sentences of this chapter are quoted in B.O., iii. 1, p. 478, col. 2.

p. 238, n. 3 He flourished about A.D. 720, and seems to have been the first Bishop of Maʿallthâ; see Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 210, note 1666 and the authorities quoted there. He was succeeded by Mâr Sergius, a monk of Bêth ʿAbhê, who was consecrated by Mâr Aḥà; see infra, Bk. II. chap. xlii.

p. 238, n. 4 ܡܲܥܲܠܬܲܝܵܐ، ܡܲܥܲܠܬܵܐ or ܡܲܥܲܠܬܲܐܝܵܐ, Arab. معلثايا, was one of the twelve dioceses under the Maphrian of Tekrît; see Bar-Hebraeus, Chron. Eccles., ii, col. 123. It is often mentioned together with Ḥĕnâithâ, and was situated about one hour to the west of Dehôk, a place about thirty-five or forty miles north of Môṣul. See Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 208; B.O., iii. ii, p. dcclx; and Le Quien, Oriens Christianus, ii. 1584 f. According to Badger, (Nestorians, vol. 1, p. 174) Maʿallthâ contained twenty families and one church in 1842–44. Yâḳût (iv, p. 578, l. 4) makes معلثايا near Gezîret ibn-ʿOmar.

p. 239, n. 1 Written ܚܵܢܝܼܬܵܐ, and ܚܢܵܝܼܬܵܐ, the latter vocalization being the correct one. Ḥnâithâ = the Χναιθα of Theophylact (V. 8. ed. Bonn p. 219, l. 9) and Χαμαιθα of Theophanes; its district seems to have reached from the valley at the mouth of the Rowandiz tributary of the Upper Zâb to Dâûdîjâ in the western valley of the Ṣapna. The modern diocese of ʿAmêdîa corresponds tolerably well to the old church province of Maʿallthâ, Beth Nûhâdhrâ and Ḥĕnâithâ. See Hoffmann, Auszüge, pp. 216–222; and the list of the villages in the ʿAmêdîa diocese in Badger, Nestorians, vol. 1, p. 174; and B.O., iii. ii, p. dcclvii.
p. 239, n. 2 See infra, chap. XLII.
p. 239, n. 3 See Book VI. chap. XV. (text p. 384).
p. 240, n. 1 See supra, p. 183, note 1.
p. 240, n. 2 Read ܕܫܒܥܐ.

p. 240, n. 3 A pure Persian, or Kurdish name. Kahnê or Kahnî = Kurdish خانى fountain, and Gàr calls to mind the al-Gàr mountain الجار discussed by Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 204, note 1618; see also note 2161 where a certain جار خانى pitch fountain is mentioned. Gâr Kahnê was probably situated near Bêth ʿÂbhê.
p. 240, n. 4 See B.O., iii. 1, p. 187, col. 2, at the foot.

p. 240, n. 5 The church province of Salakh ܐܬܪܐ ܕܣܠܟ was divided into Outer Salakh ܣܠܟ ܒܪܝܬܐ and Inner Salakh ܣܠܟ ܓܘܝܬܐ. Outer Salakh represented the country round about Arbêl, and Inner Salakh lay on the border of Adhôrbâîgân. We must look for this province in the territory of the Bâlik-Kurds. See Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 243–245.
p. 241, n. 1 Assemânî gives ܒܱܢܱܢܱܣ B.O., iii. 1, p. 479, col. 1.
p. 241, n. 2 I.e., Farrukhbhindâdh. See Hoffmann, Auszüge, pp. 289, 297. We should probably correct the Syriac thus: ܠܦܲܪܘܼܟܒܢܕܵܕ.

p. 241, n. 3 Phransê can hardly be the Syriac form of Francis. The name is probably wrongly vowelled, and perhaps stands for Farr + Narsê ܦܪܢ[ܪ]ܣܐ; cf. Mihr-Narsê, Âdhur-Narsê. Hoffmann. A Rabban Fransé is mentioned together with other holy men in the order for the burial of the priests given by Badger, Nestorians, vol. 11. p. 307.
p. 241, n. 4 Read ܘܝܼܠܸܦ.
p. 242, n. 1 The first part of this sentence is quoted in B.O., iii. 1, p. 479, col. 1.
p. 242, n. 2 This is probably the village of Shîrwân, lying in the district of Shîrwân, about eighty miles to the north-east of Môṣul. See Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 220, and notes 1749 and 1762.
p. 242, n. 3 Read ܪܟܘܼܒܹܗ here and elsewhere.
p. 243, n. 1 The following story is apparently related also in Bk. VI. chap. XV. (text p. 384, l. 3 ff.).

p. 243, n. 4 Their children made a dispute about the nut trees, and took them (text. p. 384, l. 6).

p. 247, n. 7 See supra, p. 179 ff.
p. 247, n. 8 ܚܸܪܝܵܫܵܐܝܼܬ, a rare word.

p. 248, n. 1 This appears to be the meaning of the text as it stands, but see the two following notes.

p. 248, n. 2 I.e., Thomas of Margâ did not correct this passage. Assemânî translates: Nullas eis (monachis suis) opes in terris reliquit: et quoniam eas possidere maluerunt, en amisere omnia. (Agros intelligit, quos eis Patres ipsorum legaverunt, Mar Jesujabus, videlicet, et Mar Gregorius Catholici.) Prosequitur monachos iterùm sugillans: Nullus illis egentior; laborem nihilominus inutilem patiuntur. (Ingressum nempe et exitum, sementem et messem.) Hunc auctor hymnum, seu Carmen, haudquaquam emendavit, et hactenus sine ulla correctione legitur. (B.O., iii. 1, p. 462, col. 1.)

p. 248, n. 3 Hoffmann would emend thus: I ܠܐ ܐܪܦܝ ܠܗܘܢ | ܡܕܡ ܒܐܪܥܐ | ܡܢ ܩܢܝ̈ܢܐ | ܠܝܼܚܝܼ̈ܕܝܐ | ܕܩܢܘ ܗܢܘܢ | ܗܐ ܡܣܟܢܝܢ | [ܡܢ] ܟܠܡܕܡ | ܘܡܢ ܐܪ̈ܥܬܐ | ܕܐܘܬܪܘ ܐܢܘܢ | ܐܒܗܝܗ̈ܘܢ | ܡܪܝ ܝܫܘܥܝܗܒ | ܘܡܪܝ ܓܝܘܪܓܝܣ | ܩܬܘܠܝܩ̈ܐ II ܠܐ ܐܝܬ ܕܨܪܝܟ | ܡܢ ܟܠ ܡܕܡ | ܒܕܘܡܝܐ ܕܝܠܗܘܢ | ܘܩܢܢ ܬܥܫܐ | ܡܥܠܐ ܡܦܩܐ | ܙܪܥܐ ܚܨܕܐ | ܕܠܝܬ ܒܗ ܝܘܬܪܢ ܠܕܬܥܫ ܒܗ.
p. 248, n. 4 St. Matthew xxii. 32.
p. 249, n. 1 Exodus xx. 6.

p. 249, n. 2 We should expect to read ܕܝܫܘܥ ܡܪܢ of Jesus our Lord. On this point see Badger, Nestorians, vol. ii, p. 36. The expression Jesus our God naturally suggests a Monophysite writer. See Wright, Catalogue, p. 262, col. 2, No. 5.
p. 249, n. 3 St. Luke xiii. 29.

p. 250, n. 3 Thomas of Margâ is probably quoting some apocryphal book.
p. 250, n. 4 Compare Seth the beautiful. Book of the Bee, ed. Budge, p. 27, text p. 29, l. 9.

p. 250, n. 5 There is a reference to the marvellous beauty of Adam in the Cave of Treasures (ed. Bezold, p. 12). And God formed Adam with His holy hands, in His own image and likeness. And when these angels saw his glorious appearance, they were moved at the beauty of his form ܘܓܒܠܗ ܐܠܗܐ ܠܐܕܡ ܒܐܝܕ̈ܘܗܝ ܩܕܝܫ̈ܬܐ. ܒܨܠܡܗ ܐܝܟ ܕܡܘܬܗ. ܘܟܕ ܚܙܘ ܗܠܝܢ ܡܠܐܟ̈ܐ ܠܚܙܬܗ ܫܒܝܚܬܐ. ܐܬܬܙܝܥܘ ܡܢ ܫܘܦܪܗ̇ ܕܕܡܘܬܗ܀
p. 250, n. 6 Compare יְפֵה־תאַר וִיפֵה מַרְאֶה Genesis xxxix. 6.
p. 250, n. 7 Compare כִּי־טוֹב הוּא Exodus ii. 2.
p. 251, n. 1 Compare וְהוּא אַדְמוֹנִי עֵם־יְפֵה עֵינַיִם וְטוֹב רֹאִי 1 Samuel xvi. 12.
p. 251, n. 2 Compare מַרְאֵיהֶם טוֹב וּבְרִיאֵי בָּשָׂר Daniel i. 15.
p. 251, n. 3 Read ܕܥܲܟ.
p. 251, n. 4 Read ܣܲܟܪ.
p. 251, n. 5 See Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 223.
