p. 252, n. 2 ܡܸܬܬܚܝܼܒܵܢܐܝܼܬ, a rare word.
p. 252, n. 3 ܡܕܲܒܩܵܢܵܐ.
p. 252, n. 4 Read ܕܲܒܦܛܪܵܐ.
p. 253, n. 1 Read ܥܕ ܥܨܵܬܗ.
p. 253, n. 2 See supra, p. 236, note 2.
p. 253, n. 3 Read ܒܚܝܵܪܬܐ.
p. 254, n. 1 Read ܘܐܡܲܪܘ.

p. 254, n. 2 ܛܵܫܝܿܬܵܐ a hiding place. In Brit. Mus. MSS. Or. 2441, fol. 136b, col. 1, and Rich 7203, fol. 56b, col. 2, and in Hoffman, Syrisch-Arabische Glossen, Kiel, 1874, p. 166, No. 4365. ܛܵܫ̈ܝܵܬܐ = المختفيات.
p. 254, n. 3 Read ܕܪܕܹܗ.
p. 254, n. 4 ܐܵܪܸܡܸܢܘܿܢ = ἄρμενον.
p. 255, n. 1 Read ܕܠܲܟܢܘܼܫܝܵܐ.

p. 255, n. 2 I.e., Isaias of Scete, who was a contemporary of the two Macarii, Poemen, Sisoes, Paphnutius and many other famous ascetics who lived at the end of the IVth century of our era. See Tillemont, Mémoires Ecclés., VII. p. 194, col. 2; Cotelerius, Eccles. Graec. Monumenta, t. 1. pp. 445, 596, 801, 808; Wright, Catalogue of Syriac MSS., vol. ii. pp. 458–465; Assemânî, B.O., iii. 1, p. 46, col. 2. The Isaiah referred to and quoted so often by Palladius was the brother of Paesius, and both were the sons of a merchant who carried on business in Spain ܒܢ̈ܝ ܓܒܪܐ ܚܕ ܬܓܪܐ܆ ܕܡܬܬܓܪ ܗܘܐ ܒܐܸܣܦܲܢܝܼܵܐ; one brother gave all his wealth to the poor, and the other employed his in founding and endowing a monastery.
p. 255, n. 3 I.e., Anthony the Great. See supra, p. 30.

p. 256, n. 1 ܕܲܗ̈ܩܵܢܹܐ, more correctly ܕܗ̈ܩܵܢܵܐ. Dihḳân is the Arabic form of an earlier dahyankâna. Compare the Armenian dehkan the governor of a province. In the Ḳâmûs (ed. Bûlâḳ A.H. 1303, t. IV. p. 221) الدهْقَان is explained by زَعيمُ فَلاَّحى العَجَم ورَئيسُ الاقْلِيم مُعَرَّب Plur. دَهَاقِنَة, and دهَاقِينُ. The dihkân, then, were a class of noble landed proprietors. See Hoffmann, Auszüge, note 1900, p. 239; Nöldeke, Geschichte der Perser, p. 446 f.; Bedrossian, New English and Armenian Dict., Venice, 1875–79, p. 138, col. 1; and Lagarde, Armenische Studien, p. 43, no. 603 (in Abhandlungen der Historisch-Philologischen Classe der Königlichen Gesellschaft der Wissenschaft zu Göttingen, Band XXII.). According to Masʿûdî, Wahkert وهكرت was the first man who bore the title of dihḳân, تدهقن, and the دهاقون were divided into five classes, each of which wore its own distinctive garments. See Les Prairies d'Or, ed. Barbier de Meynard, tom. ii. p. 241. From Thomas of Margâ we learn that they paid tribute to the Shahrîghân their superiors ܫܗܪ̈ܝܓܢ ܢܣܒܝܢ ܗ̄ܘ̣ܘ ܦܠܓܘܬܐ ܕܙܪܥܐ ܘܕܚܡܪܐ܆ ܘܕܓܘ̈ܙܐ ܘܟܣܦ ܪܫܐ ܡ̣ܢ ܕܗ̈ܩܢܐ Book iii, chap. 3 (Syriac text), p. 152.
p. 257, n. 1 See supra, p. 131.
p. 257, n. 2 See supra, p. 179, note 5.
p. 257, n. 3 See supra, p. 217.

p. 257, n. 4 Reading ܢܬܪܲܫܲܢ from ܪܹܫܵܢܵܐ. Compare Lagarde, Praetermissorum, (Bar-Hebraeus on the Psalms) p. 164, l. 89; ܐܬܪܫܢ ܡܢ ܪܝܫܢܘܬܐ تراُّس Duval, Lexicon Syriacum, col. 344; Cat. Bibl. Vat., t. iii, p. 354.

p. 258, n. 1 I.e., Mâr Abhâ surnamed ܒܪ ܒܪܝܟ ܨܒܝܢܗ, Bar-bĕrîkh Ṣebhyâneh, from Kashkâr. He was the second Nestorian patriarch of that name and succeeded Phethion A.D. 740; he died A.D. 750 aged one hundred and ten years, and was buried in Seleucia. He was a learned man, and skilled in the knowledge of ecclesiastical works, and he is said to have passed all his time in reading books, ܘܟܠܗ ܙܒܢܗ ܒܩܪܝܢܐ ܕܟܬܒ̈ܐ ܫܓܝܡ ܗܘܐ. See Bar-Hebraeus, Chron. Eccles., ii. col. 153. According to ʿAbhd-Îshôʿ he wrote a Book on Generals, and Commentaries and Interpretations full of learning ܟܬܒܐ ܕܐܣܛܪܛܝ̈ܛܐ ܘܢܘܗܪ̈ܐ ܥܡ ܬܘܪ̈ܓܡܐ ܡܠܝ̈ܝ ܣܘܟܠܐ ܛܟܣ. See B.O., iii. 1, p. 158 f.

p. 258, n. 2 ܟܸܠܝܵܢܵܐ = κωλύσις = ἀφορισμός = ἀκοινωνησία. See Hoffmann, Verhandlungen der Kirchenversammlung zu Ephesus am XXII. August CDXLIX aus einer Syrischen Handschrift, p. 92, note 146, p. 97, note 263, (in Schriften der Universität zu Kiel, Band XX, published by the Academia Christiana Albertina of Kiel).
p. 258, n. 3 ܟܝܼܪܝܼܛܘܿܢܝܼܵܐ = χειροτονία = ܣܝܵܡ ܐܝܼܕܵܐ
p. 258, n. 4 See Hoffmann, Auszüge, pp. 182, 210 ff.
p. 259, n. 1 Psalm lxxxiv. 7.

p. 259, n. 2 I.e., of Môṣul, (المَوْصِل, the place where two things join or meet) the town on the left bank of the Tigris opposite to the mound called Kouyunjik, which marks part of the site of ancient Nineveh. الموصل قاعدة ديار الجزيرة وهى على دجلة فى جانبها الغربى وقبالة الموصل من البرّ الآخر, الشرقى مدينة نينوى Géographie d'Aboulféda ed. Reinaud and Mac Guckin de Slane, p. 285. See also Yâḳût iv, p. 682 f. An interesting account of this town is given by Ibn-Baṭûṭah (ed. Defrémery and Sanguinetti ii. p. 134 f.), and for modern writers on Môṣul and its district see Rich, Narrative of a Residence in Koordistan, and on the site of ancient Nineveh, vol. ii, p. 29 ff.; Felix Jones, Notes on the Topography of Nineveh, in Selections from the Records of the Bombay Government, No. XLIII. New Series, p. 404 ff.; Sandreczki, Reise nach Mosul, Zweiter Theil Stuttgart, 1857; Sachau, Reise in Syrien und Mesopotamien, p. 341 ff.; Černik, Technische Studien-Expedition durch die Gebiete des Euphrat und Tigris, [forming nos. 44, 45 of Petermann's Geographischen Mittheilungen, (Ergänzungsheften)], Gotha, 1875; Layard, Nineveh and Babylon, and Fletcher, Notes from Nineveh, London, 1850.
p. 260, n. 1 ܩܪܝܼܚܬܵܐ. In Brit. Mus. MS. Rich 7203 fol. 162 b, col. 1, and Orient. 2441, fol. 348 a, col. 1, ܩܪܝܼܚܐ = ܝܕܝܼܥܵܐ, and ܩܪܝܼܚܵܐ and ܩܪܝܼܚܵܐܝܼܬ = ܢܗܝܪܐܝܬ
p. 260, n. 2 ܡܲܪ ܓܫܵܢܵܐ ܕܒܪ ܣܪܘ ܐܝܬܘܗܝ ܩܢܘܡܐ ܝܚܝܕܝܐ ܐܘ ܪܓܘܫܐ ܐܘ ܡܩܲܒܠܢܐ ܕܐܝܠܝܢ ܕܡܬܪܓܫܝܢ. Brit. Mus. MS. Orient. 2441, fol. 348 a, col. 2.
p. 261, n. 1 Read ܘܐ̄ܚܪܵܢܝܵܐܝܼܬ.
p. 261, n. 2 ܛܸܪܝܵܢܵܐ, a rare word.
p. 262, n. 1 Bishop of Rome from A.D. 432–440. See Butler, Lives of the Saints, Mar. 28; and B.O., iii. 1, p. 48.
p. 262, n. 2 See Gildemeister, Sexti Sententiarum recensiones Latinam Graecam Syriacas conjunctim exhibuit, Bonn, 1873. The Syriac text has been published by Lagarde, Analecta Syriaca, Leipzig, 1858.

p. 262, n. 3 Sapientis anima deo aptatur a deo. ψυχή σοφοῦ ἁρμόζεται πρὸς θεόν. Sapientis anima semper intuetur deum. (ἀεὶ θεὸν ὁρᾷ.) Sapientis anima semper est cum deo (σύνεστιν ἀεὶ θεῷ). See Gildemeister, Sexti Sententiarum, pp. 70, 71, Nos 416–418. In Lagarde, Analecta, p. 23, l. 30, and p. 24, ll. 1–6, the passage runs: — ܢܦܫܐ ܐܝܕܐ ܕܣܦܩ ܠܗ ܡܕܡ ܕܙܥܘܪ. ܡܝܩܪܐ ܗ̣ܝ ܠܘܬ ܐܠܗܐ. ܢܦܫܗ ܕܙܕܝܩܐ ܡܬܡܟܪܐ ܠܐܠܗܐ. ܢܦܫܗ ܕܙܕܝܩܐ ܒܟܠܫܥ ܚܙܝܐ ܠܐܠܗܐ. ܢܦܫܗ ܕܙܕܝܩܐ ܒܟܠܥܕܢ ܡܛܝܼܒܐ ܠܡܥܒܕ ܨܒܝܢܗ ܕܐܠܗܐ. ܢܦܫܗ ܕܙܕܝܩܐ ܒܟܠܙܒܢ ܥܡ ܐܠܗܐ ܥܡܪܐ. ܢܦܫܗ ܕܗ̇ܘ ܕܪܚܡ ܠܐܠܗܐ ܒܐܝܕܘ̈ܗܝ ܕܐܠܗܐ ܣܝܡܐ. ܐܘܪܚܐ ܕܡܣܩܢܗ̇ ܕܢܦܫܐ ܠܘܬ ܐܠܗܐ ܒܝܕ ܡܠܬܐ ܕܐܠܗܐ ܐܝܬܝܗ̇. ܙܕܝܩܐ ܒܟܠܙܒܢ ܠܐܠܗܐ ܢܩܝܦ ܘܚܕܐ ܒܗ ܢܦܫܗ ܕܙܕܝܩܐ ܡܬܢܣܝܐ ܡܢ ܐܠܗܐ ܒܦܓܪܐ ܡܛܘܠ ܕܬܬܝܬܪ.
p. 263, n. 1 Read ܠܐ.
p. 263, n. 2 See Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 223.

p. 263, n. 3 ܦܸܩܝܵܠܵܐ = φακεώλιον fascia qua caput involuebant olim Saraceni. See Du Cange, Gloss. Script. Med. et Inf. Graecitatis, col. 1657. ܦܸܩܝܵܠܵܐ is glossed in A by ܫܘܿܫܸܦܵܐ, a word which is explained in Brit. Mus. MS. Rich 7203, fol.(180 b, col. 2, by مِنْديل turban, the strip of cloth of which a turban is made, and شستجة head-cloth. In Orient 2441, fol. 371 b, col. 1, we have the same explanation with the addition of قِناع head-cloth, بُرْقُع veil, ܣܘܼܕܵܪܵܐ ( = ܬܟܣܝܬܐ ܗܘ ܕܪܝܫܐ = شَوْذَر, σουδάριον), and reference is made to the passage in Genesis xxxviii. 19, ܥܸܙܲܩܬܟ ܘܫܘܫܦܟ ܘܚܘܛܪܐ ܕܒܐܝܕܟ where ܫܘܫܦܟ = פְּתִילֶךָ. In the Book of Paradise ܫܘܫܦܐ = ܢܨܝܼܦܵܐ a napkin which Roman ladies wound round their heads. See the quotation in Payne Smith, Thes., col. 2442.
p. 264, n. 1 See supra, p. 236, note 2.
p. 264, n. 2 Read ܬܪ̈ܬܝܢ ܙܒܢ̈ܝܢ.
p. 265, n. 1 ܡܲܦܨܚܵܢܵܐܝܼܬ.
p. 265, n. 2 Reading with Vat. ܢܸܬܥܲܦܹܐ.
p. 265, n. 3 See Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 227, and supra, p. 236, note 2.
p. 265, n. 4 The last few lines of this chapter are quoted in B.O., iii. 1, p. 481, col. 2.
p. 265, n. 5 Chapter XXXII. see supra, p. 241.
p. 266, n. 1 The first seven lines of this chapter are quoted in B.O., iii. 1, p. 464, col. 1.
p. 266, n. 2 Read, with Vat., ܛܠܸܐ ܐ̄ܢܵܐ.

p. 266, n. 3 The words ܠܲܩܕܵܡ ܡܲܐܬܹܝܢ are corrupt, and should probably be omitted. Assemânî has ܒܫܢܬ ܡܐܬܝܢ ܘܫܒܥܣܪܐ ܠܣܝܩܘܡ ܡܠܟܘܬܐ ܕܛܝܝ̈ܐ ܕܗܠܝܢ ܘܫܪ, but some word like ܡܕܡ seems to be wanting before ܕܗܠܝܢ. The words ܠܩܕܡ ܡܐܬܝܢ may be part of a clause in which Thomas stated in years of the Christian era how long ago it was that he came to Bêth ʿÂbhê, or began to write, or we might even translate them [about] two hundred and… years ago. A.H. 217 = A.D. 832. ܣܝܼܩܘܿܡܵܐ = σήκωμα, reckoning, era. Cf. ܣܝܩܘܡ ܝܘܢ̈ܝܐ = era of Alexander, and ܣܝܩܘܡ ܡܪܢ = era of our Lord, and see the passages quoted in Payne Smith, Thes., col. 2719.
p. 267, n. 1 Compare chap. XXXII, supra, p. 240.
p. 267, n. 2 I.e., Salâkh.

p. 267, n. 3 The ܬܲܪܘܼܚܵܐ, or ܬܲܪܵܚܵܐ is the capra Caucasica described by Ainsworth in Jnl. Geogr. Soc., 11. 27, which is sculptured at Gunduk, and which I myself have seen many times near the Sinjâr mountains, and between Môṣul and Al-Ḳôsh. The Arabic form of the word is تأْرُخُ = الماعز الجبلى, and the Assyrian tu-ra-ḥu. See Hoffmann, Auszüge, note 133, p. 18; Dozy, Supplément, col. 144; and Nöldeke, Z.D.M.G., Bd. xxxiii. p. 331. Tu-ra-ḥu is the Assyrian rendering of the Accadian DA.RA. See Rawlinson, Cuneiform Inscriptions of Western Asia, i. pl. 15, col. VII, l. 6; ii. pl. 6, l. 10 c; iii. pl. 70, l. 51; v. pl. 50, l. 46 b; Strassmaier, Alphabetisches Verzeichniss, No. 9050, p. 1116; and Bruno, A Classified List, No. 2947, p. 139. Brit. Mus. MS. Orient 2441, fol. 397 b, col. 1 has (ابن اَوَى = وَاوي) ܚܝܘܬܐ ܘܐܘܝ̱ ܬܵܪܘܚܐ ܗ̄ jackal, and ܬܲܪܵܚܵܐ ܗ̄. ܬܪܘܚܐ. ܬܲܪܟܝܼܢܵܐ ܐܠܟܫܟ. In Brit. Mus. MS. Rich 7203, fol. 207 a, col. 1 ܬܲܪܟܝܼܢܵܐ = الترخين.
p. 268, n. 1 Read, with Vat., ܕܢܓܪܘ.
p. 268, n. 2 ܟܲܪܬܵܐ = الكَارَة, more correctly ܟܵܪܬܵܐ. See Hoffmann, Syrisch-Arabische Glossen, No. 4886, page 190.
p. 268, n. 3 ܬܘܼܪܣܵܝܘܿܢܐ = ܬܘܼܪܣܵܝܵܐ, = غَدَاء morning meal, = قَائِت ,قُوت food, Brit. Mus. MS. Rich 7203, fol. 198 a, col. 2.

p. 268, n. 4 The reading of B C ܡܸܬܦܪܸܣ is perhaps to be preferred here, for it is connected either with ܦܪܵܣܵܐ demensum, σιτομέτριον (Luke xii. 42), or ܦܵܪܣܵܐ See Payne Smith, Thes., coll 3276, 3279; and Bezold, Zeitschrift für Assyriologie, Bd. ii. p. 46 ff.

p. 268, n. 5 More correctly ܟܸܢܦܲܝ̈ ܫܲܒܵܚ̈ܝܼܢ = כְּנַף־רְנָנִים Job xxxix. 13. In Awṣâr Râzê Bar-Hebraeus explains the word: — ܟܢ̈ܦܝ ܫܒ̈ܚܝܢ ܗ̄. ܦܪܚܬܐ ܗ̇ܝ ܗܢܕܘܝܬܐ ܕܛܒ ܥܫܝܢܐ. ܘܡܢ ܐܢܫ̈ܝܢ ܨܦܪ ܦܝ̈ܠܐ ܡܬܩܪܝܐ. ܒܕܚܛܦܐ ܠܒܢ̈ܝ ܦܝܼ̈ܠܐ ܘܦܪܚܐ ܒܐܐܪ.

p. 269, n. 1 For accounts of the lions who were friendly with Macarius, the serpents who were at peace with Paul, and the hyaenas among whom Pachon lived, see Rosweyde, Vitae Patrum, pp. 228, 650, and 732.
p. 269, n. 2 See Rosweyde, Vitae Patrum, p. 469, col. 1, about the middle.
p. 269, n. 3 Read ܕܩܲܕܝܫܵܐ.
p. 269, n. 4 The allusion is to For I have five brethren. St. Luke xvi. 28.
p. 269, n. 5 I.e., a comparison between the five brethren and the five sins here named.
p. 269, n. 6 Read ܘܠܪ̈ܚܫܵܐ.
p. 269, n. 7 Probably the Simeon Priscus of Rosweyde, Vitae Patrum, p. 809.
p. 269, n. 8 See B.O., iii. 1, p. 51, and compare Rosweyde, Vitae Patrum, p. 39 b.
p. 270, n. 1 Read ܣܲܝܲܥܘ ܕܬܘܼܪܣܵܝ, the allusion being to the angels.

p. 270, n. 2 The offence of which this old man seems to have been guilty in the sight of the other monks was that he ate a meal cooked by fire in the morning. Strict monks ate once a day, in the evening, and they believed that the passions of the body could not be subdued if food were eaten oftener. Not understanding his manner of life they appear to have assumed that he ate a meal both evening and morning, and considering this to be a bad example for the other monks they reported the matter to Mâr Aḥâ.
p. 270, n. 3 Read ܒܲܚܝܵܪܬܐ.
p. 271, n. 1 I.e., one seized the old man's turban, unrolled it, and threw it over his neck while the others dragged it down behind like a cowl.
p. 271, n. 2 ܡܒܲܙܚܵܢܵܐܝܼܬ, a rare word.
p. 271, n. 3 Read ܗ̣̄ܘܲܝܬ.
p. 271, n. 4 For ܫܵܘ̈ܝܲܝ ܚܲܝܹ̈ܐ.
p. 272, n. 1 ܕܲܝܘܵܢܵܐ, i.e., one possessed of a ܕܲܝܘܵܐ, = διαμονιζόμενος.
p. 272, n. 2 Read ܘܲܚܙܲܘ ܠܚܝܘ̈ܬܐ.
p. 272, n. 3 Read ܚܲܕܪܘܗܝ.

p. 273, n. 1 ܚܕܲܬܐ, الحَدِيثَة. The site of this city is marked by Keshaf, near Sulṭân ʿAbdʾullah, which is situated on the left or east bank of the Tigris one farsaḥ below the Upper or Great Zâb. حديثة الموصل وهى بليدة كانت على دجلة بالجانب الشرقى قرب الزاب الاعلى Yâḳût ii. p. 222. See also Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 178; and Ritter, Erdkunde, ii, p. 665, note 2, and p. 669.
p. 273, n. 2 See Feige, Die Geschichte des Mâr ʿAbhdîshôʿ, p. 57.
p. 274, n. 1 A village which cannot have been very far from Ḥadhattâ. It is mentioned supra, p. 108.
p. 274, n. 2 On worshipping towards the East see Badger, The Nestorians, vol. ii. p. 413.

p. 274, n. 3 ܣܵܠܹܩ ܥܘܼܢܵܝܵܐ means to sing, to praise. Cf. Hoffmann, Opuscula Nestoriana, p. 93, line 2 ff., where ܣܲܩܘ = ܫܲܒܲܚܘ; and our English use of the words raise the song in Come, ye thankful people, come, Raise the song of Harvest-home. Hymns Ancient and Modern, No. 382, London 1875.

p. 274, n. 4 I.e., the service for the holy Eucharist on Easter Sunday. The lesson for the day is taken from the XXVIIIth chap. of St. Matthew. See Brit. Mus. Add. 17,923, fol. 92 a, (Wright, Catalogue, p. 184, no. 65), and B.O., iii. ii. p. CCCXXXII.
p. 274, n. 5 Read ܠܗܢܐ?
p. 274, n. 6 Read ܕܠܘ.
p. 274, n. 7 Read with BC ܝܲܠܝܼܦ.
p. 274, n. 8 ܛܲܝܵܝܵܐܝܼܬ.
p. 274, n. 9 ܠܵܥܘܿܙܵܐ a word used to express indistinct and hasty speech المتكلّم بسرعة. In Psalm cxiv. 1. עַם לֹעֵז = ܥܡܐ ܠܥܘܙܐ.
p. 275, n. 1 I.e., قوم يا راهِب ما لى ولك مُرّ بسلام من مَكانى.
p. 275, n. 2 ܥܘܼܪܵܒܵܐ = عُرْب an Arab. Compare Hoffmann, Opuscula Nestoriana, p. 95, line 6, and see Thomas of Margâ, p. 133, l. 17 (text).

p. 275, n. 3 All the MSS. read ܒܐܪܥܐ ܕܡܨܪܝܢ, but it is very doubtful if Thomas of Margâ refers to Egypt, where rain is not expected to fall regularly. Hoffmann thinks it more probable that the ܟܘܪܐ ܕܕܪܡܣܘܩ or country round about Damascus is referred to, for we know that the Nestorians who were scattered about there had a bishop. See B.O., iii. 1, p. 107, col. 1; and iii. ii. p. CCCCXXXI. Or ܕܒܐܪܥܐ ܕܡܨܪܝܢ may be a corruption of ܕܡܥܪܬ ܡܨܪܝܢ = مَعَرَّةُ مَصرِينَ, five farsaḥ south-west of Aleppo, to the west of Ḳinneshrîn and north of Idlib. See Wright, Catalogue of Syriac MSS., fol. 126 b; and Nöldeke, Zur Topographie und Geschichte des Damascenischen Gebietes und der Haurângegend, (in Z.D.M.G., Bd. XXIX, p. 420 ff.) where the list of places mentioned in Add. 14,602 is discussed.
p. 276, n. 1 Literally, I have set it down.
p. 277, n. 1 For the Babylonian original of this word see Bezold, Oriental Diplomacy, p. 88, London, 1893.
p. 277, n. 2 Read ܒܵܗ̇? Or instead of work we may understand station or position in life.
p. 278, n. 1 Luke vii. 12.

p. 278, n. 2 The allusion here is to Saint Paul, the First Hermit, (see supra, p. 30) who, when he felt that the time of his death was drawing near, sent off Antony to fetch the cloak which Athanasius, Bishop of Alexandria, had given him, in order that his body might be wrapped therein for burial. Paul wished to be left alone in prayer with God when the summons came. While Antony was on his road to bring the cloak he saw the soul of the blessed Paul being carried up to heaven by angels. See Butler, Lives of the Saints, vol. 1. p. 185, Jan. 15, London 1812.

p. 279, n. 1 For the use of ܦܪܨܘܦܐ in this sense see Payne Smith, Thes., col. 3292. And see Wright, Catalogue of Syr. MSS., p. 257, col. 1, No. 49; and p. 275, col. 2, No. 4, The Commemoration of any one Saint ܕܥܠ ܚܕ ܩܢܘܡܐ.

p. 279, n. 2 ܥܒܵܝ̈ܵܬܵܐ, i.e., two large pieces of plain or coloured cloth, one of which wrapped around him served for clothes by day, and the other formed the counterpane under which he slept at night. According to Dozy, (Supplément, ii. p. 90) عَبَآء, or عَبَآءَة is, properly speaking, the name of a kind of stuff. Compare كِسآء, the name of a stuff woven by the Arabs, or a large piece of woollen stuff used both as a blanket and mantle. (Dozy, Supplément, ii. p. 468). I have often seen the shepherds in Mesopotamia wearing these large pieces of sheep's wool cloth, and I have often been glad to borrow one from a member of a caravan to sleep under during the night. For a couple of hours they are proof against heavy rain.
p. 280, n. 1 ܒܹܣܲܕܝܵܐ = ܒܹܣܵܕܝܵܐ. The plur. fem ܒܹܣܵܕ̈ܘܵܬܵܐ (Neo-Syr. ܣܦܵܕ̈ܝܵܬܵܐ) = Heb. כְּסָתוֹת Ezek. xiii. 18.
p. 280, n. 2 ܬܘܪܣܲܝܗܘܢ for ܬܘܪܣܵܝܗܘܢ.
p. 280, n. 3 ܚܡܝܼܠܬܐ, Arab. خَمْلَة, a soft coverlet or rug with fringed edges. See Dozy, Supplément, p. 406, col. 2.
p. 280, n. 4 Genesis iii. 12.
p. 280, n. 5 Genesis iii. 3, 4.
p. 280, n. 6 Genesis iv. 8.
p. 280, n. 7 Genesis ix. 21.
p. 280, n. 8 ܡܸܬܝܲܕܥܵܢܵܐ cf. Payne Smith, Thes., col. 1562.
p. 281, n. 1 In allusion to נִלְבְּנָה לְבֵנִים Genesis xi. 3.
p. 281, n. 2 ܓܕܝܼܠܵܐ = πεπλασμένος. Cf. Bernstein in Z.D.M.G., Bd. iii, p. 407; and Budge, Book of the Bee, p. ܕ, l. 21 (ܓܵܕܠܐ ܟܟܵܪܝܬܐ).
p. 281, n. 3 ܐܸܣܩܸܛܹܐ = σκῦτος, literally, the leather whip with which boys were chastised.
p. 281, n. 4 In ܒܘܼܠܒܵܠܵܐ there is an etymological allusion to the name Babel.
p. 281, n. 5 See Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 216.
p. 281, n. 6 Or Dêndowai.
p. 282, n. 1 See Hoffmann, Auszüge, note 1640; Nöldeke, Geschichte der Perser, pp. 167, 478, 484; and infra, Bk. v. chap. 4.
p. 282, n. 2 The MSS. have ܚܘܼܓܝܪ Ḥûgîr.
p. 282, n. 3 See Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 224.

p. 283, n. 1 Sûrîn seized upon the patriarchate A.H. 1065 = A.D. 754 and held it for fifty-six days. He sat after Mâr Abhâ, and came from Seleucia. He was not guarded in his manner of life. He was formerly Metropolitan of Nisibis, but was translated to Ḥalwan (i.e., حُلْوَان = ܚܲܠܲܚ, Calah). He was deposed in the year in which a Catholicus was appointed. Bar-Hebraeus, Chron. Eccles., ii. col. 155, and see B.O., iii. 1, p. 616. According to ʿAbhd-Îshôʿ (B.O., iii. 1, p. 168) he wrote ܫܪܝ ܪܥܝܢ ܗܪ̈ܛܝܩܘܣ܆ ܒܩܘܛܥ ܡܡܠܠܐ ܝܘܢܝܐ ܘܬܚܘ̈ܝܐ ܘܒܘܚܢܐ. The Catholics who were deposed were Mâr(î)-bôkht, Narsai, Elisha, Joseph and Sûrîn or Sôrên; see Budge, Book of the Bee, p. 120.

p. 284, n. 1 Then arose Jacob and was appointed Catholicus in Seleucia, after the bishops had received from him an undertaking in writing that he would neither trangress the law nor abrogate the canon. In his days a church for the Nestorians was built at Tâgrîth (Tekrit) by the care of Ṣĕlîbhâ-zĕkhâ, Bishop of Ṭirhân, who had been cast in prison with Jacob the Catholicus. And when he was set free he began to restore the churches in Ṭirhân, and he also went to Paul the Maphrian at Tekrit and persuaded him to give permission for the Nestorians to build themselves a church in Tekrit. The Maphrian said, As far as I myself am concerned I have no objection, but I am afraid of the Patriarch and the people of Tekrit. I counsel thee, however, to go to Nisibis and to persuade the Nestorians there to give back to the Jacobites the churches which they have taken from them, for then will the people of Tekrit allow a church to be built for you here. And when Ṣĕlîbhâ-zĕkhâ had gone to Nisibis, and had made supplication to the aged Metropolitan Cyprian and to the Nestorians of Nisibis, they gave back to our people the famous Church of Mâr Domitius. And ten Jacobite merchants who were in Nisibis went down to Tekrit, and persuaded the people to allow a church to be built for the Nestorians. Bar-Hebraeus, Chron. Eccles., ii. coll. 155, 157. Jacob sat nineteen years, and died A.D. 773. See B.O., ii. p. 432; iii. 1, pp. 205, 616.
p. 286, n. 1 See infra, p. 304 ff.
p. 286, n. 2 ܓܫܝܼܡܘܼܬܵܐ embodiment, الجسمية Cf. ܓܫܝܡܘܬ ܡܠܵܐ and ܓܫܝܡܘܬ ܩܠܐ Payne Smith, Thes., col. 794.

p. 286, n. 3 ܙܢܵܓܵܐ. This very rare word is explained in Hoffmann, Opuscula Nestoriana, p. 96, l. 1f. by ܣܕܝܼܪܘܼܬܐ ܕܡܵܐܢ̈ܝ ܡܲܪ̈ܟܒܵܬܵܐ ܕܒܗܘܿܢ ܢܵܩ̈ܦܵܢ ܡܲܪ̈ܟܒܵܬܵܐ ܠܲܚܕ̈ܕܹܐ ܘܲܒ̈ܗܲܠܟܵܬܗܝܢ ܝܵܗܒܢ ܩ̈ܠܐ ܐܲܝܟ ܕܙܲܓܵܪ the arrangement in order of the furniture of chariots by means of which the chariots follow each other closely and give forth sounds like a bell as they move along. In Judges v. 28 ܙܢܵܓܵܐ ܕܡܲܪ̈ܟܒܵܬܗ (Neo-Syr. ܫܵܘ̈ܦܵܦܹܐ ܕܟܵܠܸܣܟܘ̈ܗܝ) = פַּעֲמֵי מַרְכְּבוֹתָיו. In addition to the native explanations of the word given in Payne Smith, Thes., coll. 1140, 1141 Duval gives اجراص الخيل ويقال صرير المراكب اصطفاف المراكب والتزاقها بعض ببعض Lexicon Bar-Bahlule, col. 694.
p. 287, n. 1 Lit., limb of Christ.
p. 287, n. 2 ܒܵܣܸܠܝܼܵܐ = βασιλεία = ܡܲܠܟܘܼܬܵܐ Duval, Lexicon, col. 408.

p. 287, n. 3 ܐܲܠܵܗܵܘܗ̈ܝ its gods. This custom of calling a man of rank my gods is as old as 1500 years before Christ for in the Tell el-Amarna tablets the writers of despatches frequently address Amenophis as my gods ilâni-ya. See Bezold and Budge, The Tell el-Amarna Tablets in the British Museum, p. LXI, note 1.
p. 287, n. 4 ܐܲܩܡܵܐ = ἀκμή = ܡܫܘܚܬܐ. In Bar-Bahlûl ܐܩܡܐ ܕܚܝ̈ܐ = قامة الحياة; see Duval, Lexicon, col. 276.
p. 288, n. 1 Read ܣܵܒܵܐ?
p. 288, n. 2 All the MSS. read ܐܲܟܦܵܢܵܢܝ.
p. 288, n. 3 Literally, that I should make thy glorious command in writing, and that I should paint for thee a picture.
p. 288, n. 4 Read ܘܡܢ ܐܝܠܝܢ.
p. 288, n. 5 Read ܝܼܠܝܼܦܵܐ.
p. 289, n. 1 This chapter is quoted in B.O., iii. 1, p. 177, col. 1f.
p. 289, n. 2 Read ܕܲܗܘ̤ܵܘ.
p. 290, n. 1 ܓܒܝܠܬܐ, جَبِلْتَا, a town in Ṭirhân, was situated on the east bank of the Tigris, about eighteen miles from Karḥ Sâmarrâ on the road to Môṣul. See Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 188.
p. 290, n. 2 Read ܛܝܼܪܗܵܢ, i.e., طيرهان. Ṭirhân was a district which is represented to-day by the country round about Sâmarrâ, ܫܘܡܪܐ. See Hoffmann, Auszüge, pp. 188–191; and B.O., iii. 11, p. 785.
p. 290, n. 3 In the list of his works given in B.O., iii. 1, p. 181, no mention is made of these ܫܘ̈ܐܠܐ.

p. 290, n. 4 According to Elias bar-Shînâyâ he sat from A.D. 713–729; Assemânî gives (B.O., ii. 430) 714–728. Ṣĕlîbhâ-zĕkhâ came from Karkhâ dhĕ Pêrôz, which is called to-day Karkhânê (Karkhênê), from the country of Ṭirhân. See Bar-Hebraeus, Chron. Eccles., ii. col. 149.
p. 290, n. 5 ܡܸܬܢܲܫ̈ܝܵܢܵܝܵܬܵܐ, things fallen into oblivion. A rare word.
p. 290, n. 6 ܛܵܥ̈ܝܵܬܵܐ = ܛܲܥ̈ܝܵܬܵܐ.
p. 290, n. 7 The allusion appears to be to Psalm cxxxvii. 4, How shall we sing the Lord's song in a strange land?

p. 291, n. 1 The following difficult passage is thus rendered by Assemânî, B.O., iii. 1, p. 180, col. 1: — ita pariter temporibus Sancti Magistri nostri Babaei confusi fuisse videbantur ritus Ecclesiastici sacrarum processionum, et Cantus, modi, et hirmi, et psalmodia universa ea, quae ad Psalmum, Domine clamavi ad te, peragi solet; necnon et clausulae precum, et psalmorum modulationes, et stationes, et cantiones, et hymni, qui alta voce recitantur; ita ut unaquaeque regio, urbs, coenobium, et schola suos haberet canendi modos, et sacrarum supplicationum ritus. Quamobrem factum fuerat, ut externus quisque, literis licet excultus et in scholis exercitatus, extra propriam Scholam manere velut imperitus et rudis cogeretur. Et quemadmodum quum Judaei in urbem Hierusalem postliminio rediissent, universa psalmodia restituta est, et pristinam gloriam recuperavit: et quemadmodum ante Mar Jesujabum Catholicum Adjabenum sacrarum ordinationum ritus confusi fuerant, illius autem operâ et auctoritate conveniens omnibus Ecclesiis ritus et communis factus est: similiter Spiritus sanctus beatum hunc necessariâ sapientiâ instruxit, docuitque modos suaves, et compositiones jucundas Ecclesiasticae musicae, suisque charismatibus implevit, et suis thesauris locupletatum, suae doctrinae organum et spiritualem citharam fecit. As in the early Christian Church the musical portion of the service consisted of ψαλμοὶ, ὕμνοι, ᾠδαὶ πνευματικαὶ (Ephesians v. 19, Colossians iii. 16), but I am unable to give exact renderings of the Syriac technical words. See the articles ἀκροστίχια, ἀνατρίχισμα, εἱρμὸς, κανόνες, προψάλματα, φωνὴ, τροπάριον, ᾠδὴ in Du Cange, Glossarium, coll. 45, 73, 356, 582, 1262, 1714, 1617, 1789.
p. 291, n. 2 In the text p. 142, note 1, referring to this is the observation, See the confusions in the musical system which the much enlightened Rabban Bâbhai corrected.

p. 291, n. 3 ܟܘܼܪ̈ܵܟܹܐ. Assemânî generally considers that these were connected with processions, but they seem rather to have been tunes with an oft repeated refrain; cf. ܟܘܪܟܐ لحن مضاعف مردّد دوران Payne Smith, Thes., col. 1827; and see Bk. IV. chap. 20 (text, p. 237, l. 17).

p. 291, n. 4 ܩܘܼܢܩܵܢܵܐ according to Castell p. 812, is concentus, melodia, and is rendered by Assemânî Cantus. Brit. Mus. MS. Orient. 2441, fol 330a, col. 2, explains it by song ܩܘܢܩܢܐ ܗ̄. ܪܟܢܐ ܘܡܢ ܩܝܢܬܐ ܫܩܝܠ الالحان, and in Rich 7205, fol. 152a, col. 1 ܩܘܢ̈ܘܢܐ = التفتفة الالحان.
p. 292, n. 1 ܢܝܼܫܹ̈ܐ rendered modi by Assemânî, and metra by Payne Smith, Thes., col. 2367.

p. 292, n. 2 All the MSS. have ܢܘܼܓ̈ܙܹܐ. Assemânî (B.O., iii. 1, p. 178, l. 17) and Payne Smith (Thes., col. 2280) give ܢܽܘܓܳܕ̈ܶܐ, the former rendering the word by hirmi, and the latter by hymni species. In Cardahi, Al-Lobab, Beyrut, 1891, vol. ii. p. 97, col. 2. ܢܘܓ̈ܕܐ = اّتفاق الاصوات في الغنا.
p. 292, n. 3 Psalm CXLI.
p. 292, n. 4 ܣ̈ܘܼܝܵܟܹܐ, i.e., the airs which are sung at the end of the prayer for the night السئاخين التى تقال في اخر صلاة الليل Payne Smith, Thes., col. 2551. ܣܘܼܝܵܟܵܐ = ܫܘܼܡܠܵܝܵܐ.

p. 292, n. 5 ܙܘܡܪܐ, strictly speaking, the psalms which are sung before the reading of the Epistles, cf. προψάλματα (Du Cange, Glossarium, col. 1262) and the ܫܘܪܝܵܐ of Badger, Nestorians, vol. ii. p. 20. The reader should consult the sections Hirmos, Hauptformen, Refrain, Akrostichis Reim, Gleichzeilige rythmische Gedichte, in Krumbacher, Geschichte der Byzantinischen Literatur, Munich, 1891, pp. 334–344.

p. 292, n. 6 The Psalter in the Greek Church was divided into twenty sections called καθίσματα, each of which was divided into three Στάσεις, or ܐܸܣܛܵܛܝܘܿܢܹ̈ܐ, sic dictae, quod Stationes stantes recitent Graeci, vel quod Lectionem finientes stent et quasi respirant. Du Cange, Glossarium, col. 1429. The Psalms were thus divided among the twenty καθίσματα: — καθ’ 1. Psalms 1—8. καθ’ 2. Psalms 9—17. καθ’ 3. Psalms 18—24. καθ’ 4. Psalms 25—32. καθ’ 5. Psalms 33—37. καθ’ 6. Psalms 38—46. καθ’ 7. Psalms 47—55. καθ’ 8. Psalms 56—64. καθ’ 9. Psalms 65—70. καθ’ 10. Psalms 71—77. καθ’ 11. Psalms 78—85. καθ’ 12. Psalms 86—91. καθ’ 13. Psalms 92—101. καθ’ 14. Psalms 102—105. καθ’ 15. Psalms 106—109. καθ’ 16. Psalms 110—118. καθ’ 17. Psalm 119. καθ’ 18. Psalms 120—132. καθ’ 19. Psalms 133—143. καθ’ 20. Psalms 144—150.
p. 293, n. 1 ܥܘܢ̈ܝܐ, i.e., antiphonal responses of all kinds sung by clergy and laity.
p. 293, n. 2 ܥܘܼܢ̈ܝܵܬܐ, i.e., small ᾠδαὶ sung as anthems, or ὕμνοι.
p. 293, n. 3 He sat from A.D. 647–658.
p. 293, n. 4 ܒܠܝܼܠܵܐܝܼܬ, confusedly, indistinctly.
p. 293, n. 5 Read ܘܐܲܠܦܹܗ.
p. 293, n. 6 ܩܝܵܡܘܼܬ ܩܵܠܵܐ = σύστημα, i.e., the art of singing in tune and in unison.

p. 294, n. 1 Notwithstanding the labours of Gregory Nazianzenus (born 329, died 390), of Romanos (VIth century), of Sergios and Sophronios (VIIth century), and of Andrew, Archbishop of Crete (650–720), John of Damascus (died before 754), and his friend Kosmas of Jerusalem (he became Bishop of Maiuma in Palestine about A.D. 743), vir ingeniosissimus, omnino musicam harmoniam spirans, must be regarded as the founders of Greek church music, from which the Nestorians must have borrowed largely. A dissertation on this subject, even if I possessed the knowledge necessary for writing it, would be out of place here, but the following works should be consulted by the reader who wishes to work out a comparison of the Greek and Syriac technical names: — Vincent, Ἁγιοπολίτης, (in Notices et Extraits), Paris, 1847; Wallis, Manuel Bryennios; Christ, Beiträge zur kirchlichen Literatur der Byzantiner, (in Sitzungsberichte der Bayer. Akad., phil.-hist. Cl. 1870); Christ, Ueber die Bedeutung von Hirmos, Troparion und Kanon in der Griechischen Poesie, (in Sitzungsberichte der Bayer. Akad., phil.-hist. Cl. 1870); Westphal, Metrik der Griechen; Tzetzes, Ueber die altgriechische Musik in der griechischen Kirche, Munich 1874; Reimann, Zur Geschichte und Theorie der Byzantinischen Musik; Χρύσανθος, Θεωρητικὸν μέγα τῆς μουσικῆς, Trieste, 1832; Μαργαρίτης, Θεωρητικὴ καὶ πρακτικὴ ἐκκλησιαστικὴ μουσικὴ, Constantinople, 1851; Φιλόξενος, Δεξικὸν and Θεωρητικὸν στοιχειῶδες τῆς μουσικῆς, Constantinople, 1859; Sathas, Ἱστορικὸν δοκίμιον περὶ τοῦ Θεάτρου καὶ τῆς μουσικῆς τῶν Βυζαντίνων, Venice, 1878; Bouvy, Etude sur les origines du rhyme tonique dans l'hymnographie de l'église grecque, Nîmes, 1886, Hatherly, A Treatise on Byzantine Music, London, 1892, p. 152.
p. 294, n. 2 Haggai i. 14.

p. 295, n. 1 I.e., the village of the Gazelle, ʿuzzêl being stat. abs. of ʿuzzailâ. Kĕphar-ʿUzzêl, i.e., كَفَرْعَزَّي lay on the east side of the Upper or Great Zâb. See Hoffmann, Auszüge, pp. 236, 296.
p. 295, n. 2 Read ܙܵܕܵܢܦܲܪܘܼܟ Zâdhân-parrûḥ, زَادَان فَرُّخ. See Nöldeke, Geschichte der Perser, p. 356, note 1.
p. 295, n. 3 Read ܦܲܪܘܼܟܙܵܕ Parrûḥ-zadh, فَرُّخ زَاد.
p. 295, n. 4 I.e., لُهْرَاسْپ.

p. 295, n. 6 ܗܵܦܘܿܪܹ̈ܐ, a rare word. ܗܵܦܘܿܪܵܐ = a speaker of vain things, a garrulous person = ܦܲܩܵܩܵܐ، ܒܵܕܘܿܠܵܐ، ܦܲܫܵܪܵܐ، ܗܲܕܵܝܵܐ، ܒܵܓܘܿܠܵܐ، ܒܵܕܘܿܝܵܐ، ܠܸܫܵܢܵܢܵܐ, all of which synonyms are explained by ܗ̇ܘ ܕܡܡܲܠܸܠ ܦܟ̈ܝܼܗܵܬܵܐ a man who speaketh vain and foolish things. See Payne Smith, Thes., col. 446.
p. 295, n. 7 ܦܟܝܼܗܘܼܬܵܐ, emptiness, foolishness, insipidity.
p. 296, n. 1 This chapter is quoted in B.O., iii. 1, p. 178, col. 2.
p. 296, n. 2 Literally he built the Ḥudhrâ, i.e., the service-book for the Sundays of the whole year. See supra, pp. 153, 189.
p. 296, n. 3 Or he corrected the sections, for ܨܚܵܚܵܐ = פָּרָשָׁה = περικοπή, section, chapter.
p. 296, n. 4 See supra, p. 217, note 1.
p. 296, n. 5 See Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 223.
p. 296, n. 6 Compare ܪܘܣܬܩܐ ܕܓܐܪܝܢ, Syriac text p. 346, line 8.
p. 296, n. 7 Assemânî (B.O., iii. 1, p. 178, col. 2, l. 18) omits this name.
p. 296, n. 8 See Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 223.
p. 296, n. 9 I.e., the neck of Nîram of the shepherds.
p. 296, n. 10 A village near Akra. See Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 225.
p. 296, n. 11 The account of the fortifying of this place is given in Book VI. chap. 12; see Syriac text p. 368 ff.
p. 296, n. 12 See infra, Book iii. chap. 8.
p. 297, n. 1 Perhaps the same as ܒܹܝܬ ܐܲܣܹ̈ܐ. Cf. B.O., ii. p. 221, col. 2, l. 33.
p. 297, n. 2 I.e., ܒܹܝܬ ܙܐܵܛܵܐ; see Syriac text p. 329, line 17.

p. 297, n. 3 The modern Bavian, situated on the right bank of the Gômel river, about twenty-five miles nearly north of Môṣul. For an account of the Assyrian sculptures at this place see Layard, Nineveh and Babylon, London, 1853, p. 208 ff.
p. 297, n. 4 See Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 97, note 867.
p. 297, n. 5 Assemânî (B.O., iii. 1, p. 178, col. 2, l. 28) has ܒܹܝܬ ܬܲܪ̈ܡܫܵܝܹܐ.
p. 297, n. 6 ܦܲܪܪܸܝܣܦܵܢܵܐ, formed with the Persian termination بان keeping, guarding. The word is explained by ܓܲܢܵܢܵܐ gardener, ܢܛܪ ܦܪܕܝܣܐ keeper of a garden, = بستنبانيّ.
p. 297, n. 7 ܩܝܵܡܘܼܬܵܐ ܕܩܵܠܵܐ i.e., the knowledge of singing in unison and in tune.
p. 297, n. 8 See Du Cange, Glossarium, col. 582; Badger, Nestorians, vol. ii. p. 251 ff.
p. 298, n. 1 This chapter is quoted in B.O., iii. 1, p. 179.
p. 298, n. 2 According to ʿAbhd-Îshôʿ he wrote Orations, Epistles, Hymns of Praise, Histories, Admonitions and Homilies. ܡܐܡܪ̈ܐ ܘܐܓܪ̈ܬܐ ܘܬܫܒ̈ܚܬܐ ܘܬܫ̈ܥܝܬܐ ܘܡܪ̈ܬܝܢܘܬܐ ܘܡܪ̈ܕܘܬܐ B.O., iii. 1, p. 181.
p. 298, n. 3 Better ܢܲܣܒܲܪ.

p. 298, n. 4 ܬܸܐܘܿܪܝܼܵܐ = θεωρία = spiritual vision, intellectual and divine sight or understanding. Cf. ܬܸܐܘܪܝܼܵܐ العلم ويقال البصر العقلى ܗ̄. ܚܙܬܐ ܐܠܗܝܬܐ ܗ̄. ܗܘܢܢܝܬܐ ܘܪܥܝܢܐ ܝܕܥܬܐ ܕܟܝܢܐ ܘܕܠܐ ܒܟܝܢܐ علم مقدار وراى ومعرفة النظر العقلى والتميّا بالعقل والتميا الصحيع Orient. 2441, fol. 384a, col. 2. So also Rich 7203, fol. 192b, col. 1.
p. 298, n. 5 ܬܘܼܪ̈ܓܵܡܹܐ, literally interpretations. See Badger, Nestorians, vol. ii. p. 19, ܬܘܼܪܓܵܡܵܐ = تفسير شرح تعبير ترجمة Orient. 2441, fol. 389a, col. 1, and Rich 7203, fol. 198b, col. 2.
p. 298, n. 6 ܐܘܿܫܲܥܢܵܐ = הוֹשִׁיעָה נָּא Cf. Payne Smith, Thes., col. 1639.
p. 299, n. 1 Cf. the Blessings in the Marriage service quoted by Badger, Nestorians, vol. ii. p. 254 ff.
p. 299, n. 2 Assemânî renders, De eodem sancto Jacobo cantiones magnis mysteriis refertas.
p. 299, n. 3 Assemânî renders, Ecce avolarunt dies mei. Et ad hymnum, qui incipit, Ecce mortuis, cantiones duodecim. See Bickell, Carmina Nisibena, Leipzig, 1866, De re metrica, pp. 31–35.

p. 299, n. 4 For a list of the hymns of Bâbhai extant, see Wright, Syr. Lit., p. 844, col. 1. The following hymn for the night of Sunday in Epiphany week edited from Add. 14,675, fol. 171a, and Rich 7156, fol. 163, will serve as a specimen of the metrical compositions of this eminent writer. ܫܘܒܚܐ ܠܪ̈ܚܡܐ ܕܫܠܚܘܟ ܨܐܕܝܢ܆ ܡܫܚܝܐ ܫܡܫܐ ܕܙܕܝܩܘܬܐ. ܨܡܚܐ ܕܨܡܚ ܡܢ ܒܝܬ ܕܘܝܕ܆ ܘܩܪܐ ܠܥܡ̈ܡܐ ܠܬܝܒܘܬܐ. ܩܪܘܒܘ ܬܝ̈ܒܐ ܘܫܐܠܘ ܪ̈ܚܡܐ܆ ܥܡ ܐܝܬ ܐܬܪܐ ܠܬܝܒܘܬܐ. ܘܢܫܒܘܩ ܟܠܢܫ ܡܐ ܕܒܠܒܗ܆ ܘܢܫܐܠ ܪ̈ܚܡܐ ܒܓܠܝܘܬ ܐܦ̈ܐ. ܫܡܥ ܒܥܘܬܢ ܘܗܒ ܫܐܠܬܢ܆ ܡܫܝܚܐ ܪܚܡ ܩܠ ܬܝܒ̈ܐ. ܠܐ ܡܪܝ ܬܗܡܐ ܡܢ ܬܟܫܦܬܢ܆ ܕܒܬܘܬ ܢܦܫܢ ܡܩܪܒܝܢܢ ܠܟ. ܝܵܕܥܬ ܐܘ ܡܪܝ ܕܣܓܝ ܥܘܠܢ܆ ܦܫܘܛ ܠܢ ܐܝܕܟ ܕܡܠܝܐ ܪ̈ܚܡܐ. ܒܒܪܐ ܙܥܘܪܐ ܡܬܝܼܠܝܼܢܲܢ ܠܟ܆ ܕܦܲܪܚ ܢܟܣ̈ܐ ܕܒܝܬ ܐܒܗ̈ܘܗܝ. ܚܛܲܝܢ ܘܐܪܓܸܙܢܟ ܚܘܼܣ ܘܐܬܪܚܡ܆ ܡܪܐ ܛܒܐ ܘܡܪܚܡܢܐ. ܢܓܘܠܘܢ ܪ̈ܚܡܝܟ ܥܠ ܚܘܒ̈ܬ ܕܒܕܡܟ ܚܝܐ ܙܒܝܢܝܢܢ ܠܟ. ܘܥܡ ܐܪܡܠܬܐ ܡܬܟܫܦܝܢ܆ ܠܟ ܕܝܢܐ ܣܓܝ ܪ̈ܚܡܐ. ܚܲܣܵܐ ܚܘ̈ܒܝܢ ܘܥܛܝ ܚܛܗ̈ܝܢ܆ ܛܵܒܵܐ ܕܛܥܝܢ ܝܘܩܪܗ ܕܥܘܠܢ. ܨܠܝܒܟ ܢܗܘܐ ܠܢ ܒܝܬ ܓܘܣܐ܆ ܘܢܕܚܘܩ ܡܢܢ ܚܝܠܗ ܕܒܝܫܐ. ܘܒܗ̇ܘ ܝܘܡܐ ܕܒܗ ܡܬܢܦܨܝܢ܆ ܝܠܕ̈ܘܗܝ ܕܐܕܡ ܡܢ ܕܚܝܼܚܐ. ܘܡܬܬܥܝܪ ܟܠܢܫ ܡܢ ܕܡܟܘܬ ܕܡܝܘܬܘܬܐ ܠܡܫܬܐܠܘ. ܒܗ̇ܘ ܒܝܬ ܕܝܢܐ ܕܒܗ ܡܬܦܪܥܝܢ܆ ܛܒ̈ܐ ܘܒܝܫ̈ܐ ܐܟܡܐ ܕܣܥܪܘ. ܚܢܢܟ ܢܗܘܐ ܣܢܐܓܪܐ ܚܠܦܝܢ. ܘܠܐ ܢܬܚܲܝܒ ܒܕܝܢܟ ܟܐܢܐ. ܘܒܗ̇ܝ ܫܥܬܐ ܕܕܢܚܝܢ ܪ̈ܚܡܝܟ܆ ܢܦܘܩ ܠܐܘܪܥܵܟ ܐܝܟ ܨܒܝܢܟ. ܘܥܡ ܩܕܝ̈ܫܐ ܘܟܐܢ̈ܐ ܕܐܚܒܘܟ܆ ܢܙܡܪ ܫܘܒܚܐ ܠܐܠܗܘܬܟ ܘܟܠܢ ܐܟܚܕ ܢܲܣܩ ܫܘܒܚܐ ܠܐܒܐ ܘܠܒܪܐ ܘܠܪܘܚ ܩܘܕܫܐ܆ ܕܠܗ ܬܫܒܘܚܬܐ ܡܢ ܣܓܘ̈ܕܘܗܝ܆ ܠܥܠܡ ܥܠܡܝܢ ܐܡܝܢ ܘܐܡܝܢ܀

p. 300, n. 1 I.e., Cyrus of al-Ḥîrah, surnamed the Doctor, a disciple of Mâr Abhâ; he flourished about A.D. 550. According to ʿAbhd-Îshôʿ he wrote Expositions and Funeral Orations, ܦܘܫ̈ܩܐ ܐܦ ܬܘܪ̈ܓܡܐ. See B.O., ii. p. 412, col. 1; iii. 1, p. 170, chap. XCV.

p. 300, n. 2 I.e., Narsai, called the Harp of the Spirit ܟܸܢܵܪܵܐ ܕܪܘܼܚܵܐ by ʿAbhd-Îshôʿ, and surnamed ܓܲܪܒܵܢܵܐ, the Leper. Narsai sprang from Maʿallthâ; he laboured in the school of Nisibis for fifty years, where he was a companion of Bar-Ṣaumâ, and at Edessa for twenty years; he fled from this latter town to escape the wrath of Cyrus the Bishop (A.D. 471–498), and died at Nisibis early in the next century. He was famous as a writer of hymns and other metrical compositions, his favourite metre being that of six syllables. According to ʿAbhd-Îshôʿ he wrote commentaries on Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Joshua, Judges, Ecclesiastes, Isaiah, the twelve Minor Prophets, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Daniel, twelve volumes of metrical discourses (360 in number), a liturgy, expositions of the Eucharist and of Baptism, consolatory epistles and funeral orations, hymns and sermons and exhortations, and a book entitled On the Corruption of Morals, ܥܠ ܫܟܝܪܘܬ ܕܘܒܪ̈ܐ. See B.O., iii. 1, p. 65 f.; Wright, Syr. Lit., p. 830; and Bar-Hebraeus, Chron. Eccles., ii. col. 77.

p. 301, n. 1 I.e., John, surnamed Adhramah, ܐܲܕܪܡܲܗ (see Bk. 1. chap. 14, supra, p. 67), formerly a monk in the Monastery of Mount Îzlâ when Mâr Bâbhai was the abbot. He left that monastery with Zĕkhâ-Îshôʿ and Abraham and went with them to Dâsen, and built a monastery; he is usually described as John of Bêth Rabban. According to ʿAbhd-Îshôʿ he wrote commentaries upon Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Job, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Proverbs; controversial treatises against the Magians, Jews and heretics; discourses, prayers, a Discourse upon the death of Khusrau, a Discourse upon the plague at Nisibis, Consolations, Questions upon the Old and New Testaments, hymns of various kinds, and a work upon the tones of hymns, ܩܠ̈ܐ ܕܥܘܢ̈ܝܬܐ. See B.O., iii. 1, pp. 72, 631, 708.

p. 301, n. 2 I.e., Abraham of Mount Îzlâ, the friend of John Adhramah, (see supra, p. 37, note 1). He wrote commentaries upon Joshua, Judges, the Books of Kings, Ecclesiasticus, Isaiah, the twelve Minor Prophets, Daniel, and the Song of Songs; he wrote also upon the Cause of the Sessions ܥܠܬܐ ܕܡܘܬܒ̈ܐ, and composed hymns. See B.O., iii. 1, p. 71.
p. 301, n. 3 ܡܡܲܪܝܵܢܘܼܬܵܐ, the desire to rival some one.

p. 301, n. 4 I.e., Abraham bar-Dâshandâd who flourished about A.D. 720, and who was the teacher of the Catholicus Timothy I., and of his successor Îshôʿ bar-Nôn, and of Abû Nûḥ al-Anbârî in the school of Bâshôsh in Saphsâphâ. According to ʿAbhd-Îshôʿ he wrote a book of admonition, a commentary on the discourse of Mark the monk (see Wright, Cat. Syr. MSS., p. 482, col. 1), a disputation with the Jews, the Book of the king's way, discourses on repentance, and letters upon various subjects. See B.O., iii. 1, p. 194; and Wright, Syr. Lit., p. 844. For the writings of Îshôʿ bar-Nôn and Abû Nûḥ al-Anbârî see B.O., iii. 1, pp. 165, 212.
p. 302, n. 1 A village in the country of Arbêl or Arbela. See B.O., ii. p. 251, col. 2, l. 12; iii. 1, pp. 179, 343; Bar-Hebraeus, Chron. Eccles., ii. col. 437.
p. 302, n. 2 ܦܸܠܓܘܼܬ ܒܲܪܢܵܫܵܐ. See Payne Smith, Thes., col. 2140.
p. 302, n. 3 Literally, solution.
p. 303, n. 1 Read ܠܒܲܥܵܝܹܝ̈ܗ̇.
p. 303, n. 2 ܐܘ̇ܗ = אֲהָהּ 2 Kings iii. 10.
p. 303, n. 3 There is a play here upon the name ܓܘܼܪܝܵܐ Gûryâ which means both a lion's whelp, and a puppy.

p. 303, n. 4 In Bk. IV. chap. 16 (Syriac text p. 217, l. 11) he is called, the much enlightened and famous teacher, the disciple of the master of masters, Rabban Bâbhai, the teacher and founder of schools.
p. 304, n. 1 Psalm xli. 12.
p. 304, n. 2 See supra, p. 295, note 7.
p. 305, n. 1 I.e., my poor power.
p. 305, n. 2 ܫܵܡܘܿܢܹ̈ܐ. For the weight and value of these pieces of money see under ܡܲܢܝܵܐ. Payne Smith, Thes., col. 2164.
p. 305, n. 3 St. Mark xii. 42.
p. 305, n. 4 Read always ܛܝܼܪܗܵܢ, i.e., طيرهان. See Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 191, note 1508; Lagarde, Armenische Studien, Nr. 2245, p. 152; B.O., iii. 11. p. 931.
p. 305, n. 5 Read ܚܲܛܪܸܐ, i.e., الحضر, חטרי, Ἄτραι ܚܘܛܪܐ. See Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 184, note 1440. Ḥaṭrâ of Ṭirhân must be distinguished from Ḥaṭrâ of Mârgâ, Ḥaṭrâ in Âthôr, etc.
p. 305, n. 6 I.e., our Lord [is] with him.
p. 306, n. 1 Proverbs xxix. 21. The Hebrew is מְפַנֵּק מִנֹּעַר עַבְדּוֹ וְאַחֲרִיתוֹ יִהְיֶה מָנוֹן and the Greek Ὃς κατασπαταλᾷ ἐκ παιδός, οἰκέτης ἔσται, ἔσχατον δὲ ὀδυνηθήσεται ἐφ᾽ ἑαυτῷ.
p. 307, n. 1 See Book ii. chap. 32, supra, p. 239.

p. 307, n. 2 ܡܓܘܼܫܘܼܬܵܐ, a heresy composed of paganism and Chaldeeism. It adoreth the powers of nature, (lit. elements) like the heathen, worshippeth the stars, and erreth in the computation and knowledge of the planets and Signs of the Zodiac, and in the ruling of the stars, like the Chaldeans. See Payne Smith, Thes., col. 2009.
p. 307, n. 3 See supra, p. 249 ff.

p. 308, n. 1 A village in the diocese of Salâkh, which must be sought for in the territory occupied by the Bâlik Kurds near Rawandiz; it was one of the seats of the Shahrîghân sect. See Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 245.
p. 308, n. 2 ܣܵܛܘܿܪܵܐ, Arab. سَاطُور, plur. سَوَاطير, a cook's large knife with a long, thin blade. Compare ساطر butcher, يسطير couper en longues lignes, Dozy, Supplément, i. p. 652.
p. 309, n. 1 A village in the diocese of Salâkh, and a seat of the Shahrîghân sect. See Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 245.
p. 309, n. 2 1 Kings xvii. 22.
p. 309, n. 3 2 Kings iv. 35.

p. 309, n. 4 The ܫܲܗܪ̈ܝܼܓܵܢ, or ܫܲܪܝܼܓܵܢ were the landed proprietors of the country, and took a higher rank than the Dihkânê (see supra, p. 256). According to Nöldeke (quoted by Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 239) سهريع = رئيس الكورة. The explanation of the word given in Orient. 2441, fol. 367b, col. 1, agrees with that quoted by Hoffmann from the Socin MS. of Bar-Bahlûl; but Rich 7203, fol. 176b, col. 2, gives ܫܗܪ̈ܝܓܢ = اصحاب الملكء القدم. See also Theophylact Simocatta, ed. Bonn v. 9; Nöldeke, Geschichte der Perser, p. 446 f; and Hoffmann, Auszüge, pp. 236–239. The Shahrîghân, الشهارجة, are said to have formed a noble class which ranked next to the three great castes of Sawâd. See Masʿûdî, Murûg al-Dhahab (Les Prairies d'Or), ed. Barbier de Meynard, tom. ii. p. 240, Paris 1863.
p. 310, n. 1 This sentence is quoted in B.O., iii. 1, p. 482, col. 2.
p. 310, n. 2 Psalm xcvii. 11.
p. 310, n. 3 Compare ܝܫܘܥ ܐܠܗܢ Book ii. chap. 34, supra, p. 249, note 2.
p. 310, n. 4 This sentence is quoted in B.O., iii. 1, p. 483, col. 1.
p. 311, n. 1 Vat. has ܡܘܠܐ ܐܘܟܝܬ ܟܘܕܢܬܐ, where ܡܘܠܐ is the Latin mula, بغلة
p. 311, n. 2 ܠܓܵܡܵܐ, Arab. لِجَام, plur. لُجُم, and أَلْجِمَة, and أَلْجُم (Dozy, Supplément, ii. p. 517, col. 2), i.e., Pers. لِگام.
p. 311, n. 3 A seat of the Shahrîghân in the diocese of Salâkh. See Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 245, and B.O., i. p. 194.
p. 311, n. 4 See supra, p. 309, note 4.
p. 311, n. 5 See supra, p. 256, note 2.
p. 312, n. 1 ܥܲܡܝܼܩܵܐ literally deep.
p. 312, n. 2 I.e., Ḥâtim (حاتِم) bar-Ṣâliḥ (صَالِح).
p. 312, n. 3 In the list of chapters at the beginning of the work Mâran-ʿammeh is said to have been appointed Metropolitan of Arbela.

p. 313, n. 1 I.e., لُهْرَاسْپْ, Λροοασπο, see Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 150. Lohrâsp stands for the old Arwatâspa (see Nöldeke, Geschichte der Perser, p. 2, note 1), but the Arabic form of the name is Bohrâsp بهراسف (See Masʿûdî, Les Praires d'Or, tom ii. p. 121
p. 313, n. 3 He sat from 753–772. See Bar-Hebraeus, Chron. Eccles., ii. coll. 156–158.
p. 313, n. 4 I.e., on the patriarchal throne in Arbela.
p. 313, n. 5 I.e., the place of roses.
p. 313, n. 6 ܛܘܼܓܵܪܵܐ = ܛܪܒܲܚܫܵܐ، ܡܨܘܬܐ، ܡܩܝܼܡܵܢܘܼܬܐ، ܗܲܪܵܪܘܼܬܵܐ, contention, resistance, strife, dispute.
p. 314, n. 1 See supra, p. 309.
p. 314, n. 2 See supra, p. 256.
p. 315, n. 1 Read ܠܛܚܘܼܢܵܗ̇.
p. 315, n. 2 Acts xiv. 17.
p. 315, n. 3 This chapter is quoted in B.O., iii. 1, p. 483, col. 1.

p. 316, n. 1 Assemânî has ܕܰܐܒܽܘܪ. Hoffmann transcribes Dêbhwâr (Auszüge, p. 244 and note 1936). This place is mentioned with Dâsen داسن in De Goeje, Bibl. Geogr. Arab., pars vi. p. 245, l. 13. For سا Hoffmann would read والسلق.

p. 316, n. 2 ܐܸܫܛܵܪܵܐ = الصكّ a written document, an order, and الوثيقة, an agreement, treaty. Bar-Bahlûl says that the difference between ܐܫܛܪܐ and ܩܝܵܡܵܐ (covenant) is this: ܐܫܛܪܐ is that which a man takes upon himself by the submission of love (ܒܫܘܥܒܕܐ ܕܚܘܒܬܐ), but ܩܝܵܡܐ is that which he is bound to do under a penalty. See Duval, Lexicon, col. 307. Brit. Mus. MS. Rich 7203, fol. 12a, col. 2, explains the word by كِتاب.
p. 316, n. 3 ܒܹܝܬ ܐܲܦܸܣܩܘܿܦܝܼܘܿܢ = τὸ ἐπισκοπεῖον.
p. 316, n. 4 From this it is clear that Salâkh Gawâithâ lay on the border of Âdhôrbâighân, and it is probable that it is the same place as Salaḳ al-Audî. See Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 245.
p. 316, n. 5 See Bk. ii. chap. 34, supra, p. 250, note 2.
p. 316, n. 6 ܐܹܘܬܲܢܛܝܵܐ = αὐθεντία. See Payne Smith, Thes., col. 103; and Duval, Lexicon, col. 97.
p. 317, n. 1 This monastery was situated on the Tigris, probably near some sulphur spring. Mâr Mâran-ʿammeh went thither to drink the waters of the Tigris; see Bk. iii. chap. X.
p. 317, n. 2 Compare כְּמַלְאַךְ אֱלֹהִים 1 Samuel xxix. 9; מַלְאַךְ הָֽאֱלֹהִים 2 Samuel xiv. 17; ὡς ἄγγελον θεοῦ Galatians iv. 14.
p. 317, n. 3 Literally, the legal performance. Read ܡܸܣܬܲܥܪܵܢܘܼܬܵܗ̇.
p. 317, n. 4 Read ܡܲܠܝܵܐ.
p. 317, n. 5 Read ܡܣܬܲܥܪܐ.

p. 318, n. 1 Genesis vi. 12. The state of society before the Flood is thus described in the Cave of Treasures.ܘܟܕ ܣܓܝܲܬ݀ ܫܪܝܚܘܬܐ ܕܙܢܝܘܬܐ ܕܒܢ̈ܝ ܩܐܝܢ. ܘܠܝܬ ܗ̄ܘ̣ܐ ܠܗܘܢ ܦܘܠܚܢܐ ܐܚܪܢܐ. ܐܠܐ ܙܢܝܘܬܐ ܒܠܚܘܕ. ܘܠܐ ܡܫܬܥܒܕܝܢ ܗ̄ܘ̣ܘ ܠܡܲܕܐܬܐ. ܘܠܝܬ ܗܘܐ ܠܗܘܢ ܪܫܐ ܘܡܕܒܪܢܐ. ܐܠܐ ܡܐܟܠܐ. ܘܡܫܬܝܐ. ܘܠܥܒܘܬܐ. ܘܪܘܘܬܐ. ܘܙܡܪܐ. ܘܪܩܕܐ ܘܫܥܬܐ ܫܐܕܢܝܬܐ. ܘܓܘܚܟܐ ܗ̇ܘ ܕܡܥܒܕ ܢܝܵܚܵܐ ܠܫܐܕ̈ܐ ܘܩܠ ܦܩܪܘܬܐ ܕܓܒܪ̈ܐ. ܟܕ ܨܗ̇ܠܝܢ ܒܬܪ ܢܫ̈ܐ. ܘܢܫ̈ܐ ܨܗ̇ܠܝܢ ܒܬܪ ܓܒܪ̈ܐ… ܘܟܕ ܐܡܠ̱ܟܲܬ݀ ܙܢܝܘܬܐ ܒܒܢ̈ܬ ܩܐܝܢ. ܕܠܐ ܟܘܚܕܐ ܪ̈ܗܛܢ ܗ̄ܘ̈ܝ ܢܫ̈ܐ ܒܬܪ ܓܒܪ̈ܐ. ܘܚܒܝܟܝܢ ܗ̄ܘ̣ܘ ܚܕ ܒܚܕ ܐܝܟ ܬܡܟܐ ܒܥܪܝܪܝܐ. ܘܬܪ̈ܝܢ ܘܬܠܬܐ ܓܒܪ̈ܝܢ ܢܦ̈ܠܝܢ ܗ̄ܘ̣ܘ ܥܠ ܚܕܐ ܐܢܬܬܐ. ܘܗܟܢܐ ܐܦ ܢܫ̈ܐ ܪ̈ܗܛܢ ܒܬܪ ܓܒܪ̈ܐ. ܘܪ̈ܘܚܐ ܛܢܦ̈ܬܐ ܥ̈ܐܠܢ ܗ̄ܘ̈ܝ ܒܢ̈ܫܐ. ܘܝܬܝܪ ܡܢ ܥܠܡ̈ܬܐ ܦܩܝܪ̈ܢ ܗ̄ܘ̈ܝ ܣܒ̈ܬܗܝܢ. ܐܒ̈ܗܐ ܘܒܢܝ̈ܗܘܢ ܡܛܢܦܝܢ ܗ̄ܘ̣ܘ ܒܐܡܗ̈ܬܗܘܢ ܘܒܐܚܘ̈ܬܗܘܢ܀ See Bezold, Die Schatzhöhle, p. 60 f.
p. 318, n. 2 Genesis xix. 24. 25.
p. 318, n. 3 Genesis xxxviii. 18.
p. 318, n. 4 Judges xiv. 1.
p. 318, n. 5 2 Samuel xi. 2.
p. 318, n. 6 1 Corinthians vi. 18.
p. 318, n. 7 1 Corinthians iii. 17.
p. 318, n. 8 We must follow the reading of A.
p. 319, n. 1 Genesis xii. 10.
p. 319, n. 2 Genesis xxvi. 1.
p. 319, n. 3 Genesis xliii. 1.
p. 319, n. 4 Genesis xviii. 21.
p. 319, n. 5 2 Kings xix. 35.
p. 319, n. 6 Psalm xviii. 7; Psalm xcvii. 5; Isaiah v. 25.
p. 320, n. 1 Psalm civ. 32; Isaiah xxiv. 20.
p. 320, n. 2 ܩܲܣܛܘܼܢܵܪܵܐ = quaestionarius i.e., carnifex, qui reos cruciat, examinat, Βασάνων ὑπηρέτης. Du Cange, Glossarium, Script. Med. Inf. Latinitatis, col., 1025.
p. 320, n. 3 2 Kings xix. 35.
p. 320, n. 4 2 Samuel xxiv. 15; 1 Chronicles xxi. 14.
p. 320, n. 5 Genesis xix. 25.
p. 320, n. 6 ܩܲܗܠܵܢܵܐ. Compare ܩܲܗܠܵܢܵܝܵܐ ܒܨ. ܗ̄. ܡܪܢܫܢܐ ܗ̇ܘ ܕܒܩܠ ܡܨܘܬܗ ܟܢܫ ܟܢܘܫܝܐ܀ ܩܗܠܢܝܬܐ ܬܘܒ ܗ̇ܝ ܕܐܡܝܢܐܝܬ ܡܪܝܒܐ ܘܡܪܝܡܐ ܩܠܗ̇ ܒܡܨܘܬܐ. Brit. Mus. MS. Orient. 2441, fol. 325b, col. 2.
p. 321, n. 1 ܒܲܠܚܘܿܕܵܝܘܼܬܵܐ, a rare word.

p. 321, n. 2 ܩܹܛܵܐ = κῆτος. This word is explained by سمك fish, ܢܘܢܐ ܪܒܐ great fish, ܬܢܝܢܐ dragon, تِمْساح crocodile. Brit. Mus. MSS. Rich 7203, fol. 148a, col. 2; and Orient. 2441, fol. 321a, col. 2. See also Ahrens, Buch der Naturgegenstände, (text) p. 55.
p. 321, n. 3 Jonah ii. 10.
p. 322, n. 1 ܐܸܣܛܘܼܟܣܵܐ, i.e., στοιχεῖον.
p. 322, n. 2 ܕܵܚܠܹܗ for ܕܲܚܠܹܗ.
p. 322, n. 3 ܐܵܓܡܵܐ for ܐܲܓܡܵܐ.

p. 322, n. 4 ܙܵܠܵܐ or ܙܲܠܵܐ is the name given by the Syrians to the long, slender reed which grows in marshy places in Mesopotamia from four to eight feet high; the Arabs call it قَصَب. Large patches of the reed are found in the soft ground between hills and mountains. A fine example of such a reedy swamp is that which extends from the Khâbûr to Buḥairet Khâtûnîyyeh, to the west of the Sinjâr Mountains; it affords excellent cover for wild animals of all kinds. I passed it in the late autumn of 1890, and the ride occupied more than two hours. Sir Henry Layard saw a leopard stealing from the high grass at this place. See Nineveh and Babylon, p. 324.
p. 322, n. 5 ܥܵܒܘܿܢܵܐ. A rare word.

p. 322, n. 6 All the MSS. have ܢܲܢܚܹܐ Nânḥê, and according to Stoddard (quoted in Payne Smith, Thes., col. 2387) ܢܸܢܚܵܐ means a kind of hot grass. The word ܢܸܢܚܵܐ, or ܢܵܢܚܵܐ may be a corruption of ܢܝܼܢܵܝܵܐ, Pers. نينيا = ܐܲܡܝܼ or ܐܲܡܐܘܣ, Gr. ἄμμι = نانخواة. See Dozy, Supplément, tom. ii. p. 632, col. 1; Payne Smith, Thes., coll. 223, 229, 2362. Loew in his Aramäische Pflanzennamen, No. 200, p. 259, gives the form ܢܵܢܥܵܐ, נָנְעָא Mentha.
p. 323, n. 1 See Bel and the Dragon, verse 39.
p. 323, n. 2 Read ܕܲܥܒܲܪ ܙܵܐܒܵܐ and see Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 227; and B.O., iii. 1, p. 485, col. 1 (Birtha… quae ultra Zabam fluvium).

p. 324, n. 1 Assemânî has ܒܹܝܬ ܛܵܚܘܼܢܲܝ which Hoffmann compares doubtfully with Taḥwânî (Auszüge, p. 238). In the metrical description of the destruction of this village (Syriac text p. 181, l. 7) Bêth Ṭâhônâi is said to have been situated by the side of a river ܥܠ ܝܲܕ ܢܲܗܪܵܐ.
p. 324, n. 2 This is a ὑποκοριστικόν name composed of ארמן + zâd, زاد; compare ארמנדותא Horn and Steindorff, Sassanidische Siegelsteine, p. 35, Ἀριάμνης, Ἀριαμένης? etc.
p. 324, n. 3 Read ܟܦܪ ܥܘܙܝܠ ܩܪܝܬܐ.

p. 325, n. 1 Literally a convent of daughters of the covenant. See Assemânî, B.O., iii. ii. p. 892 (De Monialibus); and Kayser, Die Canones Jacob's von Edessa, Leipzig, 1886, pp. 110–112. Among the modern Nestorians nunneries seem not to exist. See Badger, Nestorians, vol. ii. p. 170.
p. 325, n. 2 ܐܸܬܲܬ݀ for ܐܸܬܵܬ݀.
p. 325, n. 3 Strike out the point after ܘܡܫܬܕܐ.
p. 325, n. 4 Read ܐܲܪܝܼܡ.
p. 325, n. 5 For examples of ܚܲܝܲܬ used as an adverb see Payne Smith, Thes., col. 1256.
p. 325, n. 6 Numbers xvi. 32.
p. 326, n. 1 See supra, Book iii. chap. 2, p. 296.

p. 326, n. 2 All the MSS. have ܕܡܸܬܦܲܬܬܵܐ, but we must read either ܕܡܸܬܦܲܚܬܵܐ or ܕܐܸܬܦܲܚܬܲܬ݀ (compare ܘܐܸܬܦܲܚܬܲܬ݀ Syriac text p. 182, l. 5, and Brit. Mus. MS. No 17, 153, fol. 69b, col. 1, l. 19), for the roots ܦܲܚܬܸܬ and ܦܲܪܬܸܬ are unknown.
p. 326, n. 3 ܕܘܼܚܢܵܐ, دُخْن, דֹּחַן, דּוֹחִינָא. See Loew, Pflanzennamen, No. 72, p. 101.
p. 326, n. 4 Read, with BC, ܡܢܗ̇.
p. 327, n. 1 For Bêth ʿAinâthâ of Bêth Zabhdai see Bk. i. chap. 7, supra, p. 46.
p. 327, n. 2 See supra, p. 217.

p. 327, n. 3 Assemânî gives (B.O., iii. 1, p. 485, col. 1) ܚܶܒܫܽܘܫܬܴܐ Hebhshûshtâ, i.e., scarab, but both here, and in the Syriac text p. 182, l. 9, the other MSS have ܚܲܒܘܼܫܬܐ. The reading given by Assemânî is probably the more correct. For the Beetle Monastery, ܕܝܪܐ ܕܚܲܒܫ̈ܘܼܫܝܵܬܵܐ, see Bar-Hebraeus, Chronicon, ed. Bedjan, p. 517, l. 16.
p. 327, n. 4 A school was founded here by Mâr Bâbhai: see Book iii. chap. 2, p. 296.

p. 328, n. 1 He was appointed Catholicus A.H. 222 = A.D. 836 and sat for nearly thirteen years. According to Bar-Hebraeus, (Chron. Eccles., ii. col 189) he was a pure and venerable man, but on account of his lack of knowledge failed to govern the Church; before he ascended the patriarchal throne he was Bishop of al-Ḥadîtha. See B.O., iii. 1, p. 508.
p. 328, n. 2 ܩܹܢܵܪܓ seems to be the title of a high office; compare Pers. کنارَنگ Kanârang = χαναράγγης. See Nöldeke, Geschichte der Perser, p. 442, note 5.
p. 328, n. 3 Probably the school founded by Mâr Babhai; see supra, p. 296.
p. 328, n. 5 ܦܨܠ literally, to open out a way.
p. 328, n. 6 Isaiah xiv. 31.
p. 329, n. 1 The Peshîṭtâ has ܘܠܝܬ ܕܝܼܚܝܼܕܵܝ ܒܹܟܝ ܒܥܲܕܥܹ̈ܕܵܘܗܝ.

p. 329, n. 2 A place between Mardîn and Âmid. Concerning its pleasant situation compare cum ad nemorosum quendam locum vineis arbustisque pomiferis consitum Meiacarire nomine venissemus, cui fontes dedere vocabulum gelidi. Ammianus Marcellinus, xviii. 6. 16.
p. 329, n. 3 I.e., زادويه.

p. 329, n. 4 ܓܘܿܓܡܲܠ, or ܓܘܡܠ a place situated on Tell Gômel, about 40 or 50 miles east of Môṣul; here, however, Thomas of Margâ means the whole district of the Gômel valley. See Hoffmann, Auszüge, note 1534, p. 194; the map in Sachau's Reise, in which Kiepert has fixed the exact position of this town; and B.O., ii. p. LXXXIV, and p. 419.
p. 329, n. 5 Read ܘܩܘܪ̈ܝܵܟ.
p. 330, n. 1 I.e., Shâhpuhrân.

p. 330, n. 2 ܫܗܪܝܓ, the first example of the use of the singular of ܫܲܗܪ̈ܝܓܵܢ in Thomas of Margâ. The Pehlevi is shahrîg, or shahrîk, in Neo-Persian shahrî; see Nöldeke, Geschichte der Perser, p. 446.
p. 330, n. 3 I.e., Kôb near Akra; see Badger, Nestorians, vol. 1, p. 101; and Hoffmann, Auszüge, notes 1775, 1793.

p. 330, n. 4 I.e., when the first Sunday of Lent came he had not even bread to begin the fast. ܡܲܥܵܠܲܝ ܨܵܘܡܵܐ = ܚܕ ܒܫܒܐ ܕܡܥܠܵܝ ܨܘܡܐ the first day of the week (i.e., Sunday) of the beginning of the fast.

p. 330, n. 5 I.e., Lent. For the seven fasts of the Nestorians, 1. ܨܘܡܐ ܕܐܪ̈ܒܥܝܢ, 2. ܨܘܡܐ ܕܫ̈ܠܝܚܐ, 3. ܨܘܡܐ ܕܫܘܢܝܐ, 4. ܨܘܡܐ ܕܐܠܝܐ, 5. ܨܘܡܐ ܕܝܠܕܐ, 6. ܨܘܡܐ ܕܢܝܢܘܐ (or ܒܵܥܘܼܬܵܐ), 7. ܨܘܡܐ ܕܒܬܘ̈ܠܬܐ, see Assemânî, B.O., iii. ii. p. CCCLXXXVII.
p. 330, n. 6 Or Bêth Ḳardagh in Margâ; see Book iii. chap. 2, supra, p. 297. This district is also called ܩܲܪܕܵܓܝܼܵܐ; see the Syriac text p. 183, l. 5.
p. 330, n. 7 I.e., a Jacobite.
p. 331, n. 1 All the MSS. have ܬܵܩ̈ܠܹܐ, but we should probably read ܬܲܩ̈ܢܹܐ.
p. 331, n. 2 Read, with BC. ܐܸܣܬܲܟܲܠ.
p. 331, n. 3 ܗܲܪܛ, imperative of ܪܗܛ.
p. 332, n. 1 I.e., شيرزاد, lion's son. In B.O., iii. 1, p. 485, col. 1, he is said to have been the son of Maihrûḳ ܫܷܪܨܰܪ ܒܱܪ ܡܱܝܗܪܽܘܩ. See Horn and Steindorff, Sassanidische Siegelsteine, p. 41.

p. 332, n. 2 I.e., George II. He is said to have been born in Karkhâ and surnamed ابن الصياح Ibn-Eṣṣîâh. He became a monk in the Monastery of Bêth ʿÂbhê, and rose to the dignity of abbot. He was ordained Metropolitan of Gundêshâbhôr by Timothy the Patriarch, and was elected Patriarch A.H. 210 = A.D. 825, and sat for seven years (See B.O., ii. p. 435, col. 2). He died aged one hundred years, and was buried in the Monastery of Kelîl-Îshôʿ. Bar-Hebraeus (Chron. Eccles., ii. col. 187) says that he sat for forty years, but this is a mistake, as we see from the marginal note in Codex L.
p. 332, n. 3 In the Book of the Bee, (ed. Budge, p. 93 text, l. 6), the form ܡܝܼܗܵܪܘܿܩ Mîhârôḳ occurs. Compare ܕܵܕܘܼܩ Dâdhûk, Hoffmann, Auszüge, note 278; and Nöldeke, Geschichte der Perser, p. 11.
p. 332, n. 4 See Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 223, and supra, p. 297, note 3.
p. 333, n. 1 ܡܡܲܝܩܵܢܵܐܝܼܬ scoffingly. There is no example of this word in Payne Smith's Thesaurus.
p. 333, n. 2 Read ܒܪܝܼܟܵܐ.
p. 333, n. 3 I.e., Gebel Maḳlûb. See Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 175, note 1371.

p. 333, n. 4 On the margin of the MSS. is written a verse in dodecasyllabic metre which reads: — The most pious Metropolitan Mâran-ʿammeh, who excelled in mighty deeds, who was fertile in marvellous acts of strength, who spake and burned up him that dwelt insolently in a tower, avenged the blood of the righteous Mâr Nestorius.
p. 334, n. 1 I.e., How very little of this power of the Apostles hast thou seen even now!

p. 334, n. 2 Îshôʿ bar-Nôn was a native of Bêth Gabbârê, a village in the district of Nineveh, and lived for thirty-eight years in the Monastery of Saʿîd near Môṣul. He maintained a controversy against the Catholicus Timothy whom, playing upon his name, he called Tâlêmathêôs or God-reviler, and when Timothy died he was elected Catholicus A.D. 820. He sat four years, and died aged eighty-four years; he was buried in the Monastery of Kelîl-Îshôʿ (See B.O., ii. pp. 434, 435; Bar-Hebraeus, Chron. Eccles., ii. col. 181). For ʿAbhd-Îshôʿ's list of his works see B.O., iii. 1, p. 165.
p. 335, n. 1 See Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 227.
p. 335, n. 2 All the MSS. have ܥܘܼܬܩܵܐ, but read ܥܘܼܬܵܩܵܐ.

p. 336, n. 1 The ܫܵܘܒܵܐ is a hot, dry wind which dries up every pool and watercourse, and parches the ground, and destroys all vegetable life; in Deuteronomy xxviii. 22 it is mentioned with fever, fiery heat and mildew. Its effect upon the wheat crops may be gathered from Joshua the Stylite, who says that in the month of Îyâr (May, A.D. 501) there blew a hot wind for three days, and all the corn of our land was dried up save in a few places, ܢܦܩܬ ܪܘܚܐ ܕܫܘܒܐ ܝܘܡ̈ܬܐ ܬܠܬ̈ܐ. ܘܤܒ ܟܠܗ ܥܒܘܪܐ ܕܐܬܪܢ. ܣܛܪ ܡܢ ܕܘܪ̈ܝܬܐ ܙܥܘܪ̈ܝܬܐ (ed. Wright, text p. 41, translation, p. 35). The country round about Môṣul has always been, and is still, peculiarly liable to great famines. The ܫܵܘܒܵܐ wind first dries up everything, then the locusts appear, and after them the cholera. The terrible famine which took place there a few years ago, when the British Vice-Consul Mr. Russell acted so nobly, is so recent that it scarcely needs to be mentioned; those who are interested in the subject may, however, find details in Sachau, Reise in Mesopotamien, p. 344. According to Bar-Hebraeus, (Chronicle, text, ed. Bruns, p. 123) in the year 721 the water supply failed, and the villagers were obliged to go a distance of seven miles to fetch water. In the same year wheat and grain were very scarce, and in the following year the locusts came in great numbers. Two years later there was a great pestilence in Mesopotamia. In the year 784 flying locusts came and destroyed the crops, and made their way up the walls and through doors and windows into the houses which were filled with them. They filled all the water vessels, and having entered the houses from the south side they left them from the north side; having eaten up the grass and trees, they even devoured woollen garments and clothes. Three years after this plague a mighty famine took place. (B.H., Chronicle, text, p. 134) About the year 842 there was a mighty famine and terrible pestilence and suffering by reason of the heavy taxes and exactions of the rebels (B.H., Chronicle, text, p. 160). In A.H. 234 there blew over the whole of Mesopotamia a mighty, hot wind the like of which none remembered ever to have blown before, ريح شديدة وسَمُوم لم يعهد قبلها مثلها; see Gottwaldt, Hamzae Ispahanensis Annalium, Leipzig, 1844, vol. 1, p. 188; Abû-ʾl-Maḥâsm, ed. Juynboll, vol. 1, p. 801; and Bar-Hebraeus, Historia Dynastiarum, Oxford 1663, pp. 92, 93, 94, 98.
p. 337, n. 1 I.e., A.D. 819, Hoffmann thinks we should read ܗܢܐ ܒܡܐܬܝܢ ܘܬܠܬܝܢ ܘܐܪܒܥ two hundred and thirty-fourth year (i.e., A.D. 848). See the preceding note.

p. 337, n. 2 I.e., the Hebrew Fortress. Thomas of Margâ may refer to the Jewish community living round about Nebi Yûnus. This mound is called تلّ الثّوْبَة, or in Syriac ܬܠܐ ܕܬܝܒܘܬܐ the mound of repentance, because the prophet Jonah is said to have gathered the Ninevites together, and to have preached to them there, after which they repented. The position of the Monastery of Yûnus ibn-Mattai, دير يونس بن مَتَّى is described in Yâḳût, ii. p. 810. The fountain of Yûnus is about one mile distant from the mound; see Voyages d'ibn Batoutah, ed. Defrémery, tom. ii. p. 137. Nebi Yûnus is within the walls which mark the site of the ancient Nineveh, and is opposite Kouyunjik (Koyunshik) and Môṣul. The excavations which have been made there have brought to light inscriptions of Sennacherib and Esarhaddon. For a description of the plaee see Tuch, De Nino Urbe, p. 50; Rich, Narrative of a Residence, vol. ii. p. 44; Sandreczki, Reise nach Mosul, part ii. p. 48; Sachau, Reise in Mesopotamien, p. 343. It is also possible that the words Hebrew Fortress may refer to the mound of Kouyunjik, upon which stood the قلعة نينوى or Nineveh Castle; the mound was called ܬܠܐ ܕܚܣܢܐ ܕܢܝܢܘܐ the hill of the Nineveh Fortress, or حصن نينوى, or تلّ نينوى. See Rich, Narrative, vol. ii. p. 55; Bar-Hebraeus, Historia Dynastiarum, pp. 404, 441; and Tuch, De Nino Urbe, p. 49. In Bk. iv. chap. 5 ܚܣܢܐ ܥܒܪܝܐ is said to be in Nineveh and in Bk. v. chap. 2 it is said to be a town ܡܕܝܢܬܐ.
p. 338, n. 1 ܫܦܝܼܥܵܐܝܼܬ.
p. 338, n. 2 Compare الثرثار.
p. 338, n. 3 ܪܵܓܘܿܠܵܐ, in Neo-Syriac ܪܵܘܘܿܠܵܐ. See Hoffmann, Auszüge, note 1794, p. 225; and Nöldeke, Grammatik der Neusyrischen Sprache, p. 39.
p. 338, n. 5 Psalm iii. 1.
p. 338, n. 6 Psalm cxix. 84.
p. 338, n. 7 Compare Job vii. 19.
p. 338, n. 8 Compare Proverbs xv. 15; Ecclesiastes xii. 1.
p. 339, n. 1 ܚܸܕܪܵܐ i.e., what is obtained by begging. Payne Smith prefers the form ܚܕܪܵܐ (Thes., col. 1205).

p. 339, n. 2 ܣܘܿܣ̈ܝ ܡܲܥܦܪܐ, the knotted fringe or tassels of the Kaffiyyeh (كَفِّيَّة) or turban cloth. ܣܘܿܣ̈ܝ = ܣ̈ܘܿܣܲܝ from the singular ܣܸܣܵܐ or ܣܲܣܵܐ. Compare סִיסַיָּא ,סִיסִין, glomi filorum, (Buxtorf, ed. Fischer, p. 737, col. 2; Levy, Chald. Wörterbuch, p. 159, col. 2), and ܣܷܣܴܐ = القبّة Payne Smith, Thesaurus, col. 2682. In the east to this day kaffiyyehs are woven with long fringes, and when the purchaser has made his selection, the merchant hands it over to a man or woman who plaits the fringe into thin cords, each of which he knots at the end, or works it into a little round ball which is often sewn over with coloured silks and thread of gold.
p. 339, n. 3 ܡܲܚ̈ܝܵܢ for ܡܵܚ̈ܝܵܢ.

p. 340, n. 1 ܛܸܦܪܹ̈ܐ ܪܲܟܝܼܟܵܬܵܐ literally soft nails, i.e., from babyhood and tenderest childhood. The expression also occurs in Bar-Hebraeus, Chron. Eccles., I. col. 729, l. 14, and is applied to one whom Dionysius had taught from his earliest childhood in his cell.
p. 340, n. 2 Literally, a mount. ܪܵܟܘܿܒܵܐ = ܪܵܟܘܼܒܵܐ.

p. 340, n. 3 See Book iii. chap. 5, supra, p. 317. This monastery was probably situated near some sulphur spring close to the Tigris. Between Môṣul and Tekrît are many such, and a daily draught of the water or bath is most beneficial in many diseases.
p. 341, n. 1 Rêwâi appears to be a diminutive formed from some name; compare Rêw-Ardâshîr.
p. 341, n. 2 I.e., Luhrâsp, لُهْرَسْپ; for this name see Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 150; and Nöldeke, Geschichte der Perser, p. 2.
p. 341, n. 3 Read ܡܸܬܦܲܪܣܝܼܢ.
p. 341, n. 4 ܙܘܼܙܹ̈ܐ, drachmas or dirhams.
p. 342, n. 1 Read ܪܵܟܘܼܒܵܐ.

p. 342, n. 2 According to Bar-Bahlûl (Brit. Mus. Or. 2441, fol. 343b, col. 1) ܩܣܛܪ̈ܘܡܐ is the name given to the two balustrades (or banisters), between which the steps were built ܬܪ̈ܬܝܢ ܣܡܟܝ̈ܬܐ ܗܢܝܢ ܕܒܢܝ̈ܢ ܡܨܥܬܗܘܢ (sic) ܕܪ̈ܓܐ. Another lexicon, Brit. Mus. Add. 7203, fol. 159a, col. 2, says that ܩܣܛܪܘܡܐ is the raised platform (or dais) which is before the door of the altar, المَصْطَبَة التى قُدّامَ بابِ المَذْبَع; and India Office Lexicon, fol. 11b, col. 2, explains both ܩܣܛܪܘܡܐ and ܩܢ̈ܟܐ by المَذْبَع the altar. ܩܣܛܪܘܡܐ = אוּלָם in Ezechiel viii. 16; Joel ii. 17. ܩܣܛܪܘܡܐ is the whole area of the church before the ܒܝܼܡܵܐ, (not the place where the seats of the clergy stand), and was the raised or built up floor of the choir upon which the altar of sacrifice, ܡܲܨܛܒܬܵܐ, stood. (Compare Σωλέας, Pars templi quae Bemati observatur, quae uno aut altero gradu aedis sacrae pavimento eductior est. Βῆμα Sacrarium, Locus in templo ubi consistant sacerdotes, et quem nulli Laïco ingredi fas erat. Du Cange, Glossarium, coll. 195, 1513). The ܩܣܛܪܘܡܐ also included the ܕܪ̈ܓܐ ܕܩܢ̈ܟܐ, and its pavement was three steps above the pavement of the rest of the church. (See B.O., iii. ii. p. 802, note 1). ܩܣܛܪܘܡܐ seems to mean primarily a tiled pavement (compare Bekker, Anecdota Graeca, Tom. 1. p. 269, l. 27, where καλαμίδας is explained by ἢ τοὺς θηλυκοὺς καλάμους τοὺς πρὸς σύνδεσμον τῶν πλινθίνων καταστρωμάτων τῆς οἰκοδομίας), and cannot be older than the ἔδαφος πλινθοις καταστρωμένον which was laid on the ground before the temple where the altar of burnt sacrifice was placed. ܩܣܛܪܘܡܐ is also the deck of a vessel; compare καταστρώματα, τῆς νεὼς μέρος, ἐν ᾧ ἑστῶτες ναυμαχοῦσιν, Hesychius, Lexicon, ed. Schmidt, Jena, 1857, p. 435. On men-of-war the κατάστρωμα must have been the uppermost deck of all, as the combatants were posted on it when the ship went into action: see Thucydides, i. 49. 1, 3; Polybios, i. 44. 3; Plutarch, Themistocles, 14, Antonius, 67. On merchantmen the κατάστρωμα must also have been the uppermost deck, for the depth of the ship was reckoned from the κατάστρωμα to the bottom of the hold: see Lucian, navigium, V. See also Kraus, Real-Encyklopädie der Christlichen Alterthümer, Freiburg in Breisgau, 1880, articles ΑΜΒΩΝ, ΒΗΜΑ (vol. 1, pp. 43–46), and Basilica (vol. 1, pp. 109–143); De Vogüé, Syrie Centrale, Planches 119, 126, 138; L'Eglise de Saint-Jérémie à Abou-Gosch (Emmaus), with plans, by C. Mauss in Revue Archéologique, 3ième Série, Tom. xix. p. 223 ff. and Assemânî, B.O., iii. 1, p. 537, capp. 3 and 5; iii. ii. pp. 795, 821, 835. In Assemânî, Codex Liturgicus, tom. ix. Appendix, p. 281, note 2, we have ܩܣܛܪܘܡܐ explained by Cancellos qui Ecclesiae Sanctuariam a Navi, seu loco fidelium separant. From ܩܣܛܪܘܡܐ comes the Arabic مَقْصُورَة balustrade en bois ou en bronze autour du cénotaphe d'un saint. Dozy, Supplément, tom. ii. p. 358, col. 2.

p. 343, n. 1 The ܩܲܢ̈ܟܹܐ was included in the ܩܣܛܪܘܡܐ, and strictly speaking, meant the beginning of the ܩܣܛܪܘܡܐ; compare ܣܪܘܼܓܵܐ, Payne Smith, Thes., col. 2727; and ܐܣܟ̈ܦܬܐ ܕܩܢ̈ܟܐ limina Cancellorum, B.O., iii. ii. p. 821, l. 28. In Brit. Mus. Or. 2441, fol. 342b, col. 2, we have ܩܢ̈ܟܐ ܗ̄. ܒܝܬ ܡܕܒܚܐ بيت المذبح وهو البيت المقدس المحترم الذى لا يلجه الا الكهنه وارباب الراب وهو مميا من جيره.
p. 344, n. 1 ܥܵܠܡܝܸܢܵܐܝܼܬ everlastingly. A rare word.
p. 345, n. 1 In dodecasyllabic metre.
p. 345, n. 2 ܥܘܢܵܝܵܐ cantus responsorius, sic dictus quod uno canente chorus consonando respondeat. Payne Smith, Thes., col. 2927.
p. 345, n. 3 Read ܐܲܪܥܵܢܵܝܬܐ.
p. 345, n. 4 ܐܵܦܛܪܘܿܦܵܐ = ἐπίτροπος.
p. 346, n. 1 ܐܲܬܠܝܼܛܘܼܬܵܐ = ἄθλησις.
p. 346, n. 2 See Hoffmann, Auszüge, note 1440, p. 184; and supra, p. 305.
p. 346, n. 3 I.e., طيرهان. See Hoffmann, Auszüge, note 1508, p. 191; De Goeje, Bibl. Geogr. Arabicorum, pars vi. p. 245, l. 6.
p. 346, n. 4 Read ܝܘܼܒܵܠܵܐ. A reads from a beautiful root.
p. 347, n. 1 ܙܵܕ̈ܩܹܐ = ܐ̄ܚ̈ܝܵܢܹܐ.
p. 347, n. 2 Read ܕܒܹܐܘܩܝܼܢܵܐ. ܐܘܩܝܢܐ, Talm. אוקינום = ὄγκινος. For the forms of the word see Payne Smith, Thes., col. 88.
p. 347, n. 3 See Book iii. chaps. 1–3, supra, pp. 289–298.
p. 347, n. 4 Read ܐܸܣ̈ܟܘܿܠܹܐ.
p. 347, n. 5 Deut. xxxiv. 9.

p. 348, n. 1 Theodore was born at Antioch, and was the son of wealthy parents. He succeeded Olympius as Bishop of Mopsuestia in Cilicia about A.D. 394, and died A.D. 429, having filled the office of bishop for thirty-six years. In Nestorian writings he is usually called the Expositor (see Budge, Book of the Bee, p. 140), on account of his having written expositions or commentaries on the greater number of the books of the Bible. Whatever were his exact opinions upon the Natures of Christ, it is certain that the Nestorians began at a very early date to quote them in support of their own views. Maʿnâ, a Persian by race, from the town of Bêth Hardashêr, who was resident at Edessa in the earlier part of the fifth century, and is mentioned by Simeon of Bêth Arshâm among the distinguished Nestorian scholars whom he holds up to ridicule, devoted himself to the task of translating into Syriac the commentaries of Theodore of Mopsuestia during the lifetime of that great theologian (Wright, Syr. Lit., p. 830.). According to ʿAbhd-Îshôʿ, Theodore composed in all forty-one volumes. He wrote a commentary on Genesis in three volumes; a metaphysical work for the noble Alphaeus entitled ܦܠܝܼܚ ܒܙܢܐ ܘܬܐܘܪܝܐ; a commentary on the Psalms in five volumes for Ḳerdûn and his brother; a commentary on the twelve Minor Prophets in two volumes for Mâr Ṭûrîs; a commentary on Samuel in one volume for Mamarianus; a commentary on Job in two volumes for Cyril of Alexandria; a commentary on Ecclesiastes in one volume for Porphyry; and a commentary on Isaiah, Ezekiel, Jeremiah and Daniel. On St. Matthew he wrote a commentary for Julius in one volume; on Luke and John for Eusebius; on the Acts of the Apostles for Basil; on the Romans for Eusebius; on the two books of the Corinthians for Theodore; on four letters for Eustratius, and on Galatians and Ephesians; on Philippians, Colossians and the two books of the Thessalonians for Jacob; on Timothy for Peter; on Titus, and Philemon, and Hebrews for Cyrinus; and five volumes on the works of the other apostles. He wrote a book on the Sacraments; another on Faith; two volumes on the Priesthood; two volumes on the Holy Spirit; one volume on the Incarnation; two volumes against Eunomius; two volumes against those who would say, Sin is ingrained in [our] nature; two volumes against Magianism; one volume to Monks; one on obscure speech ܕܡܡܠܠܐ ܐܘܟܡܐ; one volume on Perfection of manner of life; five volumes against Allegorists, ܦܹ̈ܠܸܐܬܵܢܵܝܹܐ; one volume on behalf of Basil; one volume on the taker and that which is taken, ܢܵܣܘܼܒܵܐ ܘܲܢܣܝܼܒܵܐ; the Book of the Pearl, in which his letters are collected; and a discourse on the laying down of the Law, ܣܝܵܡ ܢܵܡܘܼܣܵܐ. See Assemânî, B.O., iii. 1, pp. 30–35; iii. ii. pp. 190, 203, 227, 228; Bar-Hebraeus, Chron. Eccles., i. col. 124; ii. coll. 58, 64, 74; Fabricius, Bibl. Graec., vol. x. p. 346 ff.; Tillemont, Mémoires, tom. vi. p. 219 (ed. Brussels 1732); and Wright, Catalogue of Syriac MSS., p. 1329, col. 1.
p. 349, n. 1 Read ܗܵܘܢܹܗ.
p. 349, n. 2 ܚܘܼܩܵܐ, an uncommon word.
p. 349, n. 3 Ezra iii. 2; 1 Esdras v. 8.
p. 349, n. 4 Arbêl, Irbîl, or Erbil إِرْبِل. See Hoffmann, Auszüge, pp. 231, 233.
p. 350, n. 1 ܒܵܕܘܿܩܵܐ is explained by اقول البحّاث المفتّش العلوم Duval, Lexicon, col. 358. See also Hoffmann, Opuscula Nestoriana, pp. XX. XXI.
p. 350, n. 2 From this we may perhaps conclude that the village or town of Kĕphar ʿUzzêl was the seat of the Bishop of Margâ; see Hoffmann, Auszüge, pp. 237, 296.
p. 350, n. 3 Here we must follow the reading of BC.
p. 351, n. 1 BC read ܥܲܩܪܵܐ. The metre requires that we should adopt this reading.
p. 351, n. 2 All the MSS. have ܠܪ̈ܓܠܘܗܝ, but we should probably read ܠܪ̈ܓܫܘܗܝ.
p. 351, n. 3 St. John xiv. 23.
p. 352, n. 1 2 Timothy iii. 8.
p. 352, n. 2 St. Matthew xxv. 15.
p. 352, n. 3 Well done, good and faithful servant: etc. St. Matthew xxv. 21.
p. 353, n. 1 Read ܒܹܝܬ ܢܵܘܵܐ. See Bk. iii. chap. 3, supra, p. 308.
p. 353, n. 2 1 Samuel, xxxi. 4.
p. 353, n. 3 Read, with BC ܩܵܥܝܐ ܗ̄ܘܼܬ ܠܗ̇.
p. 354, n. 2 Acts ix. 40.
p. 354, n. 3 1 Kings xvii. 23.

p. 354, n. 4 ܦ̈ܘܠܘܿܢܵܝܹܐ, i.e., the followers of Παυλωνᾶς or Παυλῖνος, a pupil of Ephraim Syrus (died A.D. 373). Paulonas or Paulinus is probably the same who is mentioned by ʿAbhd-Îshôʿ as having written metrical homilies, discourses against inquirers, disputations against Marcion, and a treatise concerning believers and the creed. ܣܡ ܡܕܪ̈ܫ. ܘܡ̈ܠܐ ܕܠܘܩܒܠ ܒܵܨܘ̈ܝܐ. ܘܕܪ̈ܫܐ ܕܠܘܩܒܠ ܡܪܩܝܘܢ. ܘܥܠ ܡܗܝ̈ܡܢܐ ܘܗܝܡܢܘܬܐ. See Wright, Syr. Lit., p. 828; B.O., iii. 1. pp. 170, 171, note 4; Tillemont, Mémoires, tom. iv. p. 126; Epiphanius, Haeres., LXXVII; Socrates, Hist. Eccles., iii. 6. 9; Sozomen, Hist. Eccles., v. 12. 13, etc. Compare also ܦܘܠܘܢ̈ܝܢܐ ܘܲܬܪ̈ܲܝܵܢܲܝ ܒ̈ܢܲܝܵܐ, B.O., iii. 1, p. 120, col. 2, l. 9.

p. 355, n. 2 The metre requires us to read ܠܟܠ.

p. 371, n. 1 I.e., the earthly Paradise. As to where the souls abide from the time they leave their bodies until the resurrection, some say that they are taken up to heaven, that is, to the region of the spirit where the celestial hosts dwell. Others say that they go to Paradise, that is, to the place which is abundantly supplied with the good things of the mystery of the revelation of God; and that the souls of sinners lie in darkness in the abyss of Eden outside Paradise. (Compare Animas Sanctorum, statim atque corporibus solvuntur, in Paradisum terrestrem deferri; Damnatorum verò Animas in inferiori loco apud eundem Paradisum collocari; B.O., iii. 11, p. 342, No. 4) Others say that they are buried with their bodies; that is to say, as the two were buried in God at baptism, so also will they now dwell in Him until the day of the resurrection. Others say that they stand at the mouth of the graves and await their Redeemer; that is to say, they possess the knowledge of the resurrection of their bodies. Book of the Bee, ed. Budge, p. 132. See also Badger, Nestorians, vol. ii. p. 419.
p. 371, n. 2 I.e., the temple of the flesh.

p. 371, n. 3 The whole choir, as well as the sacred table, is often called ܡܲܕܒܚܵܐ. Thomas of Margâ wishes to say that just as the body of Mâran-ʿammeh was laid on the right hand side of the choir, ܒܗܲܝܟܠܐ ܥܡ ܩܣܛܪܘܡܐ. ܕܩܢ̈ܟܐ ܒܓܒܐ ܕܝܡܝܢܐ (text. p. 171, l. 6), so he will one day stand at the right hand of the presence of God.

p. 379, n. 3 I.e., Ḥĕnân-Îshôʿ II., who succeeded Mâr Jacob as Nestorian Patriarch A. Gr., 1085 = A.D., 774 = A.H. 157; he died A.D. 780. For his writings see B.O., iii. 1, pp. 155, 157. For the famous Chinese-Syriac monument of Singan-fu, which was inscribed during the reign of this Patriarch, see B.O., iii. 11, p. 538 ff.; Yule, The Book of Ser Marco Polo, vol. ii. p. 13 ff.; Bar-Hebraeus, Chron. Eccles., ii. p. 166, note 1; B.O., iii. 1, p. 156. Copies of this interesting document have been published by Kircher, China Monumentis, Amsterdam, 1667; Pauthier, L'inscription Syro-Chinoise de Si-ngan-fou, Paris 1858; Yule, Ser Marco Polo, vol. ii. facing p. 16 (from a rubbing by Dr. Lockhart); and a new edition of these texts was promised by Heller, Prolegomena zu einer neuen Ausgabe der Nestorianischen Inschriften von Singan-fu (in Verhandlungen des VII Orient. Congresses in Wien, 1886).

p. 380, n. 3 I.e., Abraham bar-Lîphê who flourished about A.D. 750. He wrote an Exposition of the Offices ܦܘܼܫܵܩܵܐ ܕܬܸܫܹ̈ܡܫܵܬܵܐ, for which reason he is called the Expositor. He held the belief that souls are sentient things after they have left their bodies, and that after the general resurrection their memory of the Trinity would be blotted out. See B.O., iii. 1, pp. 528, 530.
p. 380, n. 1 See supra, p. 236.
p. 380, n. 2 See B.O., iii. 1, pp. 196, 197, note 2.

He held the belief that souls are sentient things after they have left their bodies, and that after the general resurrection their memory of the Trinity would be blotted out. See B.O., iii. 1, pp. 528, 530.
p. 380, n. 4 See Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 223.

p. 383, n. 3 Timothy I. was a native of Ḥazzâ in Adiabene, and a pupil of Abraham bar-Dàshandâdh at the school of Bâshosh in Saphsâphâ; he became Patriarch about A.D. 780 and died A.H., 204, or 205 = A.D. 819—820, or 820—821. The story of Timothy's accession is thus told by Bar-Hebraeus (Chron. Eccles., ii. col. 165 f.): — After Ḥĕnân-Îshôʿ II. arose Timothy, Bishop of Bâghâsh, a diocese in the mountains of Arbela. Now when Ḥĕnân-Îshôʿ was dead a schism fell among the Bishops and the people. Some of them wished Ephraim, Metropolitan of Gundê-Shâbhôr to be Patriarch, some wished for Thomas, Bishop of Kashkar, and some for this Timothy. Then Timothy acted craftily, and having filled bags (ܩܘܪ̈ܥܐ) with copper money (ܡܵܥܹ̈ܐ = ܙܘ̈ܙܐ), he sealed them, and took them with him. And he called the scholastics (ܣܟܘܠܝܣ̈ܛܝܩܘ) to him secretly by night, and said to them, I have collected all this money, dînârs and dirhams, and I wish to spend it upon [your] school; help me then, and ye shall find good [for yourselves]. And they being led astray believed his words, and went forth and fought against all those who were opposed to [the election of] Timothy. And they brought the Bishops by force, and took Timothy and carried him to Seleucia and proclaimed him Patriarch. Meanwhile Thomas, Metropolitan of Kashkar, gathered together thirteen bishops, and they came to Bagdad and tarried in the Monastery of Mâr Pethiôn, and they deposed Timothy on the third Sunday of the forty days' fast; and Timothy gathered together other [bishops] and excommunicated Thomas. Thomas and his bishops then elected the monk George, but this rival died suddenly, and Timothy having succeeded in deceiving Bêrôë the archdeacon, بيروى الاركدياقون, and the heads of colleges (as stated above), by promising them large sums of money he caused himself to be elected Patriarch. Subsequently Ephraim of Gundê-Shâbhôr, Solomon of al-Ḥadîthah, Joseph of Merv, and Sergius of Maʿallthâ held a synod at the Monastery of Bêth Ḥâlê, in which they made Rôsṭâm, Bishop of Ḥĕnâithâ, Metropolitan of Adiabene in place of Îshôʿ-yahbh, and excommunicated Timothy, who, in return excommunicated Joseph of Merv. Joseph laid the matter before the Khalif of Bagdad, al-Mahdî, but obtaining no support from him, he turned Muhammedan, and is said by Bar-Hebraeus (Chron. Eccles., ii. col. 171) to have been publicly convicted of sodomy. Timothy was excommunicated a second time by Ephraim of Gundê-Shâbhôr, and retorted by a counter-excommunication. On the whole subject see Wright, Syriac Literature, p. 845; Bar-Hebraeus, Chron. Eccles., ii. coll. 165—169; B.O., ii. pp. 433, 434; iii. 1. 158—163. According to ʿAbhd-Îshôʿ, Timothy wrote the Book of the Stars; a Disputation with al-Mahdî; a work on Ecclesiastical Judgments; Synodical Volumes, ܛܘܡܣ̈ܐ ܣܘܼܢܵܗ̈ܕܝܼܩܵܝܹܐ; two hundred Letters arranged in two volumes; a volume of Questions; a volume on Chapters; and a history. See B.O., iii. 1. pp. 162, 163.

p. 385, n. 4 Read ܘܐܲܣܒܲܪ.

p. 386, n. 2 ܩܵܬܵܪܵܣܝܼܣ = κάθαρσις = المُبَاعد. According to Brit. Mus. MS. Orient 2441, fol. 351b, col. 2, the word means ܡܬܪܚܩܢܘܬܐ ܠܐ ܡܬܥܒܪܢܝܬܐ ܕܟܠܡܐ ܕܫܪܝܪ ܘܡܬܚܘܝܐ ܒܒܪܬܩܠܐ المباعدة الابعاد عن الجماعة.

p. 386, n. 6 ܩܪܕܓ in Turkish means Black Mountain. Mâr Ḳardâgh was of noble birth, and is said to have been a descendant of Nimrod on his father's side, and of Sennacherib on his mother's; he was endowed with great physical beauty, and fine mental qualities, but he was originally a heathen. He was martyred in the forty-ninth year of the reign of Sapor II. i.e., A.D. 358. For the life, history and acts of Mâr Ḳardagh see Feige, Die Geschichte des Mâr Abhdîshô und seines Jüngers Mâr Qardagh, Kiel, 1889; Abbeloos, Acta Mar Ḳardaghi Assyriae Praefecti qui sub Sapore II martyr occubuit, Bruxelles, 1890; Bedjan, Acta Martyrum et Sanctorum, tom. ii. pp. 442—506, Paris, 1891.

p. 390, n. 1 Literally a feast of cakes of his dainty foods; ܦܘܼܚܪܵܐ = a drinking party, a banquet. According to Lagarde, Pûrîm, פּוּרִים, ܦܘܼܚܪܵܐ, Mandaïtic פוהרא are derived from فروهران the Persian name of a festival. ܙܵܘܬܪܹ̈ܐ (for ܙܲܘܬܵܪܹ̈ܐ) = cakes, and in Jeremiah vii. 18, translates the Hebrew כַּוָּנִים. The word is explained by the native lexicographers to mean, sacrifices offered to idols; sacrifices which were offered to devils in the time of the heathen, and which the Arabs still make in their festival; and cakes made of fine flour, oil and honey. For the texts see Payne Smith, Thes., coll. 1163, 1164; Duval, Lexicon, col. 684. The reading of BC Vat. ܕܙܲܦܬܵܪܹ̈ܐ is a mistake for ܕܐܲܦܬܵܪܹ̈ܐ, the sing. of which ܐܲܦܬܵܪܵܐ nausea, is also explained by the food which burneth in the stomach of gluttons, and which maketh smoke in the throat; see Payne Smith, Thes., col. 354. The form ܐܲܦܬܪܐ indigestion, is given in Duval, Lexicon, col. 269. Compare Armen. zoh sacrifice. Lagarde, Armenische Studien, p. 55, No. 792 (Abhandlungen König. Gesell. Wissen. zu Göttingen, Histor.-Philolog. Classe, Bd. XXII. No. 4).

p. 390, n. 2 Assemânî translates, Accidit enim, ut Rostamus per eos dies dum superbo sui fastus mulo vectus ab obscoeno secessu, epulisque impudicitiam redolentibus exsaturatus, etc. (B.O., iii. 1, p. 209, col. 1)
p. 390, n. 3 ܪܟܘܿܒܹܗ for ܪܟܘܼܒܹܗ.

p. 390, n. 4 This danger to strange travellers riding through villages in Mesopotamia is sometimes very great, for the dogs rush out in a body, barking and howling, and often endeavour to bite the horse's legs. Nothing but a good, long whip vigorously applied will drive them away, and I have even known it necessary to shoot one or more of them.
