p. 396, n. 1 Pachomius was born in the nome of Esneh, (Egypt. 𓋴𓈖𓊖 sen, Copt. ⲥⲛⲏ), about A.D. 292, and his parents were pagans; he became a Christian at a little village called ϣⲉⲛⲉⲥⲏⲧ, (the Χηνοβόσκιον of the Greeks) which was situated on the right or east bank of the Nile in the nome of Diospolis Parva. He lived during the time of the persecution of Diocletian, and at its ending he was about twenty years old. When the Persians threatened to make war against the Greeks (ⲛⲓⲣⲱⲙⲁⲓⲟⲥ), he was drawn as a recruit from his native village, and being fed by Christians when they stopped at the town of Esneh, he was greatly impressed by their charity. Next day he sailed as far as Antinoë, and was met there by the news that the Greeks had conquered the Persians, and that the recruits were to be sent back to their homes. On his way back he came to the desert village of Shenesêt, which was burnt up by excessive heat ⲟⲩϯⲙⲓ ⲛ̀ ⲉⲣⲏⲙⲟⲥ ϫⲉ ϣⲉⲛⲉⲥⲏⲧ ⲉϥⲣⲟⲕϩ ϩⲓⲧⲉⲛ ⲡⲁϣⲁⲓ ⲛ̀ ⲛⲓⲕⲁⲩⲙⲁ, and there God appeared to him and told him to take up his abode. Three years later he joined Abbâ Palamôn (ⲡⲁⲗⲁⲙⲱⲛ), and became his disciple. Soon after this his sister Mary came to Tabenna (ⲧⲁⲃⲉⲛⲛⲏⲥⲓ, see Quatremère, Mémoires Géographiques, tom. I. p. 281) to see him, but he refused to see her, and learning that she was disposed to lead a life of good works, he sent some of his brethren to build a habitation for her at some distance from the monastery. A number of pious women joined her, and she became the founder of a rule of nuns. Some time later Pachomius went to the north of Panopolis (ϣⲙⲓⲛ, Aḥmîm) and built monasteries at Smine, or Tesmine (see Champollion, L'Égypte sous les Pharaons, tom. 1. p. 265), and at Phenoum, ⲫⲛⲟⲩⲙ, near the mountains of Esneh. Thus in founding monasteries, in confirming the brethren, in healing the sick, and in working miracles Pachomius passed his life; and died about A.D. 351, aged sixty years. The above facts are drawn from the Coptic life of Pachomius published by Amélineau, entitled Histoire de Saint Pakhôme et de ses Communautés, (in Annales du Musée Guimet) Paris, 1889; and from Étude Historique sur Saint Pachome (in Bulletin de l'Institut Égyptien de l'année 1886, Cairo 1887) by the same author. For the Latin and Greek lives of Pachomius see Acta Sanctorum, May 14; for an Arabic life see B.O., iii. 1, p. 286; for his Regulae Monasticae see Cave, Hist. Litt., ad ann. 340, vol. 1. p. 208; Palladius, Hist. Laus., cap. 38 (for the Ethiopic text see Dillmann, Chrestomathia Aethiopica, pp. XII. No. 6, and pp. 57—69; and Wright, Catalogue of the Ethiopic MSS. in the British Museum, p. 171; and for the Syriac text see Wright, Catalogue of Syriac MSS., p. 1312); and for an account of the estimation in which he was held see Tillemont, Mémoires, tom. vii. p. 56.
p. 397, n. 1 I.e., Dĕbhar Ḥephtôn (ܚܦܬܘܢ seems to be the plain of Ḥarîr); see also Abbeloos, Acta Mar Ḳardaghi, p. 51, l. 4; and Feige, Die Geschichte des Mâr Abhdîshô, p. 31 (translation).

p. 397, n. 2 The ܛܘܼܦܵܐ, or ܛܵܘܦܵܐ, طَوْف, (called by the Arabs to-day كَلَك kalak, pronounced vulgarly tcheletch) is a raft made of skins of sheep blown out and tied in rows to poles. The poles are fastened together by other poles and ropes and thus a square or oblong structure is made. Upon it are laid planks of wood, and upon those is placed the merchandise to be carried. A small raft to carry four or five passengers and a fair amount of baggage requires about one hundred and fifty skins, and measures about 15×20 feet; but in the large wheat and alabaster carrying rafts several hundreds are required; such rafts are from thirty to forty feet square, and will carry from twenty-five to forty tons of wheat packed in sacks, each of which weighs about two hundredweight. The kalak floats down the stream, and is guided by very long oars, at the ends of which are tied pieces of reeds to form blades. The kalakje, or raftsman, every now and then pours water upon the skins to prevent the escape of the air inside, but it is often necessary to untie the neck of each skin, and to blow air into it with his mouth through a reed, which he carries for this purpose. When a raft arrives at its destination the poles are untied, and sold either for building purposes or firewood, and the skins are untied, emptied of air, dried thoroughly, and having been tied in bundles, are packed upon the backs of animals and sent up the river to be used again. The speed of a raft depends upon the current and upon the exertions of the raftsman. I made the journey by raft from Môṣul to Bagdad in February 1889 in a little over four days; but in December 1890 the journey required nearly seven days, while the huge rafts about forty feet square which I passed at the junction of the Lower Zâb with the Tigris did not arrive for some days after I had landed at Bagdad. Rafts which carry alabaster slabs for building purposes or for burning into lime are much smaller than wheat rafts, and the skins are often totally submerged. For other descriptions of the raft see Buckingham, Travels, vol. ii. p. 87; and Ker Porter, Travels, vol. ii. p. 259.

p. 398, n. 1 The word ܫܹܓܠܵܠܵܐ is new, and Hoffmann believes that it stands for either ܫܸܢ ܓܠܵܠܵܐ the tooth of a river bed, or ܪܸܫ ܓܠܵܠܵܐ the head of a river bed. It seems that Thomas of Margâ means that he brought blocks of limestone to build a pier in the peak of the mountain upon which the monastery stood, where two streams joined, to form a firm foundation for the walls of the church. The rafts would bring the stone immediately under the monastery, and mules and donkeys would bring it up the hill.

p. 399, n. 1 In Môṣul, and in Mesopotamia generally, burnt limestone is pounded by means of a large square stone, about two feet long by ten or twelve inches square, which having been pierced longitudinally is fastened to two chains by means of an iron rod running through it, and is drawn over the limestone by a horse or mule. The pounded lime is placed in basket panniers, two of which form a good load for a donkey, and in this way it is carried a considerable distance. Within the last few years the pious monks of the Monastery of Rabban Hormuzd near Alḳôsh have rebuilt part of the monastery on the plain, which travellers by the permission of the father superior use as a khân, and the monks told me on November 30, 1890, that every load of lime had to be brought thither from the place some miles away where it was burnt and crushed. The new portion of the building is very good and substantial, and the lime church is a fine specimen of its kind. Any one who has seen a mountain monastery in the East will understand the difficulties which stand in the way of building a church or monastery, and will readily perceive that the objection of the monks of Bêth ʿÂbhê to the pulling down of their church was not unnatural. The lack of roads and means of transport, the delays caused by the cold of winter and the heat of summer, and the large sums of money required for a building like a church would cause greater and wealthier men than the head of a decaying monastery to pause before beginning such a work.
p. 400, n. 1 ܘܐܸܬܦܲܪܬܲܚ = ܘܐܸܬܦܲܪܬܲܟ.
p. 400, n. 2 ܬܹܐܘܿܪܝܼܵܐ.
p. 400, n. 3 I.e., favoured him.
p. 401, n. 1 ܘܲܠܡܸܫܲܛ. Compare Arab. سَجَّ to plaster a wall with mud or lime.

p. 402, n. 1 I.e., دراهم dirhams. This was only to be expected in an eastern country. There are many places to this day in Mesopotamia where if a householder begins to make any repairs to his house, or to re-plaster it with lime, the local authorities at once assess his taxes at a higher rate and compel him to make payment immediately. Commencing to build a church when times were hard, money scarce, and provisions dear, was sufficient sign to the Muhammedan mind that the Nestorian monks of Bêth ʿÂbhê had more money than they knew what to do with.
p. 402, n. 2 Read ܬܩܝܼܡܘ. For other instances of ܐܩܝܡ ܓܒܐ to set up the back, i.e., to resist, to rebel, see Payne Smith, Thes., col. 639.
p. 403, n. 1 The ܙܘܙܐ is explained by dirham. The gold dînâr which weighed from sixty-five to seventy-two grains was equal in value to twenty dirhams, or about 10 1/2 English shillings.
p. 404, n. 1 ܐܲܒ݁ܐ a spiritual father, as opposed to ܐܲܒ݂ܵܐ a natural father.
p. 404, n. 2 He was elected Patriarch, A.D. 825. See B.O., ii. p. 435; iii. i. p. 616.
p. 404, n. 3 He was elected Patriarch, A.D. 836. See B.O., ii. p. 436; iii. 1. p. 617.
p. 404, n. 4 Thomas of Margâ means that he himself lived in the time of this Abraham.

p. 404, n. 5 From this it seems tolerably clear that the Monastery of Bêth ʿÂbhê was built upon a mountain peak between two valleys; in the valley on the east flowed the Upper Zâb, and in the valley on the west flowed a river or stream into which the spring here mentioned fell. The fortress surnamed the Little was probably on the other side of the Zâb, and could be seen from the monastery.
p. 405, n. 1 Exodus iii. 3.
p. 405, n. 2 ܩܘܼܠܬܵܐ i.e., الجرّه jar. See Brit. Mus. MSS. Rich 7203, fol. 151b, col. 1; and Orient. 2441, fol. 328b, col. 2.
p. 405, n. 3 ܨܵܘܨܝܼܘ.

p. 405, n. 4 The ܩܢܘܿܒܵܝܵܐ = κοινοβιακὸς, was a man who had decided to adopt the monkish habit but who had not yet taken up his abode in the κοινόβιον, or ܥܘܡܪܐ. It would seem that the coenobium was distinguished from the outer cells, ܩܠܝ̈ܬܐ ܒܪ̈ܝܬܐ, which were scattered about in the neighbouring mountains, although they belonged to the congregation of the monastery. The anchorites or solitaries, ܝܚܝܕ̈ܝܐ, who lived in these cells, were accustomed to go to the church of the monastery on certain occasions and on Sundays to partake of the Eucharist. The ܕܲܝܪ̈ܵܝܹܐ were the monks who lived in cells, which were separate from each other, but which were grouped round about the church, the whole cluster of buildings comprising the ܕܝܪܐ, or residence in common. The ܥܘܡܪܐ, with its outlying cells, was a later development of monastic dwelling; compare what is said of Job the Monk (he flourished about A.D. 550), وطَكَّسَ الاْعمَارَ واقَلا لى وكانَتْ من قَبْلُ كالدِّيارات and he founded coenobia and cells, which formerly were like unto places where monks dwelt in common. See B.O., iii. i. p. 431, col. 1, at the foot; Hoffmann, Auszüge, Notes 1330, 1332, pp. 171, 172; Du Cange, Glossarium, col. 677.
p. 406, n. 1 ܣܵܒܵܐ, a title of honour.
p. 406, n. 2 ܓܵܫܹܬ for ܓܸܫܹܬ.
p. 407, n. 1 I.e., which shall live again on the Day of Judgment.
p. 407, n. 2 ܣܝܼܩܘܿܡܵܐ = σήκωμα. See Payne Smith, Thes., col. 2719; Buxtorf (ed. Fisher), p. 740.

p. 407, n. 3 ܙܝܼܙܹ̈ܐ, a new word. This word seems to mean the projecting stone corbels which are laid upon the uppermost layer of bricks or stone on the walls of the church upon which rafters or beams of the roof are to rest. Compare זִיז plur. זִיזַיָּא Buxtorf, (ed. Fisher), p. 344, col. 2; Levy, Chald. Wörterbuch., p. 218, col. 1. Hoffmann thinks that ܙܝܼܙܵܐ = γεῖσα, the projecting part of the roof, the eaves, parapet, coping.

p. 410, n. 1 Compare ܠܐ ܝܫܘܥ I swear by Jesus; ܠܐ ܡܫܝܚܐ I swear by Christ (Payne Smith, Thes., col. 1869); and لاَ أَقْسِمُ بِيَوْم آلْقِيامَةِ I swear by the day of the Resurrection. Wright, Arabic Grammar, vol. 11, pp. 162, 328.

p. 417, n. 2 Basil the Great was born at Caesaraea A.D. 329, and died 379. According to ʿAbhd-Îshôʿ he wrote a book on the Six days, and several Questions, Discourses, and lengthy Epistles: ܣܡ ܟܬܒܐ ܕܫܬܬ ܝܘ̈ܡܐ܆ ܘܫܘ̈ܐܠܐ ܣܒܝ̈ܣܐ܆ ܘܡܐܡ̈ܪܐ ܘܐ ܓܪ̈ܬܐ ܒܐܪ̈ܝܟܬܐ. See B.O., iii. 1, p. 21. For the Greek text of Basil's Ασκητικά or Constitutiones Asceticae, see Migne, Patrologiae Graecae, tom. XXXI., coll. 1321—1428.

p. 418, n. 4 We should expect ܩܠܵܩܸܣܵܐ to be equal to ܩܪܵܩܸܣܵܐ = κόραξ, a raven; but it probably stands for ܩܘܪܠܐ, or ܩܘܼܪܩܵܠܐ crane (Castle, Lexicon, pp. 830, 835). Hoffmann believes that the reading of BC ܩܠܵܩܸܣܵܠܵܐ, may stand for ܩܘܼܠܓܣܵܪܐ and = Pers. کُلَنْگ سار crane-like; in this case it is the rendering of ܒܕܡܘܬ ܟܘܪܟܝܐ. For קרקם eagle, = קרגם see Lagarde, Gesammelte Abhandlungen, p. 81, No. 208; compare also Ahrens, Naturgegenstände, p. 23, No. 46; and καθεύδουσιν ἐπὶ ἑνὸς πολὸς ἐναλλαξ Aristotle, De Animalibus, lib. IX. chap. X. (ed. Didot, t. iii. p. 181).

p. 418, n. 5 Read, in any case, ܬܲܢܘܼܒܘܼܬܹܗ, but we should have expected ܬܲܚܘܼܒܘܼܬܹܗ imbecility, infirmity; compare below (text. p. 219, l. 12) ܕܬܚ̇ܒ ܗ̄ܘܼܐ he flagged, or languished. p. 426, n. 2 Probably the spring referred to in Bk. IV. chap. XI; see supra, p. 404.
p. 426, n. 3 I.e., he was to make a channel so that the water might flow down from the spring into the rock-hewn cistern of the monastery.
p. 426, n. 4 ܡܲܩܲܪܬܐ, fem. of ܡܲܩܪܵܐ. Compare Arab. مُنْقُر basin of water, reservoir; and וְאֶל־מַקֶּבֶת בּוֹר נֻקַּרְתֶּם Isaiah li. 1.
p. 426, n. 5 ܩܘܼܣܛܘܿܝ a diminutive of ܩܘܼܣܛܲܢܛܝܼܢܘܿܣ, with the Persian termination ôe; compare عَمْرَوَية.
p. 426, n. 6 Literally in his cell.

p. 426, n. 7 ܬܪܲܥ means to make an opening through which water may flow; compare the Arabic تُرْعَة, the mouth of a streamlet, the opening of a tank, and تَرَّاع a torrent filling the valley, Lane, Arabic-English Lexicon, p. 303. For examples of √ ܬܪܥ compare ܘܠܐ ܝܕܥ ܐܡܬܝ ܕܡܬܬܪܥ ܥܠܘܗܝ ܡܡܘܠܐ ܕܪܘܓܙܐ Wright, Kalîlah and Dimnah, p. 289, l. 24; ܟܢܫܝ̈ܢ ܟܢܫ̈ܝܢ ܐܬܬܪܥܘ Land, Anecdota, t. ii. p. 172, l. 20; ܕܠܐ ܢܬܬܪ̈ܥܢ ܚܢܓ̈ܬܐ ibid., p. 312, l. 20; ܬܪ̈ܥܢ ܗ̈ܘܝ ܕܡܥܘ̈ܗܝ ibid, p. 119. 24; ܕܡܥ̈ܐ ܬܪ̈ܝܥܬܐ ibid., p. 121. 14.
p. 427, n. 1 ܒܹܝܬ ܣܘܼܒܵܥܵܐ probably a part of the church, not refectory.
p. 427, n. 2 I.e., your deeds defile the Devil, and make him appear blacker than he is otherwise.
p. 428, n. 1 I.e., Cyriacus.
p. 428, n. 2 ܓܘܼܢ̄ܝܵܐ something to lie upon, a bed. Compare ܐܲܓܢܝܼ Payne Smith, Thes., col. 745.
p. 429, n. 1 ܒܵܒܵܢܘܿܫ i. e., Bâb = Pâp + anôsh (cf. Anôsh-ravân) having a blessed father.
p. 429, n. 2 After this word we should probably add ܒܲܪ ܩܲܢܟܵܝܵܐ the son of the sacristan; compare l. 16 (text).

p. 429, n. 3 The allusion is to Jeremiah xxx. 8. ܐܸܬܒܲܪ ܢܝܼܪܹܗ ܡ̣ܢ ܨܵܘܪܵܟ. ܘܲܚ̈ܢܵܩܲܝܟ ܐܹܦܲܣܸܩ. The wooden portion of the yoke is called ܨܹܦܪܵܝܬܵܐ little goat; the two ropes ܚܢܩ̈ܐ are tied to it, one at each end, and fastened under the neck.
p. 430, n. 1 Unless a priest has a Shammâshâ, i.e., a deacon or assistant . . . . to serve with him, the Liturgy cannot be celebrated. Badger, Nestorians, ii. 19.
p. 430, n. 2 ܐܸܣܛܘܵܐ = στοά, which, however, I believe we should here render aisle.

p. 430, n. 3 ܦܵܬܘܿܪܵܐ also = the table of the sacrament; see Badger, Nestorians, ii. p. 239, l. 3. This seems to be the meaning of ܦܬܘܪܐ on p. 218, l. 11 (text), where we read that Mâr Cyriacus only drank wine when he was obliged to do so in receiving the sacrament with the other brethren. Compare also the use of the word in Liturgia Sanctorum Apostolorum Adaei et Maris, Urmia, 1890, 4to., p. 6, l. 10; p. 23, l. 22; p. 24, ll. 8, 13; and p. 28, l. 14.
p. 430, n. 4 I.e., the occupier of the cell.
p. 430, n. 5 ܪܫ ܬܫܡܫܬܐ = ἀρχιδιάκονος?? or perhaps the monk who led the service.

p. 430, n. 6 ܒܹܝܬ ܐܣܛܘ̈ܢܐ = περίστυλον (Payne Smith, Thes., col. 480), and it seems, therefore, that by this word we should here understand portico or προστῷον (for a description of such a portico see Badger, Nestorians, vol. 1, p. 94). It is not probable that ܒܹܝܬ ܐܣܛܘ̈ܢܐ = ܐܣܛܘܐ ܕܗܝܟܠܐ.

p. 431, n. 1 ܒܸܝܬ ܫܵܗܪܹ̈ܐ, i.e., the place where the office for the night was sung by the ܫܲܗܵܪܹ̈ܐ or θεωροὶ. For the duties of these men see B.O., iii. 2, p. 820ff. Judging from the details given by Thomas of Margâ concerning the church used by the monks, the general arrangement of the main portions of the building must have been as shown in the following rough plan:— The altar stood in the ܩܣܛܪܘܡܐ (see supra, p. 342), or space above the three steps, and a path led through the ܩܲܢ̈ܟܹܐ, or choir, to the ܒܝܼܡܵܐ; the ܦܪܲ̈ܩܛܹܐ, i.e., φρακτὴ, or altar-screen with its veils, stood either in the middle or at the door of the ܩܲܢ̈ܟܹܐ, above the steps leading down into the nave of the church. For the various parts of the church symbolically treated see Book V. chap. 15, (text p. 306); and also Du Cange, Glossarium, s. v. κρηπὶς (col. 754), νάρθηξ (col. 986), κατηχούμενα (col. 621), ναὸς (col. 985), πρόναος (col. 1245); Waddington, Inscriptions of Syria, No. 2218, Ἐκτίση ἡ κρηπὶς καὶ ἡ κόγκ[η του] θεοῦ quoted also by Graham, Trans. Roy. Soc. Lit., vol. VI. p. 282.
p. 432, n. 1 All the MSS have ܓܘܿܪܹ̈ܐ, but read ܓܘ̈ܕܐ walls. See Hoffmann, Syr.-Arab. Gloss., No. 2764, p. 98.

p. 432, n. 2 Probably a fine specimen of the greyhound family. To this day in and around Môṣul these dogs are much used for hunting purposes, but I regret to say that when they become old the natives turn them out to starve in the streets or to be worried to death by the young and vigorous pariah dogs. They are often taken to Bagdad as gifts for Pashas.
p. 433, n. 1 I.e., the martyrium outside the church proper.
p. 433, n. 2 ܪܵܥܘܿܡܵܐ for ܪܲܥܘܡܐ.
p. 433, n. 3 ܨܠܵܒܵܐ. Compare سَلَبَة الكلاب, corde pour mener les chiens, Dozy, Supplément, t. 1, p. 672, col. 1.
p. 434, n. 1 I.e., the threshingfloor of Bâlâs. For other examples of ܐܕܪܐ with proper names, see Payne Smith, Thes., col. 41.

p. 434, n. 2 ܐܵܘܣܠܵܐ, a word explained by رَقَّة marshy land by the side of a river, and اوْسِلَة; see Hoffmann, Syr. Arab. Gloss., No. 357, p. 17; Duval, Lexicon, col. 78; Payne Smith, Thes., col. 79.
p. 435, n. 1 Read ܚܘܼܣ.
p. 435, n. 2 See Payne Smith, Thes., col. 2806.
p. 435, n. 3 ܘܲܪܝܼܕܵܐ, וַרִיד, وَرِيد; see the examples in Payne Smith, Thes., col. 1069.
p. 435, n. 4 Read ܐܝܼܕ̈ܲܝ.
p. 436, n. 1 St. Matthew xv. 22.
p. 436, n. 2 St. Luke vii. 36—50.
p. 436, n. 3 For ܒܠܵܐ read ܕܠܐ.
p. 436, n. 4 For ܠܘ ܕܗܒܐ read ܓܵܘ ܕܗܒܐ.
p. 437, n. 1 His commemoration took place on a Friday in November. See Wright, Catalogue of Syr. MSS., p. 187, No. 152.

p. 437, n. 2 ܒܹܝܬ ܣܵܕܘܿܪܸ̈ܐ i.e., the place of those who lay the tables. Hoffmann translates ܣܕܘܪܐ by Tafeldecker, compare στρώτης, στράτωρ and τραπεζάρης (Du Cange, Glossarium, col. 1598). See Hoffmann, Verhandlungen der Kirchenversammlung zu Ephesus. pp. 67, 99 (note 304, col. 2).
p. 437, n. 3 ܒܹܝܬ ܚܲܡܪܐ.
p. 438, n. 1 We should probably add ܐܢܬܘܢ after ܡܸܫܬܲܪܬܚܝܼܢ.

p. 438, n. 2 ܫܲܗܪܵܐ in Neo-Syriac ܫܵܪܵܐ church festival. For the description of the ܫܵܪܵܐ ܕܥܵܕܵܐ or festival of ʿÂdhâ (a village situated near Supurgan, four hours north of Urmî), see Socin, Die Neu-Aramaeischen Dialekte von Urmia bis Mosul, Tübingen, 1882, pp. 84, 172, notes 14 and 189.

p. 438, n. 3 The Friday of the Dead ܥܪܘܒܬܐ ܕܥܢܝ̈ܕܐ fell a little before Lent; see Wright, Catalogue of Syriac MSS., p. 183, no. 34; B.O., iii. ii. p. 382, No. 28 (ܥܪܘܒܬܐ ܛ ܕܕܢܚܐ ܘܕܘܟܪܢܐ ܕܡܝ̈ܬܐ). For a description of the festival for the commemoration of the dead now in use among the Nestorians see Badger, Nestorians, vol. 1, p. 229. The ܫܗܪܐ was celebrated in that part of the church called ܒܝܬ ܫܵܗܪܐ, into which, on solemn occasions, the laity were admitted.

p. 438, n. 4 I.e., people of Ḥîrthâ, a place the ruins of which still exist to the south-east of Meshed ʿAlî, but it seems hardly likely that a caravan going from Kûfa and Bagdad to Âdhôrbâîgân by way of Arbela would cross the Zâb and make a circuit by Môṣul. On the other hand a local caravan from Ḥedhattâ would cross the Zâb pretty soon and make its way into Margâ. For ܕܚܝܪ̈ܬܝܐ, then, we should probably read ܕܚܕ̈ܬܝܐ, to which the readings of BC point.
p. 439, n. 1 A village on the Zâb; see Bk. 1. chap. 24, supra, p. 84 (text p. 48, l. 12).
p. 439, n. 2 For ܦܵܠ̈ܚܹܐ, read ܦܲܠܵܚܹ̈ܐ.
p. 440, n. 1 St. John xiv. 12, 13.
p. 441, n. 1 Read ܩܕܡܝܐ.
p. 441, n. 2 ܢܸܒܗܹ̈ܐ motions of the mind, germinations of thought.
p. 441, n. 3 Compare St. Matthew xxii. 17.
p. 441, n. 4 Spelt also ܝܲܙܕܲܝܢܵܒܵܕ; see text p. 386, l. 16.

p. 442, n. 1 ܒܹܝܬ ܫܲܒܬܵܐ or refectory, to be distinguished from ܒܹܝܬ ܐܚ̈ܐ the common-room of the brethren. The ܒܹܝܬ ܫܒܬܐ seems to have been joined to the kitchen or place where the food was cooked (μαγειρεῖον); compare ܐܦܝܢ ܟܠܗܘܢ ܐܚ̈ܐ ܠܚܡܐ ܒܒܝܬ ܫܒܬܐ (text p. 236, l. 2). The ܫܲܒ̈ܬܵܝܹܐ (Land, Anecdota, tom. ii. p. 196, l. 22; p. 196, l. 16;) may be compared to the ἑβδομαδάριοι who had certain duties which lasted a week assigned to them in monasteries. See Du Cange, Glossarium, col. 339. For ܪ̈ܝܫܝ ܫܒ̈ܐ see Land, Anecdota, t. ii. p. 207, l. 24.
p. 442, n. 2 I.e., Mâr Cyriacus.
p. 442, n. 3 Read ܠܪ̈ܲܚܝܼܩܵܬܵܐ.
p. 443, n. 1 The Pĕshîṭtâ has ܐܘܕܥ ܗܝܡܢܘܬܗ.
p. 443, n. 2 Psalm lxxxix. 1.
p. 443, n. 3 I.e., the temple of Bêth ʿÂbhê.
p. 443, n. 4 Literally, which are said.

p. 443, n. 5 Thomas of Margâ means that he heard the Grace of the Lord sung to a tune (ܩܠܐ) which was different (ܦܪܝܼܫܐ) from that to which it was usually sung upon festivals relating to our Lord. On ܩ̈ܠܐ ܦܪ̈ܝܼܫܹܐ see B.O., iii. 1. p. 529, col. 2, l. 23. The Grace of the Lord occurs in the service for festivals relating to our Lord, and also in the service for the Consecration of Bishops, but the wording of each Grace is different. For the Grace at the Consecration of Bishops see Badger, Nestorians, vol. ii. p. 344; B.O., iii. ii. p. 685, col. 2; and for the ordinary Grace see Badger, Nestorians, vol. ii. p. 222. The verb ܐܫܬܚܠܦ refers to the tune, and the change in the tune reminded him of the Grace in the festivals relating to our Lord. Hymns with changes of tune in them were called ܫܘܚܠܦ ܩ̈ܠܐ; see Wright, Catalogue Syr. MSS., p. 376, col. 2; and B.O., iii. 1, p. 284, col. 1, l. 6, (ܩܠܐ ܒܬܪ ܩܠܐ ܥܡ ܫܘܚ̈ܠܦܝܗܘܢ); and Du Cange, Glossarium, s. v. εἱρμός, col. 356.
p. 444, n. 1 Compare ܘܐܦܝܣܩܘ̈ܦܐ ܟܕ ܡܨܒܬܝܢ ܒܒܝܪ̈ܘܢܐ ܘܒܚܘܛܪ̈ܐ B.O., iii. ii. p. 685, col. 2, l. 13.
p. 444, n. 2 See Badger, Nestorians, vol. ii. p. 17.

p. 444, n. 3 See B.O., iii. 1, p. 530, chaps. 5, 6 (ܘܡܢܘ ܦܘܫܩܐ ܕܩ̈ܠܐ ܕܫܗܪܐ); and B.O., iii. ii. p. 669, col. 2 (ܘܫܗܪܝܢ ܫܗܪܐ. ܡܢ ܪܝܫܗ ܕܕܘܝܕ ܒܩ̈ܠܐ ܘܩܢܘ̈ܢܐ. ܘܥܘܢ̈ܝܬܐ ܘܡܘ̈ܬܒܐ ܘܡܟܪܙܝܢ ܘܡܕܟܪܝܢ ܫܡܗ̈ܐ ܕܐܒܗ̈ܬܐ).
p. 444, n. 4 Psalm cxxxii. 1, in the Pĕshîṭtâ, cxxxi.
p. 445, n. 1 ܒܹܝܬ ܫܲܒܬܐ.

p. 445, n. 2 Vat. reads the brethren went into the refectory, and the other MSS. the brethren went in to table; compare Land, Anecdota, t. ii. p. 243, l. 2, for a proof that the ܫܒܬܐ and ܦܬܘܪܐ were united (ܘܫܒܬܐ ܘܦܬܘܪܐ ܐܝܟ ܚܕܐ ܐܝܬ ܗܘܐ ܠܗܘܢ). For the service of hymns to be chanted at meal-times, see Wright, Catalogue Syr. MSS., p. 372, col. 2, No. 20.

p. 445, n. 3 In the Syriac version of Pseudo-Callisthenes ܦܠܸܓ ܫ̈ܢܲܝܵܐ = μεσῆλιξ; see Budge, History of Alexander the Great, p. 10, l 17; p. 14, l. 15; p. 16, l. 5; the fem. ܦܸܠܓܬ݀ ܫ̈ܢܝܐ occurs on p. 209, l. 13.
p. 446, n. 1 ܫܲܗܵܪܵܐ vigil, excubitor, apud Syros Nestorianos vocatur, qui nocturno praesertim officio decantando praeest B.O., iii. ii. p. 820.
p. 446, n. 2 ܩܝܵܡܘܼܬܵܐ = ܩܝܵܡܘܼܬ ܘܵܠܵܐ = the art of singing correctly and in tune.
p. 446, n. 3 ܟܘܼܪܵ̈ܟܹܐ, i.e., melodies with a refrain to which different words are sung each time it is repeated. See supra, Bk. iii. chap. 1. p. 291, note 3 (text p. 142, l. 5).
p. 446, n. 4 The rest of this chapter is quoted in B.O., iii. i, p. 488, coll. 1, 2.
p. 446, n. 5 ܣܲܓܝܼ ܢܘܼܗܪܵܐ means doctissimus, and also blind = סַגִּיא נְהוֹרָא, البصير; see Wright, Catalogue of Syr. MSS., p. 162, col. 2.
p. 446, n. 6 We should read ܐܢܫ ܗܟܝܠ.
p. 446, n. 7 ܡܵܗܕܝܼ = مَهْدِى.
p. 446, n. 8 Compare ܡܲܠܒܟܝܢ ܥܘܢܝ̈ܬܐ B.O., iii. ii. p. 939, l. 18; ܡܲܠܒܟܝܢ ܥܘܢ̈ܝܐ ibid. l. 20.
p. 446, n. 9 Assemâni omits ܘܕܬܪ̈ܬܝܢ ܒܘܝܐܐ ܫܗܪܐ. We should, however, read ܒܘܝܐ ܫܗܪܐ.
p. 447, n. 1 For hymns to be sung at Vigils for the Dead see Wright, Catalogue Syr. MSS., p. 367, col. 2, No. 3; p. 370, col. 1, No. 4.
p. 447, n. 2 A Monastery of Bâʿûth دير باعوث, existed near Bâlâdh; see B.O., iii. i, p. 557, col. 1, last line.
p. 447, n. 3 Read ܪܒܢ.
p. 447, n. 4 See Book V. chap. 14 (text. p. 302, l. 4).
p. 447, n. 5 See supra, p. 220.
p. 447, n. 6 See supra, p. 220.
p. 447, n. 7 See supra, p. 68.
p. 447, n. 8 I.e., Mill-house. Assemânî has ܒܷܝܬ ܡܽܘ̈ܝܴܐܷܐ.

p. 447, n. 9 Bar-Arlâyê is probably a nickname meaning son of a giant, and is derived from ܐܱܪܻܝܱܐܝܷܠ, Heb. אֲרִיאֵל (Isaiah xxix. 1.); see Payne Smith, Thes., col. 379; Duval, Lexicon, col. 289; Hoffmann, Syr. Arab. Gloss., No. 1486, p. 52.

p. 448, n. 1 ܡܘܼܩܵܢ, i.e., موقان, was situated near Gîlân (see supra, p. 220) in Armenia and Âdhôrbâîgân. See MacGuckin de Slane, Géographie d'Aboulféda, p. 400 (وموقان فى نهاية بلاد كيلان من جهة الغرب); Yâḳût, tom. iii. p. 420; and De Goeje, Bibl. Geog. Arab., p. 17, l. 8; p. 119, l. 16; p. 120, l. 15; p. 213, l. 7. The modern form of the name is موغان. Moghân is a steppe in the corner between the right bank of the Lower Arras and the right bank of the Kurr. The town seems to have been situated near Mount Heshtâ[d]-sar, to the N. W. of Mount Tabhalân, and the town of Berzend, near the left bank of the Kara-Su in Angatieft towards the hill country. See Ritter, Erdkunde, t. viii. p. 662; t. ix. pp. 793, 796, 870.
p. 448, n. 2 The rest of this chapter is also quoted in B.O., iii. i, p. 163, col. 1.
p. 448, n. 3 I.e., China.
p. 448, n. 4 ʿAbhd Îshôʿ says of him ܘܐܝܬ ܠܗ ܐܝܟ ܡܐܬܝܢ ܐܓܪ̈ܢ ܕܒܬܪ̈ܬܝܢ ܦܢܩ̈ܝܢ ܡܛܟܣ̈ܢ; see B.O., iii. i. p. 163.
p. 448, n. 5 I.e., اليَمَنُ, see Yâḳût, tom. iv. p. 1034 f.

p. 448, n. 6 ܨܲܢܥܵܐ i.e., صَنْعَاءُ the ancient capital of Yemen. For Arabic descriptions of town see MacGuckin de Slane, Géographie d'Aboulféda, p. 95; Voyages d'ibn Batoutah, (ed. Defrémery et Sanguinetti) tom. ii. p. 176; and Yâḳût, tom. iv. p. 420.
p. 448, n. 7 I.e., Kerkuk; see supra, p. 122.
p. 449, n. 1 Compare Shushan the palace, Nehemiah i. 1; Esther ii. 8.
p. 449, n. 2 For ܐܘܿܪܵܝܵܐ read ܐܘܿܟܵܝܵܐ; for ܐܘܵܟ or ܐܘܿܟ see Bk. ii. chap. 34 (text p. 115, l. 11), and see supra, p. 250.
p. 449, n. 3 I.e., Sinn Bârimmâ = Shennâ dhĕ Bhêth Remmân = Kârdâlîâbhâdh, a place ten farsaḥ distant from Tekrît, on the east bank of the Tigris. See Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 189.

p. 449, n. 4 A town situated on the west bank of the Little Zâb just above where this river falls into the Tigris; see Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 189. خُنْيَا سابور is the Persian name of al-Bawâzîḳ La signification serait soit musique pour (l'oreille de) Sâbour quand on lui parle de la ville, soit cantatio Saporis dans le sens de laus Saporis cantibus celebrata. See De Goeje, Bibl. Geog. Arab., t. vi. p. 68, note 1, and p. 94 (text).
p. 449, n. 5 I.e., al-Bawâzîḳ.
p. 449, n. 6 ܡܫܲܡܫܵܢܵܐ ܕܣܘܼܪ̈ܛܹܐ = ܟܵܬܘܿܒܵܐ.

p. 450, n. 1 I.e., عِمْران بن مُحَمَّد. The Banû ʿImrân, بنى عمران are mentioned by Ibn Ḥauḳal as being a branch of the Azd tribe and settled in Kurdistan. See De Goeje, Bibl. Geog. Arab., Pars ii. p. 144, l. 9; Ibn al-Athîr, tom. vii. p. 117, l. 13; and Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 234 and note 1867.
p. 450, n. 2 See Book vi. chap. 16.

p. 450, n. 3 I.e., the house of Bôzâi. This name appears to have been formed originally from the Persian bôzîd; conf. Yêzdbôzedh, Horn-Steindorff, Sassanidische Siegelsteine, p. 36. For the situation of Bêth Bôzâi see Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 196.
p. 450, n. 4 See Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 223 ff.
p. 450, n. 5 Compare Psalm cvi. 23.
p. 451, n. 1 For ܠܐ in swearing an oath see supra, p. 410.
p. 451, n. 2 The allusion is to בְּעֵט בַּרְזֶל בְּצִפֹּרֶן שָׁמִיר with a pen of iron, and with the claw of a diamond, Jeremiah xvii. 1.
p. 452, n. 1 I.e., certain of the ܣܒ̈ܐ whom he specified by name.
p. 452, n. 2 A picture of the board which is beaten to call the monks together in Greek monasteries is given in Curzon's Visits to Monasteries in the Levant (frontispiece).
p. 453, n. 1 Literally, they spread out.
p. 453, n. 2 See Budge, Book of the Bee, p. 71.
p. 453, n. 3 St. John vi. 21.
p. 453, n. 4 2 Corinthians xii. 2—4.
p. 453, n. 5 ʿAmran was in bed.
p. 454, n. 1 Add a point(.) after ܘܕܩܢܟ.
p. 454, n. 2 I.e., men who lead ascetic lives.
p. 455, n. 1 I.e., during the evening service which was sung late in the night; compare τὸ ἑσπερινὸν, ὁ ἑσπερινὸς ὕμνος, Du Cange, Glossarium, col. 437.
p. 455, n. 2 I.e., شَيْخان. For another place of this name see Sachau, Reise in Mesopotamien, p. 433.

p. 455, n. 3 See supra, p. 29, note 3. ܐܡܪܝܢ ܗ̄̄ܘ̣ܘ ܬܘܒ ܥܠ ܐܒܐ ܐܪܣܢܝܣ. ܕܒܪܡܫܐ ܕܫܒܬܐ ܕܢܵܓܲܗ ܚܕܒܫܒܐ. ܫܵܒܩ ܗ̄ܘ̣ܐ ܠܫܡܫܐ ܡܢ ܒܣܬܪܗ. ܘܡܵܬܚ ܗ̄ܘ̣ܐ ܐܝܕ̈ܘܗܝ ܠܘܬ ܫܡܝܐ ܟܕ ܡܨܠܐ. ܥܕܡܐ ܕܕܵܢܚ ܗ̄ܘ̣ܐ ܫܡܫܐ ܒܐܦܘܗ̈ܝ. ܘܟܕ ܩܠܝܠ ܥܝܢ̈ܘܗܝ ܡܢ ܫܢܬܐ ܡܵܠܐ ܗ̄ܘ̣ܐ܀ ܗ̄ܘ̣ܐ ܕܝܢ ܐܒܐ ܐܪܣܢܝܣ ܐܡ̇ܪ ܗܘܐ. ܕܣܵܦܩ ܠܗ ܠܝܚܝܕܝܐ ܕܢܕܡܟ ܚܕܐ ܫܵܥܐ܆ ܐܢ ܐܝܬܘܗܝ ܚܠܨܐ܀. Sayings of the Fathers on Fasting and other labours, Nos. 105, 134. The first of these is given in Latin by Rosweyde, Vitae Patrum, p. 613.
p. 455, n. 4 I.e., his private room for services and prayer in the Abbot's house.
p. 456, n. 1 Read Elijah; see 2 Kings ii. 11.
p. 456, n. 2 I.e., his special guardian angel; compare St. Matthew xviii. 10; Acts xii. 7; Daniel iii. 25.
p. 456, n. 3 ܕܒܸܩ for ܕܒܸܩܝ.
p. 457, n. 1 Literally there is nothing to you and the Monastery of Bêth ʿÂbhê.
p. 457, n. 2 ܗܕܵܣܵܐ, a rare word.
p. 458, n. 1 Literally, let thy antiquity be renewed.

p. 459, n. 1 ܒܲܪ̈ܕܘܼܢܹܐ. There is usually no difference in meaning between ܒܪ̈ܕܘܢܐ and ܟܘܕܢ̈ܘܬܐ but here ܒܪ̈ܕܘܢܐ must have the meaning of the Arab. بَرْذَون, plur. بَراذِن. See Dozy, Supplément, tom. 1. p. 69, col. 1.
p. 460, n. 1 ܝܘܿܙܵܘ̈ܵܬܵܐ, Pers. يوز. See Lagarde, Gesammelte Abhandlungen, no. 139, p. 53.
p. 460, n. 2 ܦܪ̈ܕܝܢ i.e., hunting panthers; compare πάρδιον Aristotle, Hist. Anim., ii. 1. The native lexicons explain ܦܪܕܝܢ by النَمِر panther, and by الفَهْد panther.
p. 460, n. 3 I.e., into the προστῷον.
p. 460, n. 4 St. Luke ii. 29.
p. 461, n. 1 Read ܟܢܘܼܫܝܵܐ.

p. 461, n. 2 It is evident from this passage that ܚܣܢܐ ܥܒܪܝܐ was not situated on the left or east bank of the Tigris, close by the ruins of Nineveh, and it seems pretty certain that Môṣul itself, or some part of it on the eastern side of the town, and lying on the river bank, is meant by Ḥesnâ ʿEbhrâyâ. In a most valuable document published by Guidi, (Un nuovo testo, p. 18, at the top) mention is made of Mâr Elîyâ who built a monastery by the side of the Tigris, close to Ḥesnâ ʿEbhrâyâ ܡܪܝ ܐܠܝܐ ܕܒܢܐ ܥܘܡܪܐ ܥܠ ܓܢܒ ܕܩܠܬ ܠܘܬ ܚܣܢܐ ܥܒܝܐ (Guidi's emendation of ܥܒܪܝܐ for ܥܒܝܐ is certain). On the Monastery of Mâr Elijah, i.e., Dêr eṣ-Ṣaʿîd, see B.O., iii. 1. pp. 263, 264; iii. ii. p. 876; and see supra, p. 337.
p. 461, n. 3 For ܙܘܪ̈ܐ read ܙܘܙ̈ܐ.
p. 462, n. 1 I.e., προστῷον.

p. 462, n. 2 ܢܹܟܘܵܐܪ, i.e., نخوار, a family name or title of tolerably frequent occurrence, which appears in Greek as ὁ Ναχοραγάν, ὁ Ναχοεργάν, and with the addition of Sar Chief, ὁ Σαρναχοργάνης; see Nöldeke, Geschichte der Perser, p. 152, note 2. Hoffmann proposed a derivation in Feige, Mâr Abdhîshôʿ und Mâr Qardagh, p. 11, note 12, but that he has now abandoned, and he believes that the word is derived from نح nakh (see Lagarde, Armenische Studien, p. 110, No. 1583), as in نخستين, and bar, i.e., primam sive anticam aciem ducens. The form ܢܟܘܪܓܢ occurs in Guidi, Nuovo testo, p. 11, ll. 19, 22. Here he is called ܫܠܝܛܐ ܕܡܠܟܘܬܐ and has with him a large force of elephants.
p. 462, n. 3 I.e., Seleucia.
p. 463, n. 1 I.e., Jacobites.
p. 463, n. 2 I.e., in the Bishop's cell adjoining the church.

p. 463, n. 3 This monastery was situated on the right bank of the Tigris below Beled al-Shâbushtî, and is the دَيرُ الشَّياطِينِ which is between Balad and Môṣul. See Yâḳût, tom. ii. p. 673, l. 5; and Juynboll, Marâṣid, t. v. p. 553.
p. 463, n. 4 This monastery lay opposite to that of Rabban Pethion (i.e., Πυθίον), on the left bank of the river, about a farsaḥ below Eski-Môṣul. See Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 211.
p. 464, n. 1 I.e., of Bêth ʿÂbhê.

p. 464, n. 2 Of Bessarion it is said by his disciple, Alio quoque tempore, cum necessarium ei esset, fecit orationem, et transivit Chrysoroan fluvium pedibus; ego autem admiratus satisfeci, ei, dicens: Quomodo sentiebas pedes tuos, dum ambulares in aquâ? Et ait senex: Usque ad talum sentiebam aquam, reliqua autem erat solida sub pedibus meis. Rosweyde, Vitae Patrum, p. 649.
p. 464, n. 3 I.e., Let us cross over to the right side of the river to Bâlâdh.
p. 465, n. 1 See B.O., iii. ii. p. 878, no. 15.
p. 465, n. 2 I.e., Nekhwâr.
p. 465, n. 3 I.e., a Jacobite.
p. 465, n. 4 I.e., of Bêth ʿÂbhê.
p. 465, n. 5 See B.O., iii. i. p. 137, note 1. This work is also referred to by Îshôʿ-yahbh in his letter to Sahdônâ; see supra, p. 136, l. 12.
p. 465, n. 6 Read, with BC, ܕܒܫܪܪܐ ܡܠܦܢܐ.
p. 466, n. 1 I.e., the man of Gebhîltâ. The MSS. have ܓܒܝܼܠܬܵܝܵܐ.
p. 466, n. 2 Read with BC ܐܝܟܡܐ.

p. 466, n. 3 I.e., on the Friday preceding the Sunday which is called Nûsârdêl, the last Sunday of the Week of the Apostles, i.e., the first Sunday of the New Year. The word is compounded of the Persian nau-sard, New Year, and êl, God, meaning the Church's New Year. See Rosen and Forshall, Catalogus, pp. 31, 50; Wright, Cat. Syr. MSS., vol. 1, p. 185, col. 1, no. 101; 190, col. 1, no. 81; Nöldeke, Geschichte der Perser, p. 407, note 2; Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 59, note 523; Lagarde, Armenische Studien, p. 111, no. 1601; Payne Smith, Thes., col. 2326; B.O., iii. ii. p. 383, no. 36. (ܚܕܒܫܒܐ ܕܫܘܠܡ ܫܒܘܥܐ ܕܫܠܝܚ̈ܐ ܘܩܕܡܝܐ ܗܘ ܕܩܝܛܐ ܘܡܬܩܪܐ ܢܽܘܣܱܪܕܺܐܠ. ܘܕܘܟܪܗ ܗܘ ܕܬܪܥܣܪ ܫܠܝܚܵܐ).
p. 468, n. 1 The MSS. have ܟܪ ܕܘܵܠܹܐ, but read ܟܪ ܕܵܘܠܵܐ.
p. 468, n. 2 The MSS. have ܕܩܝ̈ܣܐ, but read ܘܩܝ̈ܣܐ.
p. 468, n. 3 Gîlân is the country by the Caspian Sea from the Russian frontier to Resht, and Dêlum, or Dailôm, is the mountainous territory behind it. See supra, p. 220, note 3.
p. 469, n. 1 I.e. Ḥêrthâ-dhĕ-Ṭaiyâyê, the ruins of which are less than half an hour distant from Meshed ʿAlî. See Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 97.
p. 469, n. 2 I.e., in Môṣul.
p. 470, n. 1 See supra, Book ii. chap. 12, p. 180.
p. 470, n. 2 He is mentioned by Palladius in his Hist. Laus.; see the following page, note 3.

p. 470, n. 3 The following is the account of this man from the Syriac version of Palladius: — ܕܥܠ ܐܦܠܘܢܝܣ܀ ܬܘܒ ܕܝܢ ܐܢܫ ܐܚܪܝܢ ܕܫܡܗ ܐܦܠܘܢܝܣ܆ ܓܒܪܐ ܬܓܪܐ ܐܬܬܠܡܕ ܗܘ̣ܐ ܠܕܘܒܪܐ ܕܝܚܝܕܝܘܬܐ. ܘܥܡ̇ܪ ܗܘ̣ܐ ܒܗ ܒܗܢܐ ܛܘܪܐ ܕܢܛܝܪܐ. ܗ̤ܘ ܕܝܢ ܗܢܐ ܐܘܡܢܘܬܐ ܡܕܡ ܕܢܦܠܘܚ ܠܐ ܐܫܟܚ. ܘܐܦܠܐ ܬܘܒ ܕܢܨܘܡ. ܐܘ ܕܢܫܗܪ ܐܝܟ ܫܪܟܐ ܕܝܚܝ̈ܕܝܐ ܒܡܫܘܚܬܐ ܪܒܬܐ. ܒܥܣܪܝܢ ܫܢ̈ܝܢ ܗܟܝܠ ܕܚܝܼܐ ܒܗ ܒܛܘܪܐ ܗܢܐ. ܗܢܐ ܕܘܒܪܐ ܘܢܨܚܢܐ ܗܘ̣ܐ ܠܗ. ܘܡܢ ܥܡܠܗ ܘܡܢ ܠܹܐܘܬܗ܆ܟܠ ܡܕܡ ܕܡܬܒܥܹܐ ܗܘ̣ܐ ܠܐܚ̈ܐ ܨܒܘ̈ܬܐ ܕܐܣܝܘܬܐ ܠܟܪ̈ܝܗܐ ܙܵܒܸܢ ܗܘ̣ܐ ܡܢ ܐܠܟܣܢܕܪܝܐ. ܘܠܟܠܗܘܢ ܐܚ̈ܐ ܕܟܪܝܗܝܢ ܡܘܒܠ ܗܘܐ. ܘܬܗܪܐ ܗܘ̣ܐ ܠܡܚܙܝܗ. ܟܠܝܘܡ ܒܡܓܗ̈ܐ ܟܕ ܢܦ̇ܩ ܗܘ̣ܐ. ܘܥܕܡܐ ܠܬܫܥ ܫܥ̈ܝܢ ܟܕ ܡܬܟܪܟ ܗܘ̣ܐ ܒܕܝܪ̈ܬܐ ܘܒܟܘܪ̈ܚܐ ܕܐܚ̈ܐ. ܟܕ ܩܐܡ ܗܘ̣ܐ ܥܠ ܬܪܥܐ ܘܐܡ̇ܪ. ܕܠܡܐ ܐܢܫ ܟܪܝܗܐ ܐܝܬ ܗܪܟܐ. ܛܥܝܢ ܗܘ̣ܐ ܓܝܪ ܪ̈ܘܡܢܐ ܘܓܠܘܣ̈ܩܐ ܝܒܝ̈ܫܐ. ܘܡܝܫ̈ܐ ܘܒܹ̈ܥܐ. ܒܗܠܝܢ ܨܒܘ̈ܬܐ ܐܝܠܝܢ ܕܡܬܒܥܝܢ ܠܟܪ̈ܝܗܐ. ܗܢܐ ܓܝܪ ܕܘܒܪܐ ܐܫܟܚ. ܕܦܫܝܩ ܗܘܐ ܠܗ ܠܡܩܢܐ ܥܕܡܐ ܠܣܝܒܘܬܗ. ܠܚܡܫܐ ܓܝܪ ܐܠܦܝ̈ܢ ܐܚ̈ܐ ܕܥܡܪܝܢ ܗܘ̣ܘ ܒܛܘܪܐ ܗ̇ܘ. ܣ̇ܦܩ ܗܘ̣ܐ ܠܣܘܥܪ̈ܢܝܗܘܢ. ܘܟܕ ܫܟܸܒ ܠܐܚܪܝܢ ܕܐܟܘܬܗ ܫܒܩ ܡܕܡ ܕܐܝܬ ܗܘ̣ܐ ܠܗ. ܘܒܥܵܐ ܡܢܗ ܕܗ̤ܝ ܗܕܐ ܬܫܡܫܬܐ ܢܫܲܡܠܐ. ܒܗ̇ܝ ܕܡܕܒܪܐ ܐܝܬܘܗܝ ܘܡܓܙܝܐ ܡܢ ܨܒܘ̈ܬܐ ܕܥܠܡܐ܀ (fol. 58b.)
p. 470, n. 4 I.e., the Nitrian desert near Alexandria; see supra, p. 39, note 3.

p. 471, n. 1 I.e., the rich Alexandrian who gave all that he had to the poor monks; the account of him as given by Palladius is as follows: — ܢܚܬ ܗܟܝܠ ܛܘܒܢܐ. ܘܚܙܐ ܓܒܪܐ ܚܕ ܬܓܪܐ ܐܠܟܣܢܕܪܝܐ ܕܕܚ̇ܠ ܡܢ ܐܠܗܐ. ܕܡܬܬܓܪ ܗܘܐ ܒܬܪ̈ܬܝܢ ܪ̈ܒܘܢ ܕܕܗܒܐ ܒܬܠܬܐ ܐܠܦܝ̈ܢ. ܕܢܚ̇ܬ ܗܘ̣ܐ ܡܢ ܬܹܒܵܐܝܼܣ ܥܠܝܬܐ. ܘܝܗ̇ܒ ܗܘ̣ܐ ܠܗ ܟܠܗ ܩܢܝܢܗ ܘܬܐܓܘܪܬܗ. ܠܡܣܟ̈ܢܐ ܘܠܐܚ̈ܐ ܝܚܝܕ̈ܝܐ. ܕܗ̤ܘ ܗܢܐ ܥܡ ܒܢ̈ܝ ܒܲܝܬܗ. ܥܣܪܐ ܣܲܩܹ̈ܐ ܕܘܩܐ ܒܟܠ ܫܢܐ ܡܲܣܩ ܗܘܐ ܠܗ ܠܛܘܒܢܐ܆ ܗ̤ܘ ܕܝܢ ܬܓܪܐ ܐܡܪ ܠܗ. ܕܦܐܪ̈ܐ ܕܬܓܘܪܬܝ ܠܢܵܝܚܐ ܕܙܕܝܩ̈ܐ ܡܩܪܒ ܐܢܐ ܠܗ ܠܐܠܗܐ. ܘܗ̤ܘ ܛܘܒܢܐ ܐܡ̣ܪ ܠܗ. ܘܥܠ ܡܢܐ ܐܝܬ ܩܢܘܡܚ ܒܫܡܐ ܗܢܐ ܕܝܠܢ ܠܐ ܡܬܝܲܩܪ ܐܢܐ. ܗ̤ܘ ܕܝܢ ܬܓܪܐ ܥܢܐ ܘܐܡܪ ܠܗ. ܡܘܕܐ ܐܢܐ ܕܐܝܬ ܗ̣̄ܘ ܠܝ ܗܢܐ ܫܩܠ ܛܥܢܐ. ܘܛܘܒܢܐ ܐܡ̣ܪ ܠܗ. ܕܥܕܡܐ ܠܐܡܬܝ ܒܗܠܝܢ ܐܪ̈ܥܢܝܬܐ ܡܬܗܲܦܟ ܐܢܬ. ܘܠܗܠܝܢ ܫܡܝܢ̈ܝܬܐ ܠܐ ܡܬܩܲܪܒ ܐܢܬ. ܐܠܐ ܐܦܢ ܗܫܐ ܠܐܚܪ̈ܢܐ ܫܒܘܩ ܗܠܝܢ. ܘܐܢܬ ܩܦ ܠܡܫܝܚܐ ܒܗܠܝܢ ܕܡܝܬܪ̈ܢ. ܒܬܪ ܩܠܝܠ ܕܝܢ ܠܘܬ ܐܠܗܐ ܐܙܠ ܐܢܬ. ܗ̤ܘ ܕܝܢ ܬܓܪܐ ܗ̇ܘ ܒܚܕܘܬܐ ܠܒܢ̈ܝ ܒܝܬܗ ܦܩܕ. ܕܫܪܟܐ ܕܩܢܝܢܗ ܠܡܣܟ̈ܢܐ ܢܦܠܓܘܢ. ܘܗ̤ܘ ܣܠܸܩ ܠܗ ܠܛܘܪܐ. ܘܢܦܫܗ ܒܐܬܪܐ ܗ̇ܘ ܚܒܫ. ܕܒܗ ܗܠܝܢ ܬܪ̈ܝܢ ܐܫܬܲܟܠܠܘ ܘܫܪ. (fol. 184b).
p. 471, n. 2 Born about A.D. 305, died about 400.

p. 471, n. 3 The account of these two brethren according to Palladius is as follows: ܕܥܠ ܐܚ̈ܐ ܟܝܢ̈ܝܐ ܦܐܣܝܣ ܘܐܫܥܝܐ܀ ܐܚܪ̈ܢܐ ܐܚ̈ܐ ܬܪܝܢ ܕܫܡܗܝ̈ܗܘܢ ܦܐܣܝܣ ܘܐܫܥܝܐ. ܒܢ̈ܝ ܓܒܪܐ ܚܕ ܬܓܪܐ܆ ܕܡܬܬܓܪ ܗܘ̣ܐ ܒܐܣܦܢܝܐ ܗܢܘܢ ܗܠܝܢ ܟܕ ܡܝܬ ܐܒܘܗܘܢ. ܦܲܠܓܘ ܝܪܬܘܬܗ ܒܝܢܬܗܘܢ ܘܡܛܐ ܠܟܠܚܕ ܚܕ ܡܢܗܘܢ ܕܗܒܐ ܥܕܡܐ ܠܚܡܫܐ ܐܠܦܝ̈ܢ ܕܝܢܪ̈ܐ. ܘܡܐܢ̈ܐ ܘܠܒܘ̈ܫܐ ܘܥܒܕ̈ܐ ܘܡܕܡ ܕܐܫܬܟܲܚ. ܘܗ̣ܢܘܢ ܗܠܝܢ ܛܘܒ̈ܢܐ. ܐܬܡܲܠܲܟܘ ܒܝܢܬܗܘܢ ܘܐܬܚܲܫܒܘ ܘܐܡܪܘ ܠܚܕܕ̈ܐ. ܒܐܝܕܐ ܬܐܓܘܪܬܐ ܢܸܚܹܐ ܒܗ ܒܥܠܡܐ ܗܢܐ. ܐܢܗܸ̤ܘ ܕܢܗܲܠܟ ܒܬܐܓܘܪܬܐ ܐܝܕܐ ܕܗܲܠܟ ܒܗ̇ ܐܒܘܢ. ܐܦ ܚܢܢ ܠܐܚܪ̈ܢܐ ܐܝܬ ܠܢ ܕܢܥܦܐ ܥܡܠܢ ܘܠܐܘܬܢ. ܘܟܒܪ ܕܝܢ ܒܐܝܕ̈ܝ ܓܝܣ̈ܐ ܢܦܠ. ܐܘ ܒܝܲܡܐ ܒܐܝܕ̈ܝ ܠܣܛܝ̈ܐ. ܘܟܕ ܒܗܠܝܢ ܚܘܫܒ̈ܐ ܡܫܬܚܩܝܢ ܗܘܘ. ܥܢܘ ܘܐܡܪܝܢ ܠܚܕ̈ܕܐ. ܢܐܬܐ ܠܢ ܠܐܘܪܚܐ ܕܫܪܪܐ. ܘܠܕܘܒܪܐ ܕܟܪ̈ܣܛܝܢܐ ܢܩܢܐ. ܐܝܟܢܐ ܕܐܦ ܡܕܡ ܕܐܪܦܝ ܠܢ ܐܒܘܢ ܢܩܲܕܹܐ. ܘܐܦ ܢܦܫܢ ܕܝܠܢ ܢܩܢܐ. ܘܫܦܪ ܠܗܘܢ ܗܢܐ ܡܘܠܟܢܐ ܕܥܡܠܐ ܕܕܝܪ̈ܝܐ. ܘܐܫܟܚ ܟܠܚܕ ܚܕ ܡܢܗܘܢ ܒܬܘܠܡܕܗ ܦܘܪܫܢܐ. ܕܐܝܢܐ ܥܡܠܐ ܢܠܒܘܟ. ܘܟܕ ܦܲܠܓܘ ܝܪܬܘܬܗ ܕܐܒܘܗܘܢ. ܗܢܐ ܚܘܦܵܛܐ ܗܘܐ ܠܬܪܝܗܘܢ. ܐܝܟ ܕܢܫܦܪܘܢ ܠܐܠܗܐ ܒܫܘܚ̈ܠܦܐ ܕܐܒܝܠܘܬܐ. ܚܕ ܡܢܗܘܢ ܕܝܢ ܟ ܡܕܡ ܕܡܛܝܗܝ. ܦܠܓܗ ܗܘܐ ܘܝܗܘܒܗ ܒܥܕ̈ܬܐ ܘܒܕܝܪ̈ܬܐ. ܘܒܕܪܗ ܠܡܣ̈ܟܢܐ ܘܠܒܝܫ̈ܐ. ܘܝܼܠܦ ܐܘܡܢܘܬܐ ܕܢܦܠܘܚ ܘܢܚܐ ܠܚܡܐ ܕܝܘܡܐ. ܘܢܬܐܡܢ ܒܨܠܘܬܐ ܘܒܨܘܡܐ ܐܡܝܢܐܝܬ. ܗ̇ܘ ܕܝܢ ܐܚܪܢܐ ܠܐ ܒܕܪ ܡܕܡ. ܐܠܐ ܒܢܐ ܠܗ ܕܝܪܐ. ܘܐܚ̈ܐ ܩܠܝܠ ܟܲܡ ܨܐܕܘܗܝ. ܘܗܕܐ ܨܝܦܘܬܐ ܗܘ̤ܬ ܠܗ. ܕܟܠ ܐܟܣܢ̈ܝܐ ܘܡܣ̈ܟܢܐ. ܘܟܠ ܣܒ̈ܐ ܘܟܠ ܟܪ̈ܝܗܐ ܕܨܝܒܝܢ ܗܘ̣ܘ ܠܘܬܗ. ܡܩܲܒܠ ܗܘ̣ܐ ܘܡܢܝܸܚ ܠܗܘܢ. ܘܟܠ ܚܕܒܫܲܒܐ ܘܫܒܬܐ ܬܠܬܐ ܦܬܘܪ̈ܝܢ ܡܬܩܢ ܗܘ̣ܐ. ܘܡܢܝܼܚ ܠܟܠ ܕܡܣܬܲܩܒܠ. ܘܗܟܢܐ ܐܦܩܗ ܠܟܠܗ ܩܢܝܢܗ܀ (fol. 59a.)
p. 472, n. 1 Read ܕܚܘܼܒܵܐ.
p. 472, n. 2 St. Matthew xxvi. 48.

p. 472, n. 3 The allusion appears to be to the three hundred and eighteen bishops who were assembled at the Council of Nice, A.D. 325, to discuss the Arian heresy. The tares were the bishops Menophantus of Ephesus, Patrophilus of Scythopolis, Theognis of Nice, Narcissus of Neroniadis, Theonas of Marmarica, and Secundus of Ptolemais in Egypt. See Theodoret, Hist. Eccles., i. 7; Socrates, Hist. Eccles., i. 8.
p. 473, n. 1 Psalm xxxv. 12.
p. 473, n. 2 Psalm xli. 9.

p. 474, n. 1 This story according to Rosweyde (Vitae Patrum, p. 579, no. 38) is as follows: — Frater quidam impugnabatur à fornicatione. Contigit autem eum venire in vicum quemdam Aegypti, et videns filiam sacerdotus paganorum, adamavit eam, dixitque patri ejus: Da mihi eam uxorem. Ille autem respondens dixit ei: Non possum eam tibi dare, nisi rogavero deum meum. Et abiens ad daemonem, quem colebat, dixit ei: Ecce quidam monachus venit ad me, volens accipere filiam meam; do ei eam? Respondens daemon, dixit: Si negat Deum suum, et Baptismum, et propositum monachi, interroga eum. Et veniens sacerdos dixit ei: Nega Deum tuum, et Baptismum, et propositum monachi, et dabo tibi filiam meam. Ille verò consensit. Et statim vidit velut columbam exire de ore suo, et volare in coelum. Pergens autem sacerdos ad daemonem, dixit: Ecce promisit se tria illa facturum. Tunc respondens diabolus dixit ei: Non des ei filiam tuam in uxorem, quia Deus ejus non recessit ab eo: sed adhuc adjuvabit eum. Et veniens sacerdos dixit illi fratri: Non tibi possum eam dare; quia Deus tuus adhuc adjuvat te, et non recessit à te. What follows in Rosweyde says that when the monk had returned to his senses he went and dwelt in the desert with a certain old man who prayed to God on his behalf. At the end of a fast of three weeks the dove again entered his body by his mouth.
p. 474, n. 2 St. Luke vi. 38.
p. 475, n. 1 I.e., Môṣul.

p. 475, n. 2 ܩܠܘܪܐ. ܩܠܘܿܪ̈ܝܼܢ (see Land, Anecdota, ii. p. 46, l. 13) = κολλύρα; compare Talmudic קילורין, Buxtorf, ed. Fischer, p. 1018. See also Du Cange, Glossarium, s.v. κολλούριον, col. 684; and Kayser, Die Canones Jacob's von Edessa, p. 107. Brit. Mus. MSS. Rich 7203, fol. 156a, col. 2, and Orient. 2441, explain ܩܠܘܪܐ by قُرْصَة a round, flat loaf, and by جَرْدَقَة. Concerning this last word Dozy (Supplément, tom. 1, p. 185) says, A Damas on donne le nom de djardaca à une pâtisserie de froment, qui est mince, puisqu'elle est à peine de l'épaisseur du dos d'un couteau, grande, ronde, cuite dans de l'huile d'abricots et arrosée de dibs tirant sur le brun.
p. 477, n. 1 St. Matthew v. 28.
p. 477, n. 2 Read ܒܪܓܬܐ.
p. 478, n. 1 Compare Genesis iv. 24.
p. 478, n. 2 See supra, p. 220, note 3.
p. 479, n. 1 St. Matthew xxv. 21.
p. 479, n. 2 This passage is quoted in B.O., iii. ii. p. 16.
p. 481, n. 1 The rest of the chapter is quoted in B.O., iii. 1. p. 491, col. 2.

p. 481, n. 2 ܡܲܪ̈ܩܝܼܘܿܢܹܐ. The heretic Marcion lived in the second century of our era. He held that there were four unbegotten existences, and that an irreconcileable opposition existed between the Creator and the Christian God. He condemned marriage, he fasted on the Sabbath, he rejected much of the Old Testament, and only accepted the Gospel of St. Luke, which he mutilated. For the history of the man, his views, his blasphemies and his sect, see Tillemont, Mémoires, t. ii. pp. 122—130. Ephraim, Zenobius and Paul, disciples of Saint Ephraem, Bôd, the Periodentes, Daniel of Ras ʿAin, and others wrote treatises against the heresy of Marcion. See B.O., iii. 1. pp. 43, 63, 170, 219 and 223.

p. 481, n. 3 Mani or Manes, the founder of the sect of the Manichees, sprang from a family of the Magians, but embraced Christianity about the middle of the third century of our era. According to Eusebius (Hist. Eccles., vii. 31) he first proclaimed himself to be Christ, and afterwards to be the very Paraclete and the Holy Spirit. He selected twelve disciples and sent them out into the world to preach his doctrine. For a history of the sect and its title see Tillemont, Mémoires, t. iv. pp. 152—171. Akin to the Manichees in belief was the famous (or infamous) Babaki sect البابكيّة led by Bâbak al-Ḥurramî بابك الخرّمىُّ. He is first mentioned A.H. 201 (see Ibn al-Athîr, ed. Tornberg, tom. vi. p. 231, l. 7), and he was slain A.H. 223 (see Ṭabarî, ed. de Goeje, ser. iii. tom. ii. p. 1015, l. 10). The doctrines and belief of this sect resembled those of the Magians in many particulars. The Arabic text of the history of Bâbak and his parentage, etc., is given by Flügel, Kitâb al-Fihrist, Leipzig, 1871, p. 343; see also Bâbek seine Abstammung und erstes Auftreten, by Flügel in Z.D.M.G., Bd. xxiii. p. 531 ff.
p. 482, n. 1 St. Matthew xxvii. 33; St. Mark xv. 22; St. John xix. 17.
p. 482, n. 2 At Jerusalem, and he was buried in Kĕphar Gamlâ.

p. 482, n. 3 I.e., James the brother of John. Herod Agrippa slew him one year after the Ascension of our Lord. He was buried in Âḳâr, a city of Marmârîḳâ. See Lipsius, Apostelgeschichten, t. ii. 2, p. 26.
p. 482, n. 4 He was slain by a blow from a fuller's staff, and by stoning. See Lipsius, Apostelgeschichten, tom. ii. 2. p. 231.
p. 482, n. 5 Head downwards (ܒܬܪ ܪܫܗ), by Nero, A. Gr. 376. See Book of the Bee, ed. Budge, p. 104.
p. 483, n. 1 For the Nestorian account of his death see Book of the Bee, ed. Budge, p. 107.

p. 483, n. 2 According to the Book of the Bee, ed. Budge, p. 106, Bartholomew was crucified by Hûrsṭî King of Armenia, where he had been an apostle for thirty years. See also Lipsius, Apostelgeschichten, tom. ii. 2, pp. 59, 99 and 104.

p. 483, n. 3 Thomas taught the Parthians, Medes and Indians. The King of India stabbed him with a spear because he had baptized his daughter. The body of Thomas was brought to Edessa by Ḥabbân. See Wright, Apocryphal Acts, vol. ii. p. 297; Acta Thomae, ed. Bonnet, p. 83 ff.; Lipsius, Apostelgeschichten, t. i. p. 236.
p. 483, n. 4 A martyr who suffered in the second year of the persecution of Sapor; see B.O., i. p. 188.

p. 483, n. 5 I.e., Pers. شاهدوست King's friend. He succeeded Mâr Simon in the Bishopric of Seleucia, and was beheaded in Bêth Lâphaṭ, the metropolis of the Hûzâyê, in the second year of the persecution of Sapor; see B.O., i. p. 188, col. 1.
p. 483, n. 6 He succeeded Shâhâdôst in the Bishopric of Seleucia, and was beheaded in Ledan, a city of the Hûzâyê, in the sixth year of the persecution of Sapor; see B.O., i. p. 190, col. 2.
p. 484, n. 1 Genesis xxxvii. 28.
p. 484, n. 2 I.e., to Bêth ʿÂbhê.
p. 484, n. 3 ܒܹܝܬ ܢܘܼܪ̈ܵܘܵܬܵܐ, literally, things in which fire was placed.

p. 484, n. 4 ܐܵܕܪ̈ܘܿܩܹܐ, a word which in A is wrongly glossed by ܒܲܝܬܐ ܕܨܠܡ̈ܐ, but which is rightly explained as things ܕܡܙܕܲܚܝܐ ܗܘܐ ܒܗܘܢ ܢܘܪܐ ܡܢ ܡܓܘܫ̈ܐ ܛܥܝ̈ܐ; see Feige, Die Geschichte des Mar ʿAbhdîshôʿ, text, p. 57, translation p. 39, at the top. The word ܐܕܪܘܩܐ is composed of âdâr = fire, and ûḳ a derivative termination; compare ܪܵܣܘܼܩܵܐ (Kalilag und Damnag, ed. Bickell, p. 13, ll. 11. 13; Z. D. M. G. Bd. xxx. p. 768) from Persian رس; ûg in ܩܪܘܓܒܪ, but read ܩܪܘܓܒܕ Ḳârûgbad, (Act. Mart., I. 345; Patkanian, Journal Asiatique, 1866, I. p. 187) chief of the workmen ܦܪܢܘܓ, φαρνοῦχος (Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 95); ܕܕܘܩ (Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 34); ܦܪ̈ܘܓܐ from parr feather; ܩܛܪܘܩܐ ܡܩܘܩܐ مَكّوٗك طسّوج.
p. 484, n. 5 See supra, p. 390, note 1.

p. 485, n. 1 ܘܹܐܠܵܐ = βῆλα, the vail or curtain with which the door or doorway of the choir is covered. See B.O., iii. 1. p. 532, chap. 13; p. 533, chap. 16; p. 528, chap. 15; Kayser, Die Canones, p. 6, l. 13.
p. 485, n. 2 ܐܦ̈ܝ ܢܵܘܣܹ̈ܐ = βελόθυρα, (Du Cange, Glossarium, col. 186) and καταπετάσματα (Du Cange, Glossarium, col. 611).

p. 485, n. 3 ܡܩܲܒܠܵܢܹ̈ܐ. The sing. ܡܩܲܒܠܵܢܵܐ occurs in Liturgia Sanctorum Apostolorum Adaei et Maris, Urmia, 1890, 4to. p. 27, l. 7 (ܘܡܲܠܒܹܫ ܠܗ ܡܩܲܒܠܵܢܵܐ ܘܣܐܡ ܦܬܘܪܐ ܥܠ ܕܪ̈ܥܘܗܝ). See Duval's review of ܛܟܣܐ ܕܩܘܕܫ̈ܐ ܕܩܪ̈ܒܢܐ ܘܕܥܡܕܐ in Revue Critique, June 20, 1892, p. 483. The ܡܩܒܠܢܐ seems also to be called ܫܘܫܦܐ and ܐܣܛܠܐ which the deacon or other ministrant uses for picking up any particle of the wafer, or for wiping up any drop of the wine while administering the Eucharist to the laity. See Badger, Nestorians, vol. 1. p. 225; and Grant in Ritter, Erdkunde, Bd. ii. p. 611. Compare also the ὡράριον, Du Cange, Glossarium, col. 1792; and the ܐܘܪܪܐ in Assemânî, Codex Liturgicus, tom. viii. p. 47, ll. 12, 13, 16.

p. 494, n. 1 I.c., Ῥαγαί, Rhages (see Tobit. i. 14; iv. 20; ix. 2) a town the ruins of which are situated about 25 miles S.E. of Teherân. It seems to have existed in the time of the last Babylonian Empire; it was rebuilt by Seleucus Nicator who called it Europus; and it was finally destroyed in the XIIIth century of our era. See Strabo, xi. 9. 1; xi. 13. 6; and Ker Porter, Travels, vol. 1, p. 358.

Compare رَوْط longue branche détachée d'un arbre, p. e. d'un peuplier (Dozy, Supplément, t. i. p. 571). In Muḥîṭ al-Muḥîṭ Buṭrus Bistânî says والرَوط عند العَامّة عود طويل من الشجر كالحَور ونخِوْهِ.

p. 497, n. 3 On the dress of monks see B.O., iii. ii. p. 898; compare also Land, Anecdota, tom. ii. p. 156, l. 22; and Usener, Der Heilige Theodosios, p. 171.

p. 497, n. 4 Compare Dixit abbas Evagrius, fuisse quemdam fratrem, qui nihil habuit in substantiâ suâ, nisi tantùm Evangelium, et ipsum vendidit in pauperum nutrimento. Dicens quodam verbo, quod memoriae dignum est commendari: Ipsum etiam, inquit, verbum vendidi, quod jubet, vende omnia, et da pauperibus. Rosweyde, Vitae Patrum, p. 582, No. 5. Interrogatus est senex quidam à fratre, quid faceret ut salvus esset. Ille autem exspolians se vestimento suo, et cingens lumbos suos, atque extendens manus, dixit: Sic debet nudus esse monachus ab omni materiâ saeculari, et crucifigere se adversus tentationem atque certamina mundi. Rosweyde, op. cit., p. 583, No. 16. The quotations from Evagrius made by Thomas of Margâ probably form part of the Μοναχὸς ἢ περὶ Πρακτικῆς, extracts from which are given by Cotelerius, Eccles. Graec. Monumenta, tom. iii. pp. 68—102; by Bigot, Palladii De Vita S. Joh. p. 525, n. 4 ܙܘܼܪܲܝܩ. Ṣadaḳa bin ʿAlîya the freed man of Azd (صدقة بن علىّ مولى الازد), also called Zuraiḳ of Môṣul (زريق بن علىّ بن صدقة الازدىُّ الموصلىُّ), who ruled over the mountainous district between Môṣul and Adhôrbâîgân, together with Wagnâ al-Azdî, did great mischief in Adhôrbâîgân in the time of al-Rashîd when, perhaps A.H. 183, Ḥuzaima bin Ḥâzim, حُزَيمة بن خازم, who drove the Ḥazars through the gates of the Caucasus and who fortified Marâga (see Al-Belâdhorî, Liber Expugnationis Regionum [ed. de Goeje, Leyden 1863], p. 330), was appointed governor of Adhôrbâîgân to resist his might (see Ibn al-Athîr, tom. vi. p. 111; Ṭabarî tom. iii. p. 648). Zuraiḳ conquered Urmiya, and together with his brother, built castles there (Belâdhorî, p. 331; Ibn al-Fakîh al-Hamadhânî [ed. de Goeje 1885] p. 284, l. 19). Zuraiḳ was appointed governor of Armenia and Adhôrbâîgân by al-Mâmûn, A.H. 209, to fight against Bâbek al-Ḥurramî بابك الخرّمىّ, by whom, however, he was vanquished (Ṭabarî, tom. iii. p. 1072; Ibn al-Athîr, tom. vi. p. 338). Previous to A.H. 211, Zuraiḳ made war against al-Sayyed bin Anas, السيّد بن أَنَس, who had been Emîr of Môṣul and Margâ since A.H. 202, and attacked him in that year with 40,000 men and slew him (Ibn al-Athîr, tom. vi. p. 248). Muḥammad bin Ḥumaid al-Ṭûsî (الطوسىّ), who had been made Wâlî of Môṣul by al-Mâmûn (see Ibn al-Athîr, tom. vi. p. 287; al-Yaʿḳubî, Historiae [ed. Houtsma], tom. ii. p. 564) conquered Zuraiḳ on the Zâb A.H. 212, and compelled him to ask for protection and a safe-conduct, الامان (Yaʿḳubî p. 564, l. 18). When Zuraiḳ came to him he sent him to the court of the Khalîfa, who at once ordered that all the wealth and possessions of Zuraiḳ and of his family should be confiscated. This order was not, however, strictly carried out, for Ḥumaid entered into negotiations with Zuraiḳ's brethren, and part of Zuraiḳ's wealth was returned to his family.

p. 530, n. 1 Pythagoras, the son of Mnesarchus a merchant or seal engraver, was born at Samos about B. C. 570. He is thought to have visited Egypt, Syria, Babylonia and India. The Pythagorean theory of happiness was that it consisted of the science of the perfection of the virtues of the soul.

p. 530, n. 2 I.e., Homer the Poet, who was reputed among the ancients to possess a great knowledge of medicine and physical science. See Fabricius, Bibliothecae Graecae, Hamburg, 1714, tom. ii. Bk. 2, cap. 6, § 13; and Tiraquellus, De Nobilitate, Frankfort 1597, tom. 1. cap. 31, pp. 133, 138. For Homer the physician who flourished about the time of Melanthus, King of the Athenians, see Fabricius, Bibliothecae Graecae, tom. xiii. Bk. VI. cap. IX.

p. 530, n. 3 For the theories of Thales, Pythagoras, Empedocles, Aristotle, Anaxagoras and others upon metals and their alloys, etc., see Hoefer, Histoire de la Chimie depuis les temps les plus reculés jusqu'à notre époque, Paris, 1842, tom. i. pp. 65, 108 ff. On the whole subject of ancient Alchemy (الكِيمِيَاء al-kîmiyâ, from Gr. χημεία or χημία, which in its turn seems to be derived from an Egyptian word meaning preparation of the black), see the excellent article Chemie by Hoffmann in Ladenburg's Handwörterbuch der Chimie (in the Encyklopaedie der Naturwissenschaften, Breslau 1884), Bd. XVI. p. 2, pp. 516—530; Kopp, Beiträge zur Geschichte der Chemie, 1869; and the article Pierre Philosophale in Migne, Encyclopédie Théologique, tom. 46, col. 1173.

p. 531, n. 1 Πλάτον δὲ ὁ φιλόσοφος, ἐκ τῶν τὰ περὶ τὴν νομοθεσίαν ὠφεληθείς; see Clemens Alexandrinus, Stromata, i. xxv; and compare the quotation from Numenius the Pythagorean in Eusebius, Praepar. Evang., xi. 10., at the end (Migne, Patrol. Cursus. Ser. Graec. tom. xxi. col. 873). Thomas of Margâ here repeats one of the many mythical stories related of Plato. Lactantius (Institut. iv. 2) made him travel to the Magi and Persians; Clemens (Cohortationes 46) made him travel to the Babylonians, Assyrians, Hebrews and Thracians; others declared that he was acquainted with the doctrines of Zoroaster and with Persian magic; but all thesestatemen ts are pure inventions, as we may see from Brucker, Historia critica Philosophiae a mundi incunabulis ad nostram usque aetatem deducta, Leipzig, 1742—67, tom. i. p. 635, and Zeller, Plato and the Older Academy (trans. by Alleyne and Goodwin), London 1876, p. 14.

p. 542, n. 1 Before the reading of the Ḳeryânâ the deacon exclaims aloud: Sit down, and be silent; and when it is ended, the people rise at the bidding of the same minister, who then gives notice of the short psalm which is to follow, and which is then taken up and sung by the officiating priest. This psalm is called Shûrâyâ, and generally consists of two verses taken from the Psalter to which the Gloria Patri is added. The Shûrâyâ, therefore, appears to hold the same place in the Nestorian liturgy, as the tractus does in the Roman, the προκείμενον in the Constantinopolitan, and the psalmellus in the Milan liturgies. Badger, Nestorians, vol. ii. p. 20.

p. 542, n. 2 The ḳeryânê, i.e., Readings, consist of extracts from the Old Testament and the Acts of the Apostles. The first ḳeryânâ is always from the Old Testament, and in a few cases the second Lesson also; but this latter is more generally taken from the Acts of the Apostles. See Badger, Nestorians, vol. ii. p. 19.

p. 543, n. 9 The ܦܪ̈ܩܛܐ, i.e., screen or lattice, which formed the middle opening part of the wall of partition, separated the chancel from the nave. It stood either upon the third or highest step leading to the ܩܢ̈ܟܐ, or by the side of the lowest step on the floor of the nave. The ܩܣܛܪܘܡܐ seems to have been the partition wall to the right and left of the door of the ܩܢ̈ܟܐ, and its width must have been equal to the depth of the three steps. According to this theory the ܩܣܛܪܘܡܐ would very well represent the ܬܘܠܬܐ ܕܫܡܝܐ.

p. 544, n. 5 Compare ܫܡܐ ܗܟܝܠ ܕܥܕܬܐ ܟܢܘܫܝܐ ܥܡ ܥܐܕܐ ܡܫܘܕܥ ܘܛܘܟܣ̈ܐ ܕܗܠܝܢ ܕܠܥܠ ܨܝܪܐ. ܐܝܟܙܢܐ ܓܝܪ ܕܬܓ̈ܡܐ ܬܫܥܐ ܗܢܘܢ ܕܠܪܒܘܬܐ ܡܫܡܫܝܢ܆ ܠܬܠܬܐ ܛܟܣ̈ܝ ܡܦܠܓܝܢܢ܆ ܗܟܢܐ ܐܦ ܗܝ. ܦܛܪܝܪܟܘ ܘܡܝܛܪ̈ܦܘܠܝܛܐ ܘܐܦܝܣܩ̈ܘܦܐ ܛܟܣܐ ܕܟܪ̈ܘܒܐ ܘܕܣܪ̈ܦܐ ܘܡܘܬܒ̈ܐ ܡܡܠܝܢ. ܘܐܪ̈ܟܝܕܝܩܘܢܐ ܘܦܪ̈ܘܕܘܛܐ ܘܩܫܝ̈ܫܐ ܒܛܟܣܐ ܕܚܝ̈ܠܐ ܘܫܘܠܛܢ̈ܐ ܘܡܪ̈ܘܬܐ ܩܝܡܝܢ. ܘܡܫܡܫ̈ܢܐ ܘܗܘܦ̈ܬܝܩܢܐ ܘܩܪ̈ܘܝܐ ܒܛܟܣܐ ܕܐܪ̈ܟܘܣ ܘܪ̈ܒܝܡܠܐܟܐ ܘܡܠܐܟ̈ܐ ܡܫܡܫܝܢ. See B.O., iii. 1. p. 355, col. 2, cap. VIII. For a long discussion on the nine orders of angels by Solomon of al-Baṣra see Budge, Book of the Bee, pp. 9—11. The Cherubim are an intellectual motion which bears the throne of the Holy Trinity, and at their head stands Gabriel; the Seraphim are a fiery motion; and the Thrones are a fixed motion. The Lords are a motion which is entrusted with the government of the motions beneath it; the Powers are the minister of the will of God; and Rulers are a motion which hath power over spiritual treasures. This class of angels governs the luminaries, the sun, moon and stars. The Principalities are a defined motion which possesseth the direction of the upper ether, of rain, cloud, lightning, thunder, whirlwinds, tempests, winds, etc.; the Archangels are a swift operative motion which governeth the animal creation and everything that hath life, from the gnat to the elephant; and the Angels are a motion which hath spiritual knowledge of everything that is on earth and in heaven. The number of each one of these classes of angels is equal to the number of all mankind from Adam to the resurrection.

p. 551, n. 2 ܒܹܝܬ ܬܸܫܡܸܫܬܵܐ, literally, the place of the liturgy. It seems to have been that part of the church which was just in front of the ܒܝܸܡܵܐ, which was called by the Greeks σωλέα (see Du Cange, Glossarium, col. 1513), and to which the Nestorians to-day give the name of ܟܘܪܘܣ. The bodies of laymen are not carried into the church as a general rule; see Badger, Nestorians, vol. ii. p. 297. The leader of the singing was called ܪܫ ܬܫܡܫܬܐ i.e., κανονάρχος (Du Cange, Glossarium, col. 583). Some interesting remarks on the singing of the Psalms and their division into kathismata, and the hours for prayer will be found in Usener, Der heilige Theodosios, p. 45, l. 19 (and note on p. 150); p. 154, and p. 49, l. 5 (and note on p. 153).

p. 553, n. 1 The overflow of the Tigris and Zâb rivers is caused by the melting of the snow in the mountains where they rise. The first spring flood takes place about the middle of February and in a few days the river rises several feet and floods all the low-lying country on each side of its banks. In February 1889, while I was at Môṣul carrying on excavations at Kouyunjik for the Trustees of the British Museum, the water reached nearly to the mound of Kouyunjik, and about two months later it actually touched its base which is several feet above the normal height of the river. The little river Ḥôser (in Assyrian ) became a mighty stream, and it was not hard to understand how very materially this river which Sennacherib tells us he brought to Nineveh (Rawlinson, Cuneiform Inscriptions of Western Asia, vol. iii. pl. 14, l. 11), must have helped to destroy the palaces of his great city. The yellow Tigris flowed along with its swollen stream at the rate of 5 1/2 or 6 miles an hour, and small rafts reached Bagdad in 4 1/2 days, including stoppages of a few hours each night. The distance from Môṣul to Bagdad viâ Kerkûk is about 300 miles, and I believe the distance by river to be about 400. The greatest flood of the Tigris and Zâb takes place in April. It may be noticed that Thomas of Margâ used the Syriac form of the Old Assyrian word for flood; i.e., ܡܸܠܐܵܐ = Assyrian mi-lum; see Strassmaier, Wörterverzeichniss, No. 5294, p. 658; Bruno, A Classified List, Leyden 1887, p. 466, No. 11538; Smith, Sennacherib, p. 146, l. 52; Rawlinson, Cuneiform Inscriptions of Western Asia, vol. 1. pl. 57, col. vii. l. 51; and Norris, Assyrian Dictionary, pt. iii. p. 789. Floods on the Tigris are often accompanied by violent south-east winds which literally blow craft up the river or into the banks, and it is necessary to cut the bridges of boats until the wind and stream subside.

p. 572, n. 3 The account of Bessarion by Palladius is as follows: — ܡܫܬܥܝܢ ܗܘܘ ܬܠܡܝܕ̈ܘܗܝ ܕܐܒܐ ܒܝܣܝܪܝܘܢ ܕܘܒܪܗ ܘܚܝ̈ܗܘܝ ܟܕ ܐܡܪܝܢ. ܕܗܟܢܐ ܐܝܬܘܗܝ ܗܘܐ ܣܒܐ ܒܗܘܦܟܗ ܐܝܟ ܦܪܚܬܐ ܕܫܡܝܐ. ܘܐܝܠܝܢ ܕܒܡܝ̈ܐ ܘܪ̈ܚܫܐ ܕܐܪܥܐ. ܘܗܟܢܐ ܕܠܐ ܫܓܝܫܘܬܐ ܘܒܗܝܠܘܬܐ ܢܦܫܗ ܠܟܠܗ ܙܒܢܐ ܕܚܝ̈ܘܗܝ. ܠܐ ܓܝܪ ܨܦܬܐ ܕܩܠܝܬܐ ܫܟܝܚܐ ܗܘܬ ܠܝܬܗ. ܘܠܐ ܒܪܓܬܐ ܕܕܘܟ̈ܝܬܐ ܐܬܬܚܕܬ݀ ܢܦܫܗ. ܠܐ ܣܒܥܘܬܐ ܕܡܐܟܘܠܬܐ ܟܠܗ ܙܒܢܐ ܕܪܗܛܗ ܫܲܡܫ. ܠܐ ܩܢܝܢܐ ܕܠܒܘ̈ܫܐ. ܠܐ ܟܬܒ̈ܐ ܟܫܐ ܘܣܡ. ܡܚܪܪܐ ܕܝܢ ܐܝܬܘܗܝ ܗܘܐܡܢ ܟܠܗܝܢ ܕܦܓܪܐ. ܟܕ ܒܣܒܪܐ ܕܛܒ̈ܬܐ ܕܥܬܝܕ̈ܢ ܡܬܒܲܣܡ ܗܘܐ. ܘܡܫܲܪܪ ܕܠܐ ܙܘܥܙܥܐ. ܘܒܫܬܐܣܬܐ ܕܗܝܡܢܘܬܗ. ܘܐܝܬܘܗܝ ܗܘܐ ܡܚܡܣܢܢܐ ܒܥܢܘܝܘܬܐ. ܘܒܕܡܘܬ ܫܒܝܐ ܙܘܥܙܥܐ. ܘܒܫܬܐܣܬܐ ܕܗܝܡܢܘܬܗ. ܘܐܝܬܘܗܝ ܗܘܐ ܡܚܡܣܢܢܐ ܒܥܢܘܝܘܬܐ. ܘܒܕܡܘܬ ܫܒܝܐ ܠܟܠ ܘܠܗܠ ܦܗ̇ܐ ܗܘܐ. ܟܕ ܐܝܬܘܗܝ ܗܘܐ ܥܪܛܠܝܐ ܒܩܘܪܫܐ. ܘܝܵܩܕ ܗܘܐ ܒܥܘܙܗ ܕܫܡܫܐ ܟܕ ܒܙܒܢ ܒܝܢܬ ܫܩ̈ܝܦܐ ܘܒܚܘܪܒܐ ܡܬܗܲܦܟ. ܘܐܢܗܸܘ ܕܢܓܕܫ ܘܢܣܬܩܒܠ ܗܘܐ ܘܢܐܬܐ ܠܕܘܟ̈ܝܬܐ ܕܡܫ̈ܝܢܢ. ܐܝܟܐ ܕܟܢܘܫܝܐ ܕܕܝܪ̈ܝܐ ܠܕܘܒܪܐ ܕܕܝܪܝܘܬܐ ܟܠܗ ܙܒܢܐ ܕܝܚܝ̈ܗܘܢ ܒܟܢܘܫܝܐ ܕܓܘܐ ܡܲܦܩܝܢ ܠܒܪ ܡܢ ܬܪܥܐ ܕܕܝܪܐ. ܗܢܝܐܝܬ ܝܵܬܒ ܗܘܐ. ܐܝܟܢܐ ܕܒܙܒܢ ܟܕ ܠܚܕܐ ܡ̣ܢ ܕܝܪ̈ܐ ܡܲܢܥ ܝܬܸܒ ܠܗ ܠܒܪ ܡܢ ܬܪܥܐ. ܘܒܵܟܐ ܗܘܐ ܘܐܵܠܹܐ ܐܝܟ ܐܢܫ ܕܐܫܬܘܙܒ ܡܢ ܡܚܫ̈ܘܠܐ. ܘܟܕ ܢܦܲܩ ܚܕ ܡܢ ܐܚ̈ܐ. ܐܫܟܚܗ. ܠܗܢܐ ܐܝܟ ܚܕ ܡܢ ܡܣܟ̈ܢܐ. ܘܚܕܘܪܐ ܕܐܝܬ ܒܥܠܡܐ. ܘܟܕ ܩܪܒ ܠܘܬܗ ܚܝܘܣܬܢܐܝܬ ܐܡ̣ܪ ܠܗ. ܡܢܐ ܒܲܟܐ ܐܢܬ ܓܒܪܐ. ܐܢ ܥܠ ܡܕܡ ܡ̣ܢ ܚܫܚܬܐ ܕܐܠܨ̈ܬܐ ܣܢܝܩ ܐܢܬ. ܐܟܡܐ ܕܐܝܬ ܒܚܲܝܠܝ ܝܗ̇ܒ ܐܢܐ ܠܟ. ܩܘܡ ܥܘܠ ܠܟ ܠܓܘ. ܘܐܬܒܲܝܐ ܒܫܘܬܦܘܬܐ ܕܒܘܪܟܬܐ ܕܦܬܘܪܐ ܥܲܡܢ. ܘܗ̤ܘ ܛܘܒܢܐ ܒܝܣܝܪܝܘܢ ܦܲܢܝ ܦܬܓܡܐ ܘܐܡܲܪ ܠܗ. ܡ̣ܢ ܩܕܡ ܕܐܫܟܚ ܩܢܝܢܐ ܕܒܝܬܝ ܗ̇ܘ ܕܐܘܒܕܬ. ܘܡܪ̈ܗܛܐ ܣܓ̈ܝܐܐ ܕܒܝܬ ܐܒܗ̈ܝ܆ ܕܒܟܠ ܙܢܝ̈ܢ ܡܫܚܠܦܐܝܬ ܚܣܪܹܬ. ܠܐ ܡܨܐ ܐܢܐ ܕܐܗܘܐ ܬܚܝܬ ܡܛܠܠܐ. ܠܣܛܝ݀ܐ ܓܝܪ ܢܦܲܠܘ ܥܠܝ ܒܓܘ ܝܡܐ. ܘܒܡܚܫܘܠܐ ܐܙܕܩܦ ܥܠܝ. ܘܡ̣ܢ ܥܘܬܪܐ ܕܩܢܹܐ ܗܘ̇ܝܬ ܐܬܓܙܝܼܬ. ܘܗ̇ܘܝܬ ܡ̣ܢ ܡܫܒܚܐ ܫܝܛܐ. ܗ̤ܘ ܕܝܢ ܐܚܐ ܐܬܬܘܗ ܒܡܠܬܐ ܗܕܐ ܘܟܪܝܬ݀ ܠܗ. ܥܠ ܐܲܦܩ ܠܚܡܐ ܘܝܗ̄ܒܠܗ ܟܕ ܐܡ̇ܪ ܠܗ. ܣܒ ܠܟ ܗܢܐ ܐܒܘܢ. ܘܗܠܝܢ ܕܫܪܟܐ ܐܚܪ̈ܢܝܬܐ ܕܐܡܲܪܬ ܡܦܲܢܐ ܠܟ ܐܠܗܐ܆ ܐܬܪܐ ܘܓܢܣܐ ܘܥܘܬܪܐ ܘܗܠܝܢ ܕܐܡܲܪܬ. ܗ̤ܘ ܕܝܢ ܝܬܝܪܐܝܬ ܐܵܠܹܐ ܗ̄ܘ̣ܐ. ܘܓܥܐ ܗ̄ܘ̣ܐ ܟܕ ܡܪܝܡ ܩܠܗ. ܘܐܡ̇ܪ. ܕܠܐ ܝܕܥ ܐܢܐ ܐܢ ܡܨܐ ܐܢܐ ܕܐܫܟܚ. ܗ̇ܘ ܡܕܡ ܕܐܘܒܕܹܬ ܕܒܥܐ ܐܢܐ. ܐܠܐ ܬܘܒ ܝܬܝܪܐܝܬ ܐܝܟ ܕܚܙܐ ܐܢܐ ܡܢܝ ܡܬܦܲܢܐ. ܟܕ ܐܠܝܼܨ ܐܢܐ ܟܠܝܘܡ ܘܡܡܲܛܐ ܐܢܐ ܠܡܘܬܐ. ܡܢ ܡܚܫܘܠܐ ܩܫܝܐ ܕܒܝܫ̈ܬܐ ܕܠܐ ܡܢܝܢܐ ܕܚܕܪ̈ܢܝ. ܗܠܝܢ ܕܡܣܝܒܪ ܐܢܐ ܥܠ ܣܒܪܐ ܕܕܠܡܐ ܐܫܘܐ ܠܟ̈ܚܡܐ ܒܝܘܡܐ ܕܕܝܢܐ܀ (fol. 131b.) The abbot Bessarion lived in the fourth century of our era. He is said to have been able to cross rivers by walking upon the water; to have caused the sun to refrain from setting until he had arrived at the cell of a certain sage; to have healed the sick and to have cast out devils; and to have been acquainted with the decrees of God before they were worked out. For his life and sayings, see Rosweyde, Vitae Patrum, pp. 518, 532, 584, 594, 609ff.; Tillemont, Mémoires, tom. viii. p. 348.

p. 576, n. 5 The village of Berbĕlî or Barbelî is mentioned in connexion with Tellà (ܬܷܠܴܐ ܘܒܱܪܒܷܠܻܝ B.O., iii. 1. p. 569, col. 1. l. 10 = التل وبربرى B.O., iii. 1. p. 564, col. 2, l. 22), and may probably be compared with the Be-Rberri mentioned by Badger (Nestorians, vol. 1. p. 397) as belonging to the diocese of Gawar; see B.O., iii. ii. p. 728; and Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 222, note 1762. Tellà lay on the east side of the Upper Zâb, north of Walto, and south of Julamerk.

p. 583, n. 2 St. Matthew iii. 13–17; St. Mark i. 5–11. Two places for fording the Jordan are mentioned in the Old Testament: one was over against Jericho (Joshua ii. 7; Judges iii. 28), and the other was at Bethabara (St. John 1. 28), which is probably to be identified with the modern Maḳṭaʿ or place of passage. It is nowhere stated expressly where Christ was baptized, but it is thought by some that His baptism by St. John took place at the upper ford. Tradition proves that from a very early date pilgrims believed that the baptism of Christ took place here, and the existence of the ruins of the Monastery of St. John (Ḳaṣr el-Yehûdî) which was built over the cave in which St. John is said to have lived, near this spot at a short distance from the river, lends support to the belief. As early as the time of Constantine baptism in the Jordan was considered a blessed thing, and in the 6th century pilgrims crowded thither from all parts; see Robinson, Biblical Researches, vol. iii. p. 353ff.; Reland, Palaestina, pp. 271–279; Socin and Baedeker, Palestine and Syria, p. 266. Antoninus Martyr, who visited Palestine about 570, says: — ……venimus in locum, ubi baptizatus est dominus noster. In ipso loco transierunt filii Israel; ibi et filii prophetarum perdiderunt securim et ex ipso loco assumptus est Elias. In ipso loco est mons Hermon modicus, qui legitur in Psalmo. At this spot both banks of the river were paved with marble steps, and a wooden cross rose in the middle of the stream …… est crux lignea intus in aqua et gradus descendunt usque ad aquam ex utraque parte marmoris. Antonini Placentini Itinerarium, ed. Gildemeister, Berlin, 1889, 8vo. pp. 7, 9. Tuch's Antoninus Martyr, seine Zeit und seine Pilgerfahrt nach dem Morgenlande, Leipzig 1864, may be consulted upon this subject with advantage.

p. 584, n. 1 It is difficult to understand what Temple Rabban Cyprian can have seen at Jerusalem. The first Temple was built by Solomon (2 Samuel vii. 5ff.), and all the arrangements were identical with those in the Tabernacle of Moses; the second Temple was built by Zerubbabel when the Jews returned from the Captivity about B.C. 510; and the third and greatest of the Temples was built by Herod and burnt down at the siege of Jerusalem by Titus A.D. 70. Julian the Apostate wished the Jews to return to Jerusalem and tried to rebuild their Temple, and before the end of the Vth century crowds of pilgrims arrived yearly to visit the places made sacred by Christ. Jerusalem suffered greatly at the hands of the Persians A.D. 614 and many of its churches were destroyed; in 637 it was conquered by the Arabs. It is thus clear that very little of any ancient building can have been left in Jerusalem by the time Rabban Cyprian arrived there.
p. 584, n. 2 See Socin and Baedeker, Palestine, pp. 189–201; and Antoninus, ed. Gildemeister, p. 14, No. 19.

p. 584, n. 3 The site of the Holy Sepulchre was discovered in the time of Constantine, but previously it is said to have been occupied by a Temple of Venus. The church which he built there was dedicated A.D. 336. For the topography of Jerusalem see D'Anville, Sur l'ancien Jérusalem, Paris, 1747; Tillemont, Histoire des Empereurs, Brussels 1732, tom. ii. p. 121–132, tom. iv. p. 107; Le Bruyn, Voyage au Levant, p. 288; Itinerarium Hierosol. ed. Wesseling, p. 592; Ammianus Marcellinus xxiii. 1; Warburton, Julian, London 1751, and the passages quoted by him; and De Vogüé, Le Temple de Jérusalem, Paris, 1863; Besant, Jerusalem, London 1888; Warren, Jerusalem, London 1884; Wilson, Jerusalem, London 1889.
p. 584, n. 4 St. Mark xiv. 14; St. Luke xxii. 11.
p. 584, n. 5 See Antoninus, ed. Gildemeister, p. 12. This pilgrim kissed the wood of the Cross and handled the label which was above it, and he saw the sponge and the reed (p. 15).

p. 585, n. 1 At the N. E. angle of the rock which bears the chapel, which is built on a small plateau at the top of Gebel Mûsâ (i.e., the Mountain of Moses), to the left is a hollow, where Moses is said to have stood when the glory of the Lord passed by, and the monks show the impression of the prophet's head and shoulders on the stone. The tradition is to the effect that Moses remained fasting for forty days in a hollow resembling a cistern near the mosque, while writing the Ten Commandments. p. 586, n. 6 Serapion the Sindonite is described by Palladius as follows: — ܬܘܒ ܕܝܢ ܐܝܬ ܗ̣̄ܘܐ ܛܘܒܢܐ ܚܕ ܕܫܡܗ ܗ̄ܘܐ ܣܪܵܦܝܼܘܿܢ ܕܐܬܩܪܝ ܕܣܸܢܕܘܿܢܵܐ. ܡܛܠ ܕܡܕܡ ܐܚܪܝܢ ܠܐ ܐܬܟܣܝ ܐܘ ܠܒܸܫ ܒܚܝ̈ܘܗܝ. ܐܠܐ ܐܢ ܣܕܘܢܐ ܒܠܚܘܕ ܕܡܥܲܛܦ ܗ̄ܘܼܐ ܘܝܬܝܪ ܪܘܪܒܐܝܬ ܐܬܕܟܪ ܗ̄ܘܼܐ ܒܡܣܪܩܘܬܐ. ܘܟܕ ܠܐ ܝܵܕܥ ܗ̣̄ܘܐ ܣܸܦܪܐ. ܬܵܢܐ ܗ̣̄ܘܐ ܟܠܗܘܢ ܟܬܒ̈ܐ ܡܢ ܠܒܐ. ܘܡܢ ܣܓܝܐܘܬ ܡܣܲܪܩܘܬܗ ܘܬܸܢܝܐ ܕܟܬܒ̈ܐ. ܐܦܠܐ ܕܢܥܡܪ ܒܩܠܝܬܐ ܡܫܟܚ ܗ̄ܘܼܐ. ܡܛܠ ܕܠܐ ܡܬܚܲܫܚ ܒܡܕܡ ܕܡܢ ܥܠܡܐ ܗܘ̣. ܐܠܐ ܡܬܟܪܟ ܗ̄ܘܼܐ ܒܟܠܙܒܢ ܘܡܬܠܡܕ ܠܣܓ̈ܝܐܐ ܘܡܙܲܒܸܢ ܗ̄ܘܼܐ ܢܦܫܗ ܒܨܒܝܢܗ. ܘܡܲܟܪܙ ܘܡܬܠܡܕ ܗ̄ܘܼܐ ܘܡܲܦܢܐ ܣܓ̈ܝܐܐ ܠܘܬ ܐܠܗܐ. (fol. 104b). Every farthing of money which he obtained he gave away to those poorer than himself, and to do deeds of charity he fasted four or five days at a time. Palladius says that he visited Rome and Athens, and that he died at the age of sixty-two. See Tillemont, Mémoires, tom. viii. p. 348, col. 2.
p. 586, n. 7 Read ܟܲܟܵܟ̈ܝܵܬܵܐ.

p. 587, n. 2 Hoffmann would read ܘܗܘܢܐ ܠܨܠܘܬܐ [he benefited by] a contemplative disposition to pray and to sing psalms.

For examples of the use of this word compare ܫ̈ܠܵܠܲܝ ܕܲܩܪܵܒܵܐ Aphraates, ed. Wright, p. 137, l. 19; ܘܥܒܝܛ ܠܠܝܐ ܒܫ̈ܠܠܘܗܝ atra erat nox, Sancti Ephraem Syri, ed. Lamy tom. 1. p. 437, l. 10; ܘܫ̈ܠܠܐ ܕܡܫܬܘܬܐ ܗܕܐ ܕܒܛܠܐ Wright, Apocryphal Acts, vol. 1. p. 183, l. 6; ܘܫ̈ܠܠܐ ܕܕܘܒܩܝܗܝܢ ܕܒܝܕ ܫܘܝ̈ܬܐ ܣܢܝ̈ܬܐ ܕܣܥܪܐ ܘܕܥܡܪܐ Land, Anecdota, tom. ii. p. 216, l. 28; and سلالة Dozy, Supplément, tom. 1. p. 670.

p. 597, n. 2 ܩܹܐܪܘܿܬܵܐ, Gr. κηρός. Compare ܘܗܕܐ ܬܘܒ ܕܥ܆ ܕܛܠܝܘܬܐ ܐܝܟ ܩܐܪܘܬܐ ܪܟܝܟܬܐ ܕܡܩܒܠܐ ܛܒܥܐ ܕܗ̇ܘ ܡܕܡ ܕܡܢ ܥܙܩܬܐ ܢܦܠ ܥܠܝܗ̇ Land, Anecdota, vol. ii. p. 121, ll. 21–23. ܩܐܪܘܬܐ = شَمَع Brit. Mus. Or. 7203, fol. 148b, col. 1. See also Payne Smith, Thes., col. 3737.

p. 600, n. 1 The ܚܢܵܢܵܐ was composed of the dust of some martyr and oil and water, and was made in the following way: — Bring, master, dust from the place in which martyrs have been crowned, and cast [it] into a vessel into which nothing has fallen except water and olive oil, throw the dust into the vessel and cast water thereupon and knead it well together. Bring a little oil in another vessel and take a portion of the mass [from the first vessel], and besmear it with that oil upon thy hand, and then cut it into pieces like the seals of the ܚܢܵܢܵܐ. Take each single piece which hath been cut and roll it upon thy left hand, with the finger of the right hand next to the thumb, until it becometh as fine as a thread, and lay it upon an outspread napkin which thou shouldst have before thee, until [the dust] hath come to an end. Let it dry for one day and one night, and then bring a ܛܝܒܘܬܐ of Mâr Thomas (i.e., a ܚܢܵܢܵܐ made of the relics of Mâr Thomas the Apostle) and cast it in the form of a cross into that vessel in which thou hast made the mass of dust, oil and water, and say, This ܚܢܵܢܵܐ is signed and sanctified by this ܛܝܒܘܬܐ of Mâr Thomas the Apostle to the healing and cure of the body and soul, in the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Ghost. ܐܝܬܐ ܐܘ ܡܪܝ ܥܦܪܐ ܕܕܘܟܬܐ ܕܐܬܟܠܠܘ ܒܗ ܣܗ̈ܕܐ ܘܐܪܡܐ ܒܡܐܢܐ ܕܠܐ ܢܦܠܘ ܒܗ ܡܕܡ ܠܓܡܪ ܣܛܪ ܡܢ ܡܝ̈ܐ ܘܙܝܬܐ. ܘܐܪܡܐ ܥܦܪܐ ܒܗ ܒܡܐܢܐ. ܘܐܪܡܐ ܥܠܘܗܝ ܡܝ̈ܐ. ܘܠܘܫܘܗܝ ܛܒܐܝܬ. ܘܐܝܬܐ ܩܠܝܠ ܙܝܬܐ ܒܡܐܢܐ ܐܚܪܢܐ ܘܫܩܘܠ ܚܕܐ ܓܒܘܠܬܐ ܘܦܬܠܝܗܝ ܥܠ ܗ̇ܘ ܙܝܬܐ ܥܠ ܐܝܕܟ. ܘܟܢ ܦܣܘܩܝܗܝ ܒܕܡܘܬ ܛܒ̈ܥܐ ܕܚܢܢܐ. ܘܫܩܘܠ ܚܕ ܚܕ ܦܘܣܩܢܐ ܘܓܠܝܗܝ ܥܠ ܐܝܕܟ ܕܣܡܠܐ ܥܕܡܐ ܕܡܬܩܲܛܢ ܐܝܟ ܚܘܛܐ ܒܨܒܥܐ ܕܝܡܝܢܐ ܕܠܘܬ ܟܪܬܐ. ܘܦܪܘܣܝܗܝ ܥܠ ܣܕܘܢܐ ܦܪܝܣܐ ܕܗܘܐ ܩܕܡܝܟ ܥܕ ܓܡܪ ܟܠܗ. ܘܫܒܘܩ ܕܝܵܒܫ ܚܕ ܝܘܡܐ ܘܚܕ ܠܠܝܐ. ܘܟܢ ܐܝܬܐ ܛܝܒܘܬܐ ܕܡܪܝ ܬܐܘܡܐ܆ ܐܪܡܐ ܒܛܘܦܣܐ ܕܨܠܝܒܐ ܒܗ̇ܘ ܡܐܢܐ ܕܓܒܠܬܝܗܝ ܒܗ. ܘܐܡܪ. ܡܬܪܫܡ ܘܡܬܩܕܫ ܚܢܢܐ ܗܢܐ ܒܛܝܒܘܬܐ ܗܕܐ ܕܡܪܝ ܬܐܘܡܐ ܫܠܝܚܐ ܠܚܘܠܡܢܐ ܘܠܐܣܝܘܬܐ ܕܦܓܪܐ ܘܕܢܦܫܐ ܒܫܡ ܐܒܐ ܘܒܪܐ ܘܪܘܚܐ ܕܩܘܕܫܐ܀ See B.O., iii. ii. p. 278; Payne Smith, Thes., col. 1316; Duval, Lexicon, col. 764; Mai, Scriptorum Veterum Nova Collectio, tom. v. p. 21. The Christians who went to Malabar and visited the spot where Saint Thomas was slain were in the habit of bringing back with them some of the dust or earth which they mixed with water and gave sick folk to drink; see B.O., iii. ii. p. 279.

p. 612, n. 2 Thomas means to say that as the fame of the Abbot Cyprian spread abroad in the countries round about people of all ranks flocked to his monastery, and that they either made offerings in money, or in kind, to it, or gave gratuities to the monks to conduct services and prayers on their behalf. The offerings in kind were eaten at a common table by monks and visitors, and the gifts in money enabled them to indulge in many of the comforts of life. In a short time the monks lost their keen appreciation of the pleasures of the ascetic life and grew to love the services of Saints' days and holidays, and Satan was enabled to work his will upon them. At this time the Abbot by means of a flask of bad oil, which was introduced into the monastery by a heretic, showed them that this perpetual and wearisome crowd of visitors was as injurious to their spiritual life as was bad oil if used to anoint children and sick people before baptism, and that the odour of such visits was symbolically as the smell of bad oil; he caused the flask of bad oil to be burned, and thus symbolically burned up the disease which was eating away the spiritual life of the ascetics.
p. 612, n. 3 For ܣܐܘܪ̈ܝܢܐ see supra, p. 41, note 2.
p. 612, n. 4 Literally, oil of wickedness, which typified a wicked spirit.

p. 628, n. 2 With the form ܩܲܪܕܘܿ, Arab. قرْدَى, compare ܟܘܼܣܪܵܘ, Arab. كِسْرَى. Mount Ḳardô is, according to tradition, the spot upon which the ark rested and where it was swallowed up by the earth. According to a story told in the history of Mâr Âwgîn, a certain Mâr Jacob made up his mind to go to the mountains of Ḳardô, and to pray to the Lord to show him the ark and to bring back a plank therefrom. Having taken the advice of Mâr Âwgîn he set out for Ḳardô, and upon his arrival at the skirts of the mountain an angel met him and led him to the spot where the ark had been swallowed up. The Lord then appeared to him and told him that he had arrived at the place wherein the ark was laid, and when Mâr Jacob had asked Him to give him a plank therefrom, He caused a plank of the wood of the ark to be set before him. Mâr Jacob received it with joy and returned to Mâr Âwgîn who straightway made from it a cross which he wore upon his neck, and which he afterwards buried in his monastery. See Bedjan, Acta Martyrum, tom. iii. Paris, 1892, pp. 435–437.
p. 629, n. 1 I.e., between the services.
p. 630, n. 1 ܢܸܡܪܵܐ does not make sense here and the word must be corrupt. Hoffmann suggests that we should either read ܢܵܡܲܪܬܵܐ cage, or ܢܲܚܫܝܼܪܵܐ hunting.

p. 632, n. 1 The meaning of ܢܐܪܒܐ has been pointed out by Hoffmann, in Auszüge, p. 225. With the word we may compare the Assyrian 𒉌𒊑𒁉 niribi, plur. 𒉌𒊑𒁉𒋼 niribiti; see Lotz, Die Inschriften Tiglathpileser's I, Leipzig, 1880, p. 143.

p. 632, n. 2 ܢܹܐܪܲܒ ܒܲܪܙܲܝ i.e., the glen of Barzai. Barzai, sometimes written Barzî, seems to be derived from Barz (for Burz) high, and a second word; the form ܒܪܙܘܝ, برزوى Barzôe also seems to exist. It is possible also that Barzai may be connected with the Persian Barâz wild boar, a beast which in early times was much prized by the Persians; compare Βαράζης, Οὐαράζης, Βράζης, Nöldeke, Geschichte der Perser, p. 240, note 1.
p. 632, n. 3 See supra, p. 577.
p. 632, n. 4 It is clear from this passage that ܢܐܪܒܐ is a mountain glen or valley with only one place of entrance.
p. 632, n. 5 ܡܲܠܟܘܼܢܵܐ diminutive from ܡܲܠܟܵܐ; see Payne Smith, Thes., col. 2143.
p. 633, n. 1 Extracts from this chapter are quoted in B.O., iii. 1. p. 499, coll. 1, 2.
p. 633, n. 2 All the MSS. have ܪܵ̈ܟܒܹܝܗ̇, but we must read ܟܪ̈ܵܒܹܝܗ̇ furrows; compare Job xxxi. 38; Psalm lxv. 10.

p. 651, n. 1 I.e., سِنْجَار, the famous city situated about three days' journey W. of Môṣul. For an Arabic derivation of the name of the place, and for the legends which relate that the ark of Noah rested near here, see Yâḳût, tom. iii. p. 158f.

p. 651, n. 2 The name of this town occurs in the Assyrian inscriptions under the forms D. P. Na-ṣib-na, D. P. Na-ṣi-bi-na, and D. P. Na-ṣib-i-na; see Rawlinson, Cuneiform Inscriptions, vol. ii. pl. 52, ll. 17b, 36b and 38a; vol. ii. pl. 53, l. 43; and Bezold, Catalogue, p. 224.

p. 651, n. 3 I have been told at Môṣul that the journey from Môṣul to Baghdad was once made in less than two days by a man sitting upon two inflated sheep-skins at the time of the spring floods, and with a very full river it is just possible that a man might be carried from Bâlâdh near Eski-Môṣul to Baghdad in forty-eight hours. The journey from Baghdad to Môṣul is performed by the post in from three and a half to five days; the distance by road viâ Kerkûk is about 300 miles.
p. 652, n. 1 Read ܚܢܵܝܬܵܐ Ḥĕnâithâ. See Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 216ff.

p. 656, n. 1 I.e. عِمْران بن مُحَمَّد الازدىّ. According to Ibn Ḥauḳal, the Banû ʿImrân, a branch of the tribe of el-Azd, were settled in Kurdistân. See Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 254, note 1867; and Thomas of Margâ, Bk. iv. chap. 21, supra, p. 450, note 1.

p. 656, n. 3 ܬܲܝܡܲܢ translates the Heb. תֵּימָנָה, דָּרוֹם and נֶגֶב (Payne Smith, Thes., col. 1606) Taiman is the district called Yemen, اليَمَن, by the Arabs. For the place called ʿImrânîya, see Hoffmann, Auszüge, pp. 200, 224, and compare Corpus Inscriptionum Semiticarum, Pars ii. tom. 1. Fasc. 1. p. 107.
p. 656, n. 4 ܝܲܙܕܲܝܢܵܒܵܕ, also written ܝܲܙܕܝܼܢܵܒܵܕ; see Nöldeke, Geschichte der Perser, p. 384; and Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 218, note 1739.

p. 658, n. 2 The children of Bôzî seem to have been a Kurdish or Persian family from whom the place ܒܹܝܬ ܒܘܿܙܝܼ took its name, and it would appear from Thomas of Margâ's report of ʿAmran's conversation that they had been driven out of their dwelling-place by the Banû ʿImrân; see Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 196.
p. 659, n. 1 I.e., part of April and May.

p. 659, n. 2 It is not probable that ܡܲܠܒܲܕ is the ملبّد بن حرملة الشيبانىُّ whose acts are described in Ibn al-Athîr, tom. v. pp. 369–371. We are told by Thomas of Margâ, (supra, p. 650) that Gabriel was a contemporary of Mâr Aḥâ, Mâr Mâran-ʿammeh and Mâr Îshôʿ-yahbh [of Adiabene], and we know that these Metropolitans lived in the VIIth century of our era; ملبّد بن حرملة, however, died about A.H. 137 (A.D. 754), and if he had been a contemporary of Mâr Aḥâ he must have been considerably more than 100 years old at the time of his death. For the account of Malbadh's monastery see Bk. VI. chap. 13, supra p. 639.

p. 661, n. 4 All the MSS. have ܘܡܲܩܪܸܒ, but Hoffmann thinks that we should read ܘܡܲܩܢܸܒ and lurketh in secret places, which gives much better sense. The noun ܡܩܢ̈ܒܐ occurs also in the Chronicle of Bar-Hebraeus, ed. Bruns, p. 336, l. 16 (rendered exploratores); and in Cureton, Eccles. Hist. of John of Ephesus, p. 345, l. 22 (rendered hordes by Payne Smith in his translation, Oxford, 1860, p. 371). The word is explained by ܟܡܹܐܢܵܐ ambush, and by ܣܝܥ̈ܬܐ ܕܠܣ̈ܛܝܐ ܕܡܩܲܢܒܝܢ. ܐܘܟܝܬ ܡܠܲܣܛܝܢ ܠܒܢܝܢ̈ܫܐ ܐܝܠܝܢ ܕܡܬܚܲܒܪܝܢ ܠܐܚܪ̈ܢܐ ܒܫܓܘܫ̈ܝܐ ܘܢܩܦܝܢ ܠܡܓܢܒ ܘܠܡܟܲܕܒܘ܀ bands of thieves who lie in wait, that is to say, thieves who plunder people, and who band themselves together with others in revolt, and unite together to rob and steal; see Duval, Lexicon, col. 1147. Compare مقْنَب band of brigands, and قَنَّاب voleur, Dozy, Supplément, p. 408, col. 2.

p. 666, n. 7 Genesis iii. 6.
p. 667, n. 1 ܩܘܼܦܕܵܐ. This word is explained by قدر لحم; قطعة لحم, and ܩܘܦܕܐ ܐܝܟ ܒܪ ܣܪܘ ܗ̄. ܦܣܩܐ ܕܒܣܪܐ ܕܗ̣ܘ ܢܩܣܐ; see Brit. Mus. MSS. Rich. 7203, fol. 152a, col. 2; Orient. 2441, fol. 330b, col. 1.

p. 667, n. 3 ܩܲܛܵܐ or ܩܲܛܘܼ, plur. ܩܲܛ̈ܘܵܬܵܐ; see Budge, Book of the Bee, p. ܩܡܘ, l. 19, where the word is explained by ܟܵܟܘܼܫ̈ܝܵܬܵܐ (sing. ܟܵܟܘܼܫܬܐ, Chald. כַּרְכּוּשְׁתָּא), and Wright, Kalilah and Dimnah, pp. 172, l. 22; 175, l. 15; 209, 22; 263, 11; and 367, 16 (on p. 263, l. 18, ܩܲܛܘ is feminine). Compare the Arabic قِطّ, plur. قِطاط; and Payne Smith, Thes., col. 1790. ܩܛܐ = سِنَّوُر in Brit. Mus. MS. Orient. 2441, fol. 333b, col. 1.

p. 668, n. 5 Read ܥܘܼܪܒܵܐ.

p. 669, n. 1 ܫܘܼܢܵܪܵܐ, Talm. שׁוּנְרָא (Buxtorf, ed. Fischer, p. 1232, col. 1), Arabic سِنَّوُر. In Masʿûdî (Les Prairies d’Or, ed. Barbier de Meynard and Pavet de Courteille, tom. iii. p. 13, l. 10) we have السنانير وهى القطاط.
p. 669, n. 2 I.e., أُمْ الخَيْر. See Hoffmann, Auszüge, p. 195.
p. 669, n. 3 See supra, p. 613, note 1.
p. 669, n. 4 Read ܨܠܘܿܬܵܐ.
p. 670, n. 1 Read ܟܸܢܦܵܗ̇.

p. 670, n. 2 ܒܹܝܬ ܣܵܗ̈ܕܐ. This martyrium is, in Nestorian Monasteries, a chapel lying on the left or north side of the ܩܲܢ̈ܟܹܐ, κόγχη, or square in which the altar stands; it is entered through two doors, one being to the north of the κόγχη, and the other at the east end of the left aisle or side nave. Here the ܒܝܬ ܣܘܒܥܐ, or place where Compline was sung, must have been immediately before the door of the martyrium and have formed the left part of what Badger calls the chancel, i.e., the space before the closed κόγχη, where the lecterns stood. In this case that part of the church was accessible to every body, and the appearance of this woman in it can be readily explained.
p. 671, n. 1 ܙܵܘܬܪܹ̈ܐ see supra, p. 390, note 1.
p. 671, n. 2 I.e., the Ḥâzer, خازِر.
p. 671, n. 3 ܪܵܗܹܐ, see supra, p. 661, note 3.
p. 672, n. 1 I.e., بيت عُبَيْد.

p. 672, n. 2 Compare 2 Kings ix. 30; and Jeremiah iv. 30. The √ כחל occurs in Ezekiel xxiii. 40; compare تَكَحَّل, to paint the eyes with كُحْل. The use of mestchemet or eye-paint in Egypt is as old as the time of Unas, who reigned about B.C. 3300, and a wall painting at Beni-hasân in Upper Egypt proves that as early as about B.C. 2500 mestchemet or eye paint was brought to Egypt from Syria.

p. 673, n. 1 ܒܹܝܬ ܚܣܝܼܟܹ̈ܐ, i.e., the dense thicket of the forest which hid and protected the monastery. For the word ܚܣܝܟܐ used in this sense compare ܠܒܪ ܡܢ ܥܒ̈ܐ ܘܚܣܝ̈ܟܐ ܕܩܝܣ̈ܐ outside the woods and places defended by trees; see Cureton, John of Ephesus, p. 402, l. 24; and Payne Smith, Thes., col. 1331. A Monastery of ܚܣܝܟܐ is mentioned in B.O., ii. p. 65, l. 26.
p. 673, n. 2 Read ܥܵܒܵܐ.

p. 678, n. 5 ܣܲܗܪ̈ܵܢܹܐ, Heb. שַׂהֲרֹנִים, Chald. סַהֲרָנַיָּא little moons. In Hoffmann, Opuscula, p. 96, l. 5, this word is explained by ܗܲܡܢܝܼ̈ܟܹܐ ܕܗܢܘܢ ܨܲܡܒܪܹ̈ܐ ܕܫܕܡܘܬ ܣܗܪܐ ܢܣܝܟܝܢ crescents-haped collars (or neck-chains), that is torques, which are cast in the shape of the new moon. Another explanation is (Payne Smith, Thes., col. 2539) Chains of gold like unto the moon, that is to say the half moon, in which are set precious stones; they also call ܣܗܪ̈ܢܐ that [piece of] iron which is made like the half moon, and which the Arabs put on their camels above their nostrils. The Arabs call every thing which has the form of a crescent or new moon أَهِلَّة.

p. 43, n. * The hill on which Mâr Daniel, another old Christian Church, is situated, and of which it occupies the highest and central point, is abrupt on its western and sloping on its eastern side. The river Gomel, about as large as the Khozer, falls into the Ḥâzir (near Mâr Mattai), which in turn falls into the Upper Zâb. Rich, Narrative, vol. 2, p. 80.
unnumbered The capital of Shensi, originally called Changgan. It was the metropolis of Shi-Hoangti of the Thsin dynasty.
